title: Buffalo Bills could still pull off a trade for DT Vita Vea before Week 1
summary: NFL training camps are heating up, and so is the rumor mill regarding Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea, who recently asked the team for a trade. In the last year of his current deal set to pay him $18 million for the 2026 NFL season, Vea is now unhappy with that figure after […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - DECEMBER 12: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Nose Tackle Vita Vea (50) rushes the passer during the regular season game between the Buffalo Bills and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on December 12, 2021 at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images NFL training camps are heating up, and so is the rumor mill regarding Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea, who recently asked the team for a trade. In the last year of his current deal set to pay him $18 million for the 2026 NFL season, Vea is now unhappy with that figure after the market was recently reset. Despite Vea’s request, Tampa Bay’s front office is on record as saying he will not be traded. However, not everyone is convinced that’s true. In an appearance on “The Pat McAfee Show” ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Shefter said that he wouldn’t be surprised to see the Bucs’ stance change in the coming weeks if “Vea continues to be dug in, and (he thinks) Vea will continue to be dug in.” The 31-year-old two-time Pro Bowler has been a top-tier defensive lineman for Tampa Bay since being drafted by the Buccaneers 12th overall in the 2018 NFL Draft. Though good, his individual stats don’t even accurately paint the best picture of his impact. Just how important has Vea’s presence been to the Buccaneers? As shared by McAfee and company, since 2018 (Vea’s rookie season) Tampa Bay’s defense has “allowed the fewest yards (65.5/game) and 1st downs (3.9/game) on between-the-tackle runs.” It’s obvious that the Buffalo Bills could benefit by adding someone of Vea’s ability to their defense. But there are some reasons for pause. First of all, is the financial strain — where having to account for his $18 million on this year’s salary books is a tough ask. Not impossible given the right moves, but tough. Second on that front is coming to terms with Vea on a new deal, likely also key to his playing a complete 2026 season. Yes, the financial ramifications aren’t all there is to consider. Yes, under prior head coach Sean McDermott, Buffalo had picked up a troubling recurrent trend of suspect run defense. Vea would almost single-handedly solve that issue. However, we don’t know what Buffalo’s new defensive coordinator, Jim Leonhard, has in store with his 3-4 base system. It’s possible that the Bills’ current defensive line roster is set to surprise as run defenders, or that the system overall creates the type of havoc to negate an opponent’s rushing onslaught. The Bills have a fairly crowded defensive tackle group, and adding Vea likely means giving up on someone president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane selected in any one of several recent drafts. Does that make sense in this scenario? What starter/significant contributor among Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, T.J. Sanders, DeWayne Carter, Landon Jackson, Zane Durant, Phidarian Mathis, Tommy Akingbesote, Zion Logue, or Kody Huisman would Buffalo be willing to cut loose? That’s on top of whatever in the way of draft pick compensation Tampa Bay demands. The hard truth is that at 31, Vea’s best years could be in the rearview mirror. Sure, his pretty good may still be better than someone else’s great. Importantly, though Vea is a grizzled vet, he’d enter pretty far behind the eight ball if traded to the Bills today (and that’s assuming they manage to get a new deal done). Despite all of that above, it’s almost guaranteed that Beane has already contacted the Bucs to see what’s happening with Vea, because he always checks in on talented players. At this point, it still feels like a pipe dream for Buffalo to land Vea. The money, the new contract, and the roster management, the lack of time in the system… it’s a lot to overcome. Perhaps the only question needing asked is whether or not Vita Vea is the one player to take the Bills over the top, sending quarterback Josh Allen and the franchise to its first-ever Super Bowl victory. Anything short of an emphatic “yes” should give One Bills Drive pause. "I think Vita Vea being traded is certainly a possibility.. I don't see this situation anytime soon and he wants to be traded.. It wouldn't surprise me if Tampa traded him later in the summer" ~ @AdamSchefter #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/uVmoY3KbvS — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) August 4, 2026
author: Matt Byham

title: How many targets will Buffalo Bills running backs have in 2026?
summary: Buffalo Bills new head coach Joe Brady has described himself as a “Sean Payton disciple”. One of the foundational pieces of a Sean Payton offense has been usage of running backs in the passing game. Now that we have the two main points out of the way, let’s elaborate. Alaina Getzenberg, Buffalo Bills beat reporter […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 15: Ty Johnson #26 of the Buffalo Bills makes a catch in the second quarter against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on December 15, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills new head coach Joe Brady has described himself as a “Sean Payton disciple”. One of the foundational pieces of a Sean Payton offense has been usage of running backs in the passing game. Now that we have the two main points out of the way, let’s elaborate. Alaina Getzenberg, Buffalo Bills beat reporter for ESPN, noted recently that the team’s running backs have been more involved in the passing game throughout training camp compared to camps under the previous coaching regime. Bills RBs have been noticeably more involved as pass catchers in practices, per @agetzenberg . pic.twitter.com/aWIalyfOOG — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) August 2, 2026 Apart from the obvious points-per-reception fantasy football implications for running backs James Cook, Ty Johnson, and Ray Davis (who have all seen degrees of success as pass catchers in their careers), this shift also naturally begs the follow up question: how many targets will the Bills runners get in 2026? Is there even a noteworthy and statistically significant shift coming or is this more of a “oh that was a fun idea” moment that passes and becomes the turkey burgers of the 2026 training camp: a fun story for a moment, but ultimately forgotten when the real games start getting played. Let’s establish exactly what we mean by the statement “one of the foundational pieces of a Sean Payton offense has been usage of running backs in the passing game”. What is “foundational”? Since 2013, offenses under current Denver Broncos and former New Orleans Saints head coach Sean Payton have ranked inside the top eight in running back target share every single year: 2013 – 32% running back target share (rounded to the nearest full percentage point), 1st in the NFL per FantasyPros. 2014 – 26%, 4th 2015 – 24%, 6th 2016 – 25%, 1st 2017 – 32%, 1st 2018 – 28%, 2nd 2019 – 28%, 4th 2020 – 27th, 3rd 2021 – 28%, 1st 2023 – 32%%, 1st 2024 – 21%, 6th 2025 – 20%, 8th Ironically enough, a Sean Payton offense being eighth in the league in running back target share was low enough relative to established expectations that it generated conversation around the changes that might be made to the offensive structure under new play-caller and former Buffalo Bills backup quarterback Davis Webb. Are those numbers even representative of a significant increase relative to the Buffalo Bills’ historic rates? Not last year. In 2025, the Bills running back target share was 18.4%, 12th in the NFL and less than two percentage points behind the Broncos. If the Bills go from “2025 Buffalo” to “2025 Broncos”-level of running back involvement in the pass game, none of us will even notice. But in 2024, the Bills were almost a full five percentage points behind the Broncos in this measures stat (16.6 to 21.4). 2023? The delta was over 15 points (25.8 to 32.1). 2021 represented a 12.9 point delta (between the Bills and the Saints). 2020 was a 14.6 point spread (13.5 to 28.1). I’ll spare you the remainder of the years but suffice it to say, you have to go all the way back to 2013 and 2014 to find years where the Bills were at the top of the league in running back target share, which logically trends given that two of their most dynamic offense weapons were running backs (Fred Jackson and C.J. Spiller). Here’s the thing: passing the ball to your running back doesn’t necessarily mean your passing offensive will be good. In fact, most of the time it’s essentially a net neutral play for the offense; better than taking a sack or throwing an incompletion, but nothing that moves the offense forward in a meaningful way. The Bills, however, have been an outlier in that department. They averaged an EPA per pass of 0.228, 2nd in the NFL and a good chunk ahead of the third-place Atlanta Falcons (0.216 EPA per pass attempt). For reference, the league median in this metric was 0.003 last year. Over the last four seasons, it’s actually a negative number (-0.040). The Bills threw the ball 495 times in 2025 (535 called pass plays). This represented an almost exact 50/50 run/pass ratio (50.55%/49.45%). If former head coach Sean McDermott did in fact have an impact on that and the team heads toward a league average run/pass split (56/43 last year), the Bills should have about 606 called pass plays. Assuming a 92.5% throw rate on those called plays, that would leave 561 pass attempts. If the Joe Brady offense lands the Bills at about a 28% running back target share, that means 157 running back targets may be in store for the Bills, up from 92 last year. If that number is too high for your taste, a 22% running back target share would lead to 123 running back targets. Either outcome would represent a huge and statistically significant increase and could change the way the offense flows for the team in their first year under a new head coach since 2017. Ultimately, this could all just be another example of a training camp narrative that doesn’t bear fruit come week one. But the premise is fair, the process is good, and it’s certainly something worth keeping an eye on in the early parts of the 2026 season. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!
author: Bruce Nolan

title: Buffalo Bills first fully padded training camp practice highlighted by multitude of fights
summary: Pittsford, N.Y. | The first day of full pads at Buffalo Bills training camp brought a new level of physicality that spilled over into multiple scuffles between teammates, including a pair of rookies in the middle of it all. While everyone expects an elevation of intensity when the pads can pop at camp, it’s been […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Rochester, NY, USA; Buffalo Bills outside linebacker TJ. Parker (99) leaves the field after a training camp session at St. John Fisher University. Mandatory Credit: Mark Konezny-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Pittsford, N.Y. | The first day of full pads at Buffalo Bills training camp brought a new level of physicality that spilled over into multiple scuffles between teammates, including a pair of rookies in the middle of it all. While everyone expects an elevation of intensity when the pads can pop at camp, it’s been a very long time that the Bills had four fights in the course of one practice at St. John Fisher University. Here’s more on the group fisticuffs along with other general observations from Tuesday’s practice: Alec Anderson looks to have an early led in the left-guard battle. He took the opening session in 11-on-11 with the first team. Austin Corbett did get first-team reps at that position, his turn just came later in practice. Sam Franklin Jr. was everyone on Monday — hardly taking a break. That probably led to his lighter day on Tuesday, as many combinations of Damar Hamlin, Geno Stone, and Jalon Kilgore took safety and nickel reps alongside Cole Bishop for the majority of the morning. The Josh Allen to DJ Moore connection is locked and loaded. Whether it was Moore working back to the football on comebacks, finding space on in-breakers, or getting over the top for the longest play of camp thus far — which featured a ridiculously pinpoint throw and spectacular grab — these two have demonstrated an instant rapport. Moore to come. 👀 pic.twitter.com/uQYxqTxoCN — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) August 4, 2026 Allen had a few more incompletions in the sun than he did through a rainstorm on Monday, yet there were periods in which the ball didn’t hit the turf on five or six plays in a row. Khalil Shakir probably made the most catches, and Dalton Kincaid was found down the seam on multiple occasions. Jordan Hancock mostly worked with the 2s and had an interception of a Kyle Allen throw he undercut perfectly. Dee Alford missed two diving pass-breakup attempts in one-on-ones but showcased plus tenacity with a serious run-game stick later in team drills. Deone Walker spoke after practice briefly and said he tweaked his elbow which is why he hasn’t practice the past two days. He followed by stating he’ll be returning to practice soon. Christian Benford closed quickly on a deep out-breaker from Allen to Moore that he should’ve intercepted. On that note, rookie Toriano Pride Jr. closed the separation gap on a long ball from Shane Buechele to Mecole Hardman — who, by the way, looked noticeably twitchy in one-on-ones — to break up the pass at the last second in the end zone. Ray Davis went down and looked to be a lot of pain after being tackled on one of his carries. About 15 minutes later he was cutting at full speed and ultimately finished practice with a few handoffs, one in which he fumbled. Kaleb Elarms-Orr was everywhere, including in the middle of one of the skirmishes in the second half of camp. He rotated in with the 1s all morning. Critically, he didn’t only assert his will with sticks against the run. There was textbook coverage downfield on a wheel route run by Ty Johnson in which KEO kept stride with the speedy veteran back downfield. He also sniffed out a screen play perfectly and plugged a running lane on Johnson. Elarms-Orr started one of the scuffles after he hit Kincaid on a grab in which the tight end was going to the ground. Keon Coleman was largely invisible but did make an acrobatic grab after Max Hairston undercut a short in-breaker but couldn’t knock the ball to the ground. The third-year receiver quickly reacted to the tipped pass and snagged it with one hand. Early in one-on-ones, Josh Palmer was open. A lot. Allen did miss him by a half yard on a go ball. After a few of those wins, Davison Igbinosun demonstrated his suffocating nature in press man that led to an Allen throwaway with Palmer as the target. T.J. Parker sparked another fight after a hard tackle in the flat. Unsurprisingly, Alec Anderson got right into the thick of it, and it took a while to separate everyone. I noticed Keleki Latu throw a very light punch into the mix. Tyler Bass still hasn’t kicked at training camp… four practices in. Hmmmm. The Bills will have a walkthrough closed to the public and media on Wednesday before two more SJFU practices on Thursday and Friday ahead of the Return of the Blue & Red scrimmage on Saturday evening at the new Highmark Stadium.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bijan Robinson’s record extension proves Buffalo Bills got ahead of the market with James Cook
summary: When the Buffalo Bills signed James Cook to a four-year, $46 million extension before the 2025 season, there was no shortage of criticism.  “Never pay running backs.” That familiar sentiment echoed throughout Bills Mafia, with many questioning whether Buffalo should commit $11.5 million AAV per year to a position long considered disposable. The majority didn’t […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 07: James Cook #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball against the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter at Highmark Stadium on September 07, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Buffalo Bills signed James Cook to a four-year, $46 million extension before the 2025 season, there was no shortage of criticism. “Never pay running backs.” That familiar sentiment echoed throughout Bills Mafia, with many questioning whether Buffalo should commit $11.5 million AAV per year to a position long considered disposable. The majority didn’t care that the contract came in way under what most “experts” had predicted. Fast forward one year, and that narrative looks increasingly outdated. The Atlanta Falcons just reset the running back market by signing Bijan Robinson to a three-year extension worth up to $75 million. While incentives can push the deal to $25 million AAV annually, the base value sits at $66.75 million, an average of $22.25 million per season, now ranking him first amongst NFL running backs now over Saquon Barkley’s $20.6 million AAV per year. The market has moved…and it has moved quickly. . @Bijan5Robinson is now the highest-paid RB in the league: 1. Bijan Robinson: $22.25M per year 2. Saquon Barkley: $20.6M per year 3. Christian McCaffrey: $19M per year 4. De’Von Achane: $16M per year 5. Derrick Henry: $15M per year pic.twitter.com/dgBmFwBR3f — NFL (@NFL) August 4, 2026 James Cook and Kyren Williams signed extensions one year earlier that averaged less than $12 million annually. At the time, Cook’s deal placed him comfortably among the league’s highest-paid backs. Today, he ranks just 12th in average annual value, and that number is expected to fall again once Detroit’s Jahmyr Gibbs signs what will almost certainly be another market-setting extension. The fascinating part is that Cook’s production stacks up with almost anyone in football. He has rushed for more than 1,000 yards in three consecutive seasons. In 2025, he led the NFL with 1,621 rushing yards while finishing just shy of 2,000 yards from scrimmage. He’s also scored double-digit touchdowns in back-to-back seasons, including leading the NFL in rushing touchdowns during the 2024 campaign. That’s elite production. Could anyone honestly name 12 or 13 running backs they would rather have than Cook today? Probably not. That’s what makes the criticism of his extension feel misplaced. The Bills didn’t overpay Cook. They paid him before the market exploded. General manager Brandon Beane recognized where elite running back contracts were headed and locked in one of the league’s most productive offensive players at what is now beginning to look like an absolute bargain. An $11.5 million average annual salary seemed significant in 2025. Twelve months later, it represents barely half of what Robinson will earn and sits closer to the middle tier of starting running back contracts than the top. The “don’t pay running backs” philosophy still exists across parts of the NFL, but the league has also shown a willingness to reward truly elite, versatile backs who can change games as runners and receivers. Cook belongs in that conversation. As the salary cap continues to climb and stars like Gibbs inevitably sign larger deals, Cook’s contract should only become even more team friendly. Sometimes the best contracts aren’t the ones that look cheap on the day they’re signed. They’re the ones that look like steals a year later.
author: Sara Larson

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: OLB Mike Danna
summary: The Buffalo Bills overhauled their defense this offseason, adding numerous players who have no connection to former head coach Sean McDermott. That might be a welcome sign for some of us who were growing tired of seeing familiar old faces like Shaq Lawson and Dane Jackson come back for second turns with the club. Am […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JUNE 9: Mike Danna #51 participates in drills during the Buffalo Bills mandatory minicamp at Kaleida Health Performance Center on June 9, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills overhauled their defense this offseason, adding numerous players who have no connection to former head coach Sean McDermott. That might be a welcome sign for some of us who were growing tired of seeing familiar old faces like Shaq Lawson and Dane Jackson come back for second turns with the club. Am I cherry-picking by leaving out Tre’Davious White and Jordan Poyer, whose second acts with the Bills were more successful? Yes, yes I am. The Bills even added a player from one of their great AFC rivals, poaching an edge rusher who was released in February. The last time the Bills added a player from that team, it was safety Mike Edwards, and it didn’t turn out well for either the team or the player. In today’s installment of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a veteran edge player who will have to prove himself worthy of remaining with the Bills through September. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Mike Danna Number: 51 Position: OLB Height/Weight: 6’2”, 261 pounds Age: 28 (29 on 21/1/2026) Experience/Draft: 6; selected by the Kansas City Chiefs in the fifth round (No. 177 overall) of the 2020 NFL Draft College: Central Michigan Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 5/11/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Danna’s one-year contract is worth $1,402,500 overall. Thanks to the veteran’s salary benefit, Buffalo’s cap hit if Danna makes the 53-roster counts slightly less than that, as it comes in at $1,262,500. That’s also the total guaranteed amount on the contract, so Buffalo will eat that figure as a dead-cap charge if Danna is released. 2025 Recap: Danna spent last season with the Chiefs, his sixth year with the club that drafted him. It was the second year of a three-year, $24 million extension he had signed with Kansas City in April 2024. Danna played 15 games last season, making 14 starts. He appeared on less than half of Kansas City’s defensive snaps for the first time since the 2021 season, and as a result, he had his worst year statistically. He tied career-lows with 25 tackles and three tackles for loss, and he set a new career low with just one sack. He did notch his first career interception, however, returning it for 10 yards against the Washington Commanders. The two games he missed were early in the season, Weeks 3 and 4, thanks to a quadriceps injury he suffered during Kansas City’s Week 2 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. Positional outlook: Danna is one of eight players listed at outside linebacker on the current roster. T.J. Parker, Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, Michael Hoecht, Javon Solomon, Andre Jones Jr., and Cade Denhoff are the others. 2026 Offseason: Danna is healthy and has participated in offseason work to date. 2026 Season outlook: Danna signed what essentially amounts to a fully guaranteed contract in May, so the Bills are going to eat his cap number whether he’s on the 53-man roster or not. The numbers crunch at OLB is tighter than it is at a lot of positions, though, as Buffalo will enter the season with Rousseau, Chubb, Parker, and Hoecht on the team barring some kind of injury or strange happenstance. That leaves room for one or two other edge players at most, and that may also depend on what the team decides to do at some other positions. Will new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard be a bit more multiple with his fronts? If he is, the Bills might keep an extra defensive end type who might seem like he’d be better suited for a four-man front. That would benefit Danna, who played in such a defense under Steve Spagnuolo in Kansas City. In that scenario, Buffalo might also go a little lighter on players listed at defensive tackle, especially with those “tweener” types who might not have a clear home along the line. Between DTs and OLBs, I expect the Bills to keep 10 total players at most, and eight players at least. If we already have four locks in the players listed above, then we throw in clear roster locks at defensive tackle like Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, and T.J. Sanders, we’re already at seven players. I give Javon Solomon a leg up on the other outside linebackers thanks to his ability to play special teams at a high level combined with his untapped pass-rush upside. There’s eight right there, and we haven’t kept a backup down lineman or two. In short, while Danna’s contract might say that he’s a shoo-in for the roster, his positional group and his fit in Buffalo’s defense tell me he’s more of a bubble player than anything else. Barring injury, I don’t anticipate that he’ll be on the roster once the season starts, but a strong preseason combined with some other players suffering some dings could change that outlook.

Greene played for the Panthers from 1998-99. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #39. Kevin Greene The Carolina Panthers had one of the most successful integrations into the NFL of any expansion franchise in league history. Kevin Greene was a big part of that, as he led the team in sacks in all three of his seasons in Carolina, anchoring an overachieving defense for such a new team. Greene entered the NFL with the Rams. After three modest seasons, he broke out as a pass rusher with his first of 10 double digit sack seasons. He left the Rams after eight seasons for greener pastures and joined the Steelers, where he continued to dominate the league as a pass rusher. After the 1995 season, he joined up with his former defensive coordinator Dom Capers, who was then the head coach of the Carolina Panthers. Greene led the league in sacks and was named a first team All Pro at 34 years old. Despite the success, Greene and the team could not work out a new contract, and Greene was released. He spent one year with the 49ers, after which he returned to the Panthers and picked up where he left off. He racked up 27 more sacks and more Pro Bowl nomination at age 36 and 37 before calling it a career. Greene finished his career with 160 sacks, good for third all time. 41.5 of those came in his three seasons with the Panthers, which ranks sixth in franchise history. His time with the team was short and sometimes tumultuous given the contract dispute, but there’s no denying that Greene was one of the best pass rushers to ever come through Charlotte. He unfortunately passed away from a heart attack back in 2020, but he will always be immortalized in the Hall of Fame and in Panthers history. His massive production and contributions to the unlikely rise of the Panthers land him at number 39 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Panthers vs Cardinals: Offensive Preview
summary: The preseason is upon us, and if you’re like me, it snuck up on you pretty quick. I guess that’s what happens when your team is playing in the Hall of Fame game and gets the honor of playing an early and extra preseason game that nobody wants. The opponent in this game that no […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - DECEMBER 08: Carolina Panthers offensive coordinator Brad Idzik looks on during the game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Carolina Panthers on December 08, 2024 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The preseason is upon us, and if you’re like me, it snuck up on you pretty quick. I guess that’s what happens when your team is playing in the Hall of Fame game and gets the honor of playing an early and extra preseason game that nobody wants. The opponent in this game that no one wants to play in is the Arizona Cardinals, who have the lowest win total over/under you’ll ever see at 3.5 games. All that’s good for is making people freak out if the Panthers struggle in this game. You’ll see takes along the lines of “it might be a long season for us if our backups are worse than the Cardinals backups” and things of that nature. I’m here to remind you that the result of this game means absolutely nothing knowing full well people are going to ignore this and try to read into it either way. Anyway, there are some things we can pay attention to as we scratch our itch to watch football on our TVs. Whether or not the Carolina Panthers win or not isn’t worth analyzing, but there are some more micro-level things we can watch for. Kenny Pickett’s viability as a backup quarterback This is going to be more of an eye test thing than a stats thing. Given the context of the game and the players that are going to be on the field, Pickett might not have great protection or windows to throw through. More important will be how decisive and poised he looks operating the offense and how accurate he is when he gets a chance to deliver the football. Pickett has a lot of real NFL games under his belt, so he should be fine, but a strong performance can quiet some concerns Panthers fans have about him as the team’s backup. Can the backup tackles block people? The Panthers got dealt a rough bit of news with Taylor Moton missing time with a blood clot in his lung. That means both of last season’s starters are on the shelf for the foreseeable future, which pushes free agent signing Rasheed Walker and rookie first round pick Monroe Freeling to the starting spots. After them is anyone’s guess. The Panthers are walking a dangerous line at that position group right now. They need one of their inordinately tall depth guys to be better than expected to make the depth at that position look a little less scary. The mechanics of Brad Idzik as a play caller There isn’t going to be a whole lot in terms of scheme for the preseason, but we’ll get our first look at Brad Idzik calling plays. We’re not going to worry about play design, but it will be interesting to see some of his tendencies start to show in different situations. Like what does he call in 3rd and short, or how often does he run or pass the ball on first down. And perhaps most importantly for this setting, is he quick at getting the personnel groupings and play calls down to the field. It’s not the end of the world if it’s a little choppy given this is a new gig, but it’ll be interesting to see how the debut goes. Jonathon Brooks? We’ve hardly seen Brooks since the Panthers picked him in the second round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He’s been a full go throughout training camp, and with the starters not getting the call for the Hall of Fame game, I’d expect Brooks to get at least a few looks. We’ll see how well he’s bounced back from multiple ACL tears, and the game reps will be paramount to get him back in a rhythm going into the regular season.

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. full_text: 8 Dec 1996: Linebacker Lamar Lathon of the Carolina Panthers celebrates during a game against the San Francisco 49ers at 3Com Park in San Francisco, California. The Panthers won the game, 30-24. | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #40. Lamar Lathon Lamar Lathon started his career as an off-ball linebacker out of the University of Houston. The hometown Houston Oilers selected Lathon 15th overall in the 1990 NFL Draft. After a rookie season that saw mostly backup and special teams duties, he took the starting role at strong side linebacker in his second season. That year just so happened to be his best year in Houston, logging 116 tackles, two sacks, three interceptions, and six forced fumbles. A couple years later, an injury and a coaching change cost him that starting role. During training camp in 1993, Lathon suffered a broken forearm. Newly hired defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan kept Joe Bowden as the starter even after Lathon was healthy. Lathon moved to more of an edge rusher role the following season, notching 8.5 sacks. Despite showing some pass rush promise, Houston released Lathon after the season. The Carolina Panthers had just come into existence in 1995 as Lathon hit the open market. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio liked Lathon’s fit in his 3-4 as an outside linebacker, and the team signed Lathon. The team was rewarded with one of Lathon’s best seasons to that point. He then followed up that campaign with a 1996 season full of accolades. He combined with fellow edge rusher Kevin Greene to terrorize opposing quarterbacks. Lathon alone logged 77 tackles and 13.5 sacks (still good for fifth most in franchise history for a single season), leading to him being named to the Pro Bowl and All Pro Second Team. He even got seventh place in the Defensive Player of the Year voting, proving how dominant he truly was. After Kevin Greene left for San Francisco the following year, Lathon’s production took a huge hit, as did his health. He started the year with foot and ankle injuries and suffered a major knee injury in Week 3. Though he played through the injury for most of the rest of the season, the knee would need major reconstructive surgery during the offseason. Lathon tried to return the following season, but being 31 years old and coming off a major knee injury ultimately ended his career. Lamar Lathon showed incredible ability as both an off ball linebacker and edge rusher, essentially being a Micah Parsons or Abdul Carter before they were even born. His true home, like Parsons and Carter, was at edge. The “Salt and Pepper” combination of Greene and Lathon drove the Panthers defense to be second in points allowed, leading the team to a 12-4 record and a NFC Championship Game appearance. Though his time in Carolina was cut short, his dominance for the then expansion franchise helped catapult the Panthers into the hearts of the people of Charlotte. For this contribution, Lamar Lathon earned the No. 40 spot on our countdown.

title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Gervon Dexter
summary: In the last 16 months, we have seen some serious turnover on the defensive side of the football. Several of Matt Eberflus’ guys are already out the door, and Dennis Allen has spent the last two offseasons building a defense in his vision. The Bears have added a couple new names to the defensive line […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 10: Gervon Dexter Sr. #99 of the Chicago Bears runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the last 16 months, we have seen some serious turnover on the defensive side of the football. Several of Matt Eberflus’ guys are already out the door, and Dennis Allen has spent the last two offseasons building a defense in his vision. The Bears have added a couple new names to the defensive line since Allen took over, but there’s still a handful that remain from Eberflus as well. Those names are Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, and Gervon Dexter. Dexter is the name we are going to focus on in this article (although you’ll be reading about Sweat and Booker in later articles in the series), and I think Dexter is an interesting player to discuss because he’s another player where I think his future is up in the air. Gervon Dexter: Stash After his rookie season, Dexter certainly was showing promise, and he built upon that in season two. Dexter still had some success in season three, but some of the weaknesses in his game hadn’t improved as many had hoped. Dexter now enters year four, and we most likely know what type of player Dexter has become. Yes, there’s a chance that Dexter can still break out from where he was and elevate his game and become a player closer to a game-wrecker that teams love to have penetrating from the interior defensive line, but what we are most likely looking at is a defensive tackle who is a good pass rusher and a below-average run defender, making him an above-average defensive tackle. Having someone of Dexter’s skills starting on your defensive line is fine for a team that is looking to play solid football around .500, but is Dexter capable of being a starting defensive tackle for a team contending for a Super Bowl? My answer to that is no. I do think, however, that if Dexter was a team’s third defensive tackle and part of a rotation, that would be a strong enough defensive line to contend for a Super Bowl, as long as the players in front of him were stronger, more skilled players. I don’t think Dexter is a perfect fit for Dennis Allen’s defense, but he is a good fit, especially being that he can get interior pressure from time to time, something Allen does like out of his tackles. Dexter is going to become a free agent in 2027, and I would say that the sensible move would be to let Dexter walk after this year and let someone else pay him the contract dollars he’s most likely seeking. However, the Bears are in a unique spot. Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo are almost certainly not going to be here next year. Montez Sweat is also going to be a free agent after the 2027 season as well. The Bears don’t have a lot of certainty in the long term on the defensive line, so it might make it more likely, because of that, that Dexter sees a second contract. It’s quite possible that if the Bears had more stability in the defensive line room, they may not consider keeping Dexter as much. But let’s look at this: going into 2027, if the Bears want to keep 10 DL, they’ll have Sweat and Austin Booker with Daniel Hardy; they’ll have Neville Gallimore, Shemar Turner, and Jordan van den Berg. That means they need to find 4 more DL for the 2027 season, and that’s if every one of the above names returns. The Bears need to find a starting-caliber edge (unless Booker breaks out) and two starting-caliber DTs, and they will need to use one or two day one or day two draft picks on defensive linemen as well. With that kind of turnover, if Dexter is willing to take a shorter contract, even if he doesn’t improve from the last couple of seasons, he may be worth bringing back to stabilize the DL a little bit. However they want to handle Dexter, it’s going to come down to how he plays this year. If Dexter plays as he has or regresses a little, he’s going to be firmly on the bubble as to whether or not the Bears want to bring him back for 2027. But if he improves, it might be worth trying to find some common ground if the contract is affordable and bringing Dexter back. But under no circumstances is this a player that should be offered a contract extension before the 2026 season. The Bears should let Dexter play out this season and see where the chips fall.

title: Bears sign All-Pro RT Darnell Wright to 4-year, $116M extension
summary: The Bears have signed right tackle Darnell Wright to a four-year extension worth $116 million with $93 million guaranteed, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported on Tuesday. With an annual average of $29 million, he will now become the highest-paid right tackle in NFL history. Wright, 24, has seen steady improvement each year in the NFL […]
full_text: The Bears have signed right tackle Darnell Wright to a four-year extension worth $116 million with $93 million guaranteed, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported on Tuesday. With an annual average of $29 million, he will now become the highest-paid right tackle in NFL history. Wright, 24, has seen steady improvement each year in the NFL since the Bears used the No. 10 overall pick on him in the 2023 NFL Draft. Most notably, he ended 2025 with an 85.0 PFN OL Impact Score , ranking him No. 7 among all offensive tackles and No. 4 among right tackles. He earned second-team All-Pro recognition for his performance last year, which marked his third season in the league. Coming off a strong season which saw the Bears’ offensive line jump from the No. 24 ranking in PFN Team OL Impact Scoring in 2024 all the way to No. 3 in 2025, general manager Ryan Poles saw firsthand just how important having a strong offensive line was to their offense improving as a whole last season. Wright was their second-best offensive lineman behind Protector of the Year left guard Joe Thuney, but given each player’s age, the former is certainly the more valuable long-term asset for the organization. The Bears picked up the fifth-year option on Wright’s contract in April, and they’ve now locked him down beyond the end of his rookie deal. As a result of the deal, Chicago has Wright under contract through the end of the 2031 season.

title: Chicago Bears roster 2026: Kyle Monangai, Devin Bush, and Malik Muhammad are underrated
summary: If you want to feel better about the fact that the Chicago Bears are the only NFL team without a 4,000-yard passer in its history, consider that 12 other teams hadn’t seen it happen for them until the new millennium turned around. And some of the league’s best current teams — the Houston Texans, Philadelphia […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears completes a catch and carries the ball during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you want to feel better about the fact that the Chicago Bears are the only NFL team without a 4,000-yard passer in its history, consider that 12 other teams hadn’t seen it happen for them until the new millennium turned around. And some of the league’s best current teams — the Houston Texans, Philadelphia Eagles, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Buffalo Bills, and Seattle Seahawks — didn’t see it for their franchises until the last few years . The larger point, of course, is that Caleb Williams, who threw for 3,942 yards in the 2025 regular season — and 4,560 if you include the postseason — is on the verge of getting the Bears off the schneid. Williams is also the man to finally break the Bears’ epic quarterback curse , which started after Sid Luckman and World War II. How far can the 2026 Bears go with a quarterback of Williams’ caliber? This will be Williams’ second season with Ben Johnson as his head coach and offensive mastermind, and everybody’s pretty psyched about that. “He’s had two offseasons and one training camp so far, and a full season to where he’s had a lot of the similar concepts repeat for him,” Johnson said of Williams a few days ago . “Now, we’re at the point where he’s not thinking about the play call, he’s not thinking about the cadence, the motion and all the rigmarole before the snap. “Things are starting to slow down. So, what we need to see here in camp is that anticipation. Take it up a notch. I think with that, the coverage recognition gets taken up another notch. There are other ways we’re going to continue to challenge and push him, more of which are going to happen post-snap. Last year we talked about that pre-snap operation quite a bit. [We] feel a lot better about that this time of year than we did [last summer], so now we’re just moving onto the next stage.” Williams agrees. “Plays get more detailed,” the quarterback said of his current work with Johnson. “He’s adding more on my plate of figuring out the coverage before, and having an idea of where I can go with the ball faster and sooner. I haven’t thrown a lot of picks in my career, because I can see the coverage and feel the coverage. It’s a little more detailed from play to play, and specifics within the play, towards the coverage that we are attacking. Then, adding more plays in there so that we can kill, alert and check to these different man checks, Cover-2 checks, single-high or whatever the case may be. “We are excited about that. I’m excited. The challenge that he’s giving me to be able to take the next step and progress is what I’m most excited about. It’s going to be hard. It’s going to be tough like it is every year. That’s what you embrace, that’s what you enjoy. Because when it shows up on game days and Sundays or whatever day we play on, it’s really rewarding.” Last season, the 11-6 Bears got as far as the Divisional Round of the playoffs for the first time since 2010, and there’s no reason to assume that they can’t do it again — or go even further in the tournament. If that’s the case, of course, it can’t just be about Johnson and Williams. Everyone on the roster must be at their best, including the lesser-known names. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the Bears’ new season — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: RB Kyle Monangai There are times when you watch a draft prospect’s tape, and you then see how the NFL values him, and you tend to wonder what the hell the NFL is thinking. When I saw that the Bears were able to lift Rutgers running back Kyle Monangai with the 235th overall pick in the seventh round of the 2025 draft, I must admit that I thought a lot of pro personnel people had lost their damned minds. Because what I saw from the 5′ 8¼, 211-pound Monangai made it pretty clear in my mind: Forget about the height. Forget about the 4.6-second 40-yard dash at the combine . This guy is a football player , and I don’t care what anybody says in any other direction. Rutgers RB Kyle Monangai is a one-cut-and-go Pocket Hercules with serious lateral juice, hatred in his heart for anybody trying to tackle him, and a SERIOUS stiff-arm. Probably a third-day guy who could turn himself into more. pic.twitter.com/qG9Mpvuuue — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) April 24, 2025 Monangai proved the point in a rookie season that had him gain 846 yards and score five rushing touchdowns on 190 carries, adding 23 catches on 34 targets for 222 yards. His first start came in Week 9 against the Cincinnati Bengals when D’Andre Swift was out with a groin injury. All Monangai did in that game was to blow up Cincy’s defense to the tune of 176 yards on 26 carries. “When you come into the building like he does, and have his approach every single day, and it doesn’t matter whether it’s in the meetings or in walkthroughs or practices, you know what you’re going to get,” Johnson said of Monangai last November . “He is a very consistent player. He ran hard; he lowered his pads. I thought that he played some inspiring football for anybody that was watching it, whether you were on the field or on the sidelines. No one was surprised.” Swift was more succinct, but equally complimentary. “He doesn’t carry himself like a rookie, and he [darn] sure doesn’t play like one.” Kyle Monangai was ignored by the NFL until the seventh round of the 2025 draft. Monangai responded by taking it out on the rest of the league throughout his rookie season. @ChicagoBears pic.twitter.com/cyFMStXX5h — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 2, 2026 Monangai’s high-contact playing style does come with some danger — he’s been dealing with a soft tissue injury in training camp — but when he’s healthy, he will undoubtedly be proving the doubters wrong yet again. Underrated free agent: LB Devin Bush Just because you don’t succeed in the NFL right away doesn’t mean that you can’t do so over time. Some players have everything it takes to create legitimate careers, but the growth takes a while. Or, they’re in the wrong systems. Or, trends haven’t quite caught up to what they can do. Or, on and off-field issues get to them for a while. Take the example of linebacker Devin Bush. The Pittsburgh Steelers selected the 5’11, 234-pound Bush with the 10th overall pick in the 2019 draft out of Michigan, and it never quite worked out. Bush had his moments in Pittsburgh’s defense, but not nearly enough for such a high pick — especially a high pick that the team had to trade first- and second-round picks in 2019, and a third-round pick in 2020, just to take in the first place. The Steelers refused to exercise Bush’s fifth-year option, so he was out after the 2022 season. Bush signed with the Seattle Seahawks for a nondescript 2023 season, and then, the turnaround started to happen when Bush signed a one-year, $1.5 million contract with the Cleveland Browns in 2024 and had his best season to date under Jim Schwartz. That led to a one-year, $3.25 million contract with the Browns in 2025, whereupon Bush had his best season to date under Schwartz once again. Last year, Bush totaled 50 solo tackles, 24 stops, seven tackles for loss, a forced fumble, three interceptions, and five pass breakups. He had three more picks than he allowed, and with his two pick-sixes and 164 return yards, Bush was as dangerous an interceptor as you could get in the NFL. Very quietly, Devin Bush was a DUDE for the @Browns last season. Led the NFL in pick-sixes (two) and interception return yards (164). Now, the @ChicagoBears can benefit from his skill set. pic.twitter.com/e74yHS3z04 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 3, 2026 “I’m going into Year 8,” Bush said after the…

title: Injuries put more pressure on Dennis Allen, Bears defense to simply survive in 2026
summary: It can happen to anyone, any team, at any time. Right now, unfortunately, the Chicago Bears are going through it. Safety Coby Bryant, arguably the centerpiece of this year’s free-agent haul, will reportedly miss 8-10 weeks after suffering a knee injury in yesterday’s practice—better than the alternative, as it won’t require surgery, but not ideal […]
full_text: It can happen to anyone, any team, at any time. Right now, unfortunately, the Chicago Bears are going through it. Safety Coby Bryant, arguably the centerpiece of this year’s free-agent haul, will reportedly miss 8-10 weeks after suffering a knee injury in yesterday’s practice—better than the alternative, as it won’t require surgery, but not ideal for the Bears. He’ll now join fellow safety Elijah Hicks (shin) and cornerback Kyler Gordon (calf) on the PUP list, putting additional strain on the defensive back room. When you take into account that edge Dayo Odeyingbo is coming off of an Achilles injury and second-year defensive lineman Shemar Turner (knee) is also on the PUP list from the injury he suffered last year, this defense has a lot of question marks heading into a critical 2026 season. That’s especially concerning given that Chicago largely kept their defensive core the same—aside from adding quality starters like Bryant and linebacker Devin Bush and rookies like first-round pick Dillion Thieneman—rather than making a high-upside splash move this offseason. And Ryan Poles likely doesn’t have a major move up his sleeve to change the calculus, with adding veteran secondary depth probably his only consideration right now. In the end, all of that points toward the same thing: all the pressure is on Dennis Allen to make this defensive roster work. Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen on leading a group dealing with injuries: “I want to see 11 fricken dudes on the field competing their ass off.” pic.twitter.com/vrwlzOrmup — Chris Emma (@CEmma670) August 4, 2026 Despite ranking poorly in most advanced metrics and missing true blue-chip talent last season, the Bears’ defense broke even, more or less, by generating a league-leading 33 takeaways (including 23 interceptions) in 2025. Moreover, players like Nahshon Wright (now with the New York Jets) stepped up when called upon and turned in strong seasons, suggesting the Bears can likewise get big plays out of backups and young players in 2026 as well. Is it wise to count on the whole of the Bears’ defense being greater than the sum of its parts again? Probably not. Turnovers are famously finicky, as many rely on good luck. Just take the drop-off between the Bears’ record-setting 2018 season (36 takeaways) and their underwhelming 2019 campaign (19 takeaways) as evidence. History would suggest Chicago is in for a similar regression to the mean this season when it’s all said and done. For those interested, Allen’s teams (as either a DC or head coach) have had eight seasons ranked in the bottom half of the league in takeaways against seven in the top half of the NFL. Do they have the talent to withstand that variance? I’m not sure they do. But they seem ready to roll the dice. Allen’s defenses, aside from a few peak years in New Orleans from 2022-2024, have rarely been among the league’s best in terms of points per game and yards allowed . Some units, like last year’s, were basically turnstiles. But the trick is that they’re usually good enough to survive even without top talent, adhering to the old “bend, don’t break” philosophy and using mind games and simulated pressure as much as possible to disrupt an offense’s thought process. They don’t usually dominate; they keep the bleeding to a minimum and try to get key stops/takeaways in big moments. That’s a tough way to live, but last year was proof it can be done. And with Ben Johnson seemingly trying to score 40 points a game with his stacked offensive unit, Allen and the Bears defense just have to allow no more than 39 on their end. As the San Francisco 49ers game last year demonstrates, that approach can get you burned. But, as seen in the playoffs against the Packers and Rams, Allen’s squad proved it could step up when the chips are down. Without the assurance of Bryant, Gordon, and several other players being available or as effective as they could be, that’s what Allen and this defense must do: enough.

(Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images With safety Coby Bryant’s injury sidelining him for eight to ten weeks, and with safety Elijah Hicks still on the PUP list, the Chicago Bears signed safety Marlen Sewell today. Sewell (6′, 199), a 2026 undrafted free agent from Vanderbilt, was originally signed by the Kansas City Chiefs after a May tryout, but was released in June. During his five years in college with the Commodores, he had 102 tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, .5 sack, 3 passes defended, a forced fumble, and a fumble recovery. He has a lot of special teams experience while a reserve early in his collegiate career, but last year he emerged as a leader for their defense. At his Pro Day, he ran a 4.48 forty, had a 36′ vertical, and a 10’6″ broad jump. He’s no relation to the Sewell brothers currently on the Bears, and he goes by Marlo. He’ll compete with Anthony Johnson Jr., Gervarrius Owens, and Skyler Thomas to win a backup safety spot or a place on the practice squad. To make room for Sewell on the roster, the Bears placed defensive end Jonathan Garvin on injured reserve.

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: What offseason narrative is most tired?
summary: It’s been a long offseason, but real football is back. In less than two weeks time the Bears will be taking the field against the Cleveland Browns to open the preseason. Already a handful of days into training camp and some players are already trying to reset narratives that have occurred throughout the summer break. […]
full_text: It’s been a long offseason, but real football is back. In less than two weeks time the Bears will be taking the field against the Cleveland Browns to open the preseason. Already a handful of days into training camp and some players are already trying to reset narratives that have occurred throughout the summer break. A few that I have seen pop up consistently since season’s end: Luther Burden will be the Bears #1 WR in 2026 and beyond Subtext, Rome Odunze will not be Dayo Odeyingbo and Grady Jarrett were flops Subtext, these two players will be minimal contributors in 2026 and will get cut next offseason Kyler Gordon’s soft tissue injuries are a major problem Subtext, the Bears are assessing replacements for him after the 2026 season at NB The Bears have problems at LT and C Subtext, Braxton Jones, Jedrick Wills, Garrett Bradbury, and Logan Jones will be worse than their 2025 starting counterparts The Bears will regress in 2026 Subtext, their defense, turnover differential, and 4th quarter comebacks are unsustainable and will lead to a regression to the mean There might be others, but these were some that I consistently gleaned from the media, other blogs, and even here at WCG. So which of these are the most tired? Which do we need to set straight and pull out of the offseason echo chamber? This is the basis of this week’s question: Which offseason Bears narrative is most tired? For me, it’s the conversation around Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo. I get it — these two failed to live up to their lofty contracts in 2025. A reminder of each contract below: Grady Jarrett signed a 3 year, $42.75 million deal including cap hits of $18.9 and $16.8 million in 2026 and 2027 (but only $4 million in dead money in 2027) His annual average salary of $14.5 million ranks 24th in the NFL amongst IDL. Dayo Odeyingbo signed a 3 year, $48 million deal including cap hits of $20.5 and $19.5 million in 2026 and 2027 (but only $4.5 million in dead money in 2027) His average annual salary of $16 million ranks 29th in the NFL among Edge rushers. Neither of these are small cap hits, and one might argue that they kept the Bears from pursuing other defensive upgrades this offseason. I get it. But I think we are confusing sunken cost with a player that is no longer on the team. In case the offseason narrative has convinced you otherwise, Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo are still members of the 2026 Chicago Bears — and I think they are both severely underrated for what they can do for the 2026 defense. Let’s start with the veteran, Grady Jarrett. Jarrett came in with a pedigree and something to prove after his long tenure with the Atlanta Falcons came to a close following a cut in March of 2025. Ryan Poles viewed him as the interior rusher and veteran presence that the Bears DL desperately needed. Unfortunately, in 14 games last season, Jarrett only tallied 1.5 sacks, 39 tackles, 1 TFL, 8 QB hits, and 3 PDs. Those numbers aren’t enough to justify his cost. But that’s not to say that Jarrett doesn’t have anything left in the tank. Jarrett himself has owned up to his 2025 season by saying: No, so we hear it, man. But it also comes with the job, you know, it comes with the job. And at the end of the day, we gotta really take it personal and get back to work. Even if sometimes your best ain’t good enough. So you gotta find out ‘Where can I be better at? Jarrett isn’t a stranger to down years, either. He also isn’t a stranger to bounce backs. In 2021, his age 28 season, Jarrett had a down year following two Pro Bowl seasons, where he only notched 1 sack, and 3 TFLs in 17 games. The next season, Jarrett responded with 6 sacks and 12 TFLs — a massive improvement that shows his ability to right the course. Additionally, he has noted being in better shape this offseason, after working through a knee injury that sidelined him for portions of 2025. So it should not be outlandish to expect a better Grady Jarrett in 2026, something that I have seen consistently discounted this offseason. As for Dayo Odeyingbo. It’s safe to say that Dayo has become the newest punching bag for Bears fans. Reports of a “Motivated Dayo” has become a sarcastic refrain for fans that expect him to be a non contributor in 2026. While I understand why people are questioning his impact, I think it is far too premature to write him off at this stage in his career. Dayo was but 26 years old with 3.5 seasons under his belt when he joined the Bears last offseason. Odeyingbo has draft pedigree and prototypical size for the position as a 2nd round pick that measures at 6’-5” and 282 lbs. While he still hasn’t put together a spectacular season in his career, he mustered 11 sacks, 16 TFLs, and 34 QB hits in his age 24 and 25 seasons combined — numbers that suggest a jump still may be warranted. Still, in his 8 starts in 2026, Odeyinbo struggled to string together strong performances and eventually ended with 1 sack and 2 TFLs — disappointing numbers that have led many to write him off. I think that’s a mistake. Odeyingbo had seen steady improvement under the tutelage of Gus Bradley, and found himself under a new defensive scheme for the first time in his career in 2025. When revisiting tape, I saw a player that frequently looked indecisive — which often led to him playing slower. I see an extra year under Allen, an offseason of good health, and more “motivation” as being key to a turnaround for Dayo. Will he ever be a 10 sack player? Unlikely. But to write him off would be a mistake. I think there is a very good chance of him tallying 6+ sacks and being a powerful counterpunch to Austin Booker’s speed/length. In total — I suppose my primary gripe is that we simply cannot write off two players after one season on a team and defense that feature a lot of new. I’ll eat my words if we continue to see the same issues 4-5 games into 2026. But until then, let’s give these two a chance to change the narrative. Now it’s your turn! Which offseason Bears narrative is most tired? Sound off in the comments!

full_text: DALLAS, TX - November 01: SMU Mustangs safety Isaiah Nwokobia (#23) looks up field during the college football game between the SMU Mustangs and the Miami Hurricanes on November 1, 2025, at Gerald J. Ford Stadium in Dallas, TX. (Photo by Matthew Visinsky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have waived safety Isaiah Nwokobia, the team announced on Tuesday. It’s the first player the team has cut since the start of training camp. An undrafted free agent out of SMU, Nwokobia was quickly scooped up by the Bengals following the 2026 NFL Draft. The hope was he could challenge guys like Daijahn Anthony and PJ Jules for one of the final safety spots, but that obviously didn’t pan out. The 6-foot, 206-pound Nwokobia was listed as a safety but has the potential to play nickel cornerback. Over the last two seasons while playing in the ACC, he racked up 180 tackles, 10 pass deflections, 5.5 tackles for loss, and five interceptions. Because this move comes so early in camp, it could signal that the team has someone else they’d like to compete for a spot on the final 53-man roster, though no subsequent move has been made.

Joe Burrow on what the Bengals are bringing to training camp 👀 🎤: @EvanWashburn pic.twitter.com/b8iL39BG2L — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) August 3, 2026 Evan Washburn does a terrific job covering the NFL for CBS. He’s always been effusive in his praise for Joe Burrow and the Bengals’ gameday experience. Everything Joe Burrow says here is encouraging. Hearing Burrow talk about the sense of urgency from the players is motivating going into the season, and it’s what you want to hear going into a crucial season; Burrow is speaking with confidence. It’s confidence we saw in 2021 and 2022, and we all know what happened in those seasons. Under center, play action. Off Ja’Marr’s fingertips on the deep ball. pic.twitter.com/TX28AmlePH — Caleb Noe (@CalebNoeTV) August 4, 2026 First of all, this is so close to being perfectly executed. On the play, notice T.J. Slaton bursting through the offensive line to pressure Joe Burrow. It looks like, from the clip, that Dylan Fairchild was trying to hold him back, practically wrapping his arm around him. Perhaps Burrow had to rush the throw and put just slightly too much on it to Chase, but you can see the development of the play as promising as training camp continues to unfold. But considering how bad the defense has been the last three years, seeing them make plays throughout this training camp has been awesome. Bryan Cook’s impact and leadership are both already being felt. DJ Turner has been outstanding in training camp so far. Watch him step in the pocket to avoid the rush, and then create separation to throw the ball. Not only that, but the throw was a perfect spiral, line-drive dart to Tee Higgins. Good pressure from Myles Murphy, with Drew Sample blocking on the right side of the line. Remember prior to 2021 when we heard Burrow got stronger with better arm strength while rehabbing his left knee? There’s a reason he did that. This was an absolute rocket throw. Bryan Cook pick 6 vs Burrow pic.twitter.com/gwIWkWSX0l — Jay Morrison (@ByJayMorrison) August 4, 2026 Again, playmakers making plays. This Bengals’ defense has playmakers for the first time in multiple years. Good tracking from andrei iosivas pic.twitter.com/0NnzmWvklS — John Sheeran (@John__Sheeran) August 4, 2026 This is an encouraging sign from Andrei Iosivas. Working against DJ Ivey, Iosivas was able to locate the ball and keep his body in bounds on a tough catch. Iosivas is having a really good training camp, and hopefully this time he can translate that into the regular season. The Colbie Young training camp hype train is gaining steam. Kid keeps making plays. #Bengals @FOX19 — Jeremy Rauch (@FOX19Jeremy) August 4, 2026 If anything, Young is providing competition for Andrei Iosivas at WR3. title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: Which position battles matter the most?
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are back to work, the pads are on, and training camp is in full swing. Before we know it, they’ll be taking the field for their first preseason game, and the process of trimming the roster from 90 players down to 53 will begin in earnest. Some positions are already set in […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor looks on during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals are back to work, the pads are on, and training camp is in full swing. Before we know it, they’ll be taking the field for their first preseason game, and the process of trimming the roster from 90 players down to 53 will begin in earnest. Some positions are already set in stone. Quarterback is one of them. Joe Burrow and Joe Flacco are QB1 and QB2, and only an act of the football gods will change that. There are also position battles we can debate until we’re blue in the face, but they probably won’t have much impact on Sundays. WR6, for example, is unlikely to see meaningful snaps outside of special teams. But which camp battles will actually affect the Bengals once the regular season begins? Here are a few that stand out—in no particular order. CB4 Dax Hill and DJ Turner II appear to be the Bengals’ starting outside corners, while Jalen Davis is currently penciled in as the starting nickel. But who becomes the first corner off the bench when Al Golden dials up extra defensive backs? Josh Newton and DJ Ivey both return with experience in the system, while free-agent addition Ja’Sir Taylor brings versatility. They’re joined by third-round rookie Tacario Davis, along with Jalen Kimber, Bralyn Lux and Ceyair Wright. The Bengals didn’t make a major investment at cornerback this offseason, signaling confidence in Hill and Turner. Still, depth at the position always matters. Injuries happen, and today’s NFL demands that defenses play with five or six defensive backs for large portions of the game. Whoever earns the CB4 role could end up playing far more snaps than fans expect. Backup Guard Cody Ford appears locked in as the Bengals’ top swing lineman. I originally considered listing backup tackle as the more important battle, but it’s hard to envision anyone on the roster taking that role away from Ford. That shifts the focus inside. The Bengals believe they have their center of the future in Connor Lew, and with Ford likely handling tackle duties when needed, players like Jalen Rivers and Liam Brown could find themselves battling to become the primary backup at guard. It’s not the flashiest competition, but interior offensive line depth has a way of becoming important at the worst possible time. Hopefully, whoever wins the job isn’t forced into extended action. Backup Tight End Mike Gesicki sits atop the depth chart, but the competition behind him could end up being just as important. The Bengals have frequently lined up in 13 personnel (one running back, one wide receiver and three tight ends) during training camp with Joe Burrow under center. If that’s going to become a regular part of the offense, the depth chart behind Gesicki suddenly matters a lot more. Drew Sample and Tanner Hudson have both carved out productive roles over the past few seasons. Erick All is back from injury, and rookie Jack Endries is looking to make an impression after being selected in the 2026 NFL Draft. They can’t keep everyone, and they won’t play everyone. It’ll be fascinating to see which three tight ends the coaching staff trusts most when those heavier personnel packages become part of the game plan. Safety No. 4 The Bengals signed Kyle Dugger for a reason. He may not leap over Jordan Battle as the starter next to Cook at safety, but he’ll be on the field, and he’ll push Battle. This isn’t about Dugger and Battle, though. This is about who takes up the fourth, and possibly final, safety spot on the roster. It’ll come down between PJ Jules and Daijahn Anthony. The winner of this battle keeps their spot on the 53-man roster and also becomes a special-teams contributor. There are plenty of other camp battles worth following, but these feel like the ones most likely to influence what we see once the games start counting. Which position battle do you think will have the biggest impact on the Bengals this season? Sound off. title: Cincinnati Bengals roster 2026: Dax Hill, Jonathan Allen, Connor Lew are Hidden Gems
summary: It was not too long ago that the Cincinnati Bengals were right up top in the AFC pecking order. In 2021 and 2022, they got as close as you can get to winning a Super Bowl without actually winning it. There was the 23-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams in Super Bowl LVI at […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals cornerback Dax Hill (23) catches a pass during the Cincinnati Bengals Training Camp 2026 at Kettering Practice Field in Cincinnati on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It was not too long ago that the Cincinnati Bengals were right up top in the AFC pecking order. In 2021 and 2022, they got as close as you can get to winning a Super Bowl without actually winning it. There was the 23-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams in Super Bowl LVI at the end of the 2021 season and the 23-20 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in the 2022 AFC Championship game. Of course, after those two 23-20 games in a span of less than a year, things started to come apart. Joe Burrow’s health became more of a concern in 2023 and 2025, and when Burrow played at a thermonuclear level in 2024, he did so with a Lou Anarumo defense that ranked 25th in points allowed and 27th in DVOA . Last season, Burrow played in just eight games, and in the first half of the season, Al Golden’s defense was one of the worst… like, ever. According to FTN’s data, Cincinnati’s defensive DVOA of 30.1% in Weeks 1-9 was the worst in the history of the metric, which currently goes back to 1977. Running back Chase Brown and receiver Ja’Marr Chase were yowling about said defense in October , and for good reason. Then, it all turned around. From Week 10 through the end of the season, the Bengals improved their Defensive DVOA to -2.2% (Defensive DVOA is better when it’s negative), up from 32nd to 13th. And though the sins of the season’s first half would not be erased by that improvement — the 2025 Bengals finished 30th in Defensive DVOA behind only the Dallas Cowboys and the New York Jets — there was enough on the bone for management to spend in both draft capital and actual dollars to improve things on that side of the ball. Hence, the trade for ex-New York Giants game-wrecker Dexter Lawrence, as well as the signings of former Seattle Seahawks edge-rusher Boye Mafe, veteran defensive lineman Jonathan Allen, former Kansas City Chiefs safety Bryan Cook, and veteran defensive back Kyle Dugger. Adding Texas A&M edge-rusher Cashius Howell and Washington cornerback Tacario Davis in the second and third rounds of the 2026 draft should provide even more enforcement potential. So, here’s what the plan for the Bengals this season seems to be: Bank on a healthy Joe Burrow and all of his weapons, and give the defense enough juice to be league average or better after that historical awfulness. It worked not too long ago, and it could work again. For that to happen, of course, the Bengals will need the best possible performance from everybody on the roster. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 team — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Here are the Hidden Gems for your 2026 Cincinnati Bengals. Underrated veteran: DB Dax Hill A primary reason for the aforementioned defensive improvement in the second half of the 2025 season was the decision to move Dax Hill outside from the slot more often. Since the Bengals took the Michigan alum with the 31st overall pick in the 2022 draft, Hill has alternated between the two spots, with varying degrees of distinction. 2024 was a complicated season for Hill: he missed all but the first five games with a knee injury, but he came back strong, especially when the team needed someone to bookend the estimable DJ Turner II. From Weeks 1-11 last season, Hill took just 20% of his 666 ( Iron Maiden riff here ) snaps outside; the rest of the time, he was either a slot defender or a box guy. But starting in Week 12 against the New England Patriots, Hill’s outside reps increased exponentially. 76% of his 366 reps in that time period came on the outside, and when targeted there, Hill allowed 12 catches on 19 targets for 6.7 yards per catch, no touchdowns, no interceptions, four pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 76.2. Most importantly. Hill’s outside deployment told opponents that they couldn’t just avoid Turner and get away with THAT all day long. If you blinked or looked away for a second, you probably missed the @Bengals ' massive uptick in defensive efficiency in the second half of the 2025 season. Moving Dax Hill from slot to outside had a lot to do with it. pic.twitter.com/kMtGnSQuiV — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 30, 2026 After the season, the Bengals named Hill their winner of the NFL’s Ed Block Courage Award , which credits players who show “professionalism, great strength and dedication” in the face of adversity. “I want to thank the entire organization and my teammates for thinking highly of me in coming back from my injury,” Hill said. “Representing the team well, coming back, and making an impact was my big focus. I thank everybody for being in my corner, and I’m happy being back with the guys.” “There is not a more deserving player than Dax Hill for the Ed Block Courage Award,” said Bengals Director of Sports Medicine/Head Athletic Trainer Matt Summers. “Dax is a very consistent ‘everyday’ guy. His unwavering work ethic and trust in the rehab plan allowed him to return to the field in 2025 without hesitation. Dax is also very gracious with the time he commits to community service, and his humility further reflects the values he poses for his teammates to vote him as this year’s recipient.” If Hill’s on-field community service continues to be the ability to shut receivers down as that outside guy, that’s one more box for the team to check off as they fight for relevance again. Underrated free agent: IDL Jonathan Allen Dexter Lawrence was obviously the big move the Bengals made this offseason, but it wasn’t the only contract signed to bolster the defensive line. Getting nine-year veteran Jonathan Allen on a two-year, $25 million contract with $7.5 million guaranteed should provide some sneaky dividends. Last season in Brian Flores’ crazy-quilt defense for the Minnesota Vikings, Allen had four sacks, 34 pressures, 44 solo tackles, 34 stops, and seven tackles for loss. That was Allen’s first season in Minnesota after eight with the Washington (YOUR NAME HERE) franchise, which selected him with the 17th overall pick in the 2017 draft out of Alabama. At his peak, Allen lived up to all that draft capital spent, and while he may not be the pressure machine he was in 2021 and 2022, he’s not that far off. At 6’3” and 300 pounds, he brings all the movement skills and a surprising amount of power to displace double teams for his size. As long as Sexy Dexy is on the field, Allen won’t see as many doubles as he did in 2025 — 190— and 17 of his 34 pressures came when he had more than one guy on him. So, there could be a bump in the numbers for the veteran. And the run defense is already *chef’s kiss.* Jonathan Allen spending time in yo' backfield. Moving Allen around with Sexy Dexy as the epicenter should be fun. @Bengals pic.twitter.com/7rh2meKKGk — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 30, 2026 Allen is certainly happy about the prospects for that interior line. “I don’t think there’s ever been a guy to play like Dexter,” Allen said in June. “Dexter is a unique guy, and I’m just excited for the opportunity. “It’s funny. After I left Minnesota (last season), I just sat down and had to really think what I wanted. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t want to come up here and put up great numbers. That proves your worth and why they brought you in. But, honestly, I just want to play meaningful football in December, and I want to help the team any way I can. I believe if I do that, the numbers will come. “At this point in my career, it’s all about winning, man.” It’s been a while since anybody voiced that reason for signing with the Bengals, but here we are, and it could happen more quickly with Allen’s contributions. Underrated draft pick: Center Connor Lew You obviously don’t know how NFL teams feel about your draft binkies until one actually selects one of them. In the case of…
