title: Packers add 2 tight ends
summary: With the injuries to tight ends Tucker Kraft, Luke Musgrave, Luke Lachey and R.J. Maryland, the Green Bay Packers were in a pinch for bodies at the position going into Tuesday’s practice. It had already been reported that the team signed McCallan Castles, a former practice squadder from the 2025 team, to help them while […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 22: Drew Biber #87 of the Minnesota Golden Gophers looks on against the Northwestern Wildcats at Wrigley Field on November 22, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the injuries to tight ends Tucker Kraft, Luke Musgrave, Luke Lachey and R.J. Maryland, the Green Bay Packers were in a pinch for bodies at the position going into Tuesday’s practice. It had already been reported that the team signed McCallan Castles , a former practice squadder from the 2025 team, to help them while their tight end room was banged up. On Tuesday, though, it was revealed that the Packers had apparently signed another tight end, too: Drew Biber. Like Castles, Biber had worked out with Green Bay last week, one of six tight ends that the team brought in throughout the week. Between Castles, Biber and international exemption Thomas Yassmin, the Packers have now signed half of the tight ends from that batch of workouts. Here was what we wrote about Biber following the announcement of his workout: Like Beetham, Biber is another 2026 UDFA. He participated at the American Bowl with Team Guardians, where he shared the tight end room with Packers signing R.J. Maryland. Biber played at Purdue for four seasons before transferring to Minnesota for his senior year. He posted 33 receptions for 271 yards (8.2 per) and a touchdown in his college career. He was listed as the 37th tight end in the 2026 class per The Beast, which reported that he was 6’3.5” and 247 pounds at his pro day and ran a 4.88-second 40-yard dash. Neither R.J. Maryland, who is dealing with a hamstring injury, nor Luke Lachey, who was seen on a scooter and wearing a boot after practice yesterday, were seen at practice on Tuesday, so the assumption right now is that the team has waived those players to make room for the additions of Castles and Biber. The Packers’ roster was full going into the day, so two corresponding roster moves need to be made for Castles and Biber to join the team.

summary: The Packers’ defensive line is facing a lot of questions this season. How will they answer them? If it comes down to a single player, the answer might have to be Chris McClellan. full_text: Chris McClellan #55 of the Green Bay Packers rides a bicycle while pointing toward the crowd during the Green Bay Packers Training Camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Packers’ defensive line is facing a lot of questions this season. How will they answer them? We’ve written quite a bit about McClellan in the months since he was drafted , but it’s been a waiting game to see if any of our analysis would find the mark. So far, it looks like the Packers were on the money with their faith in the rookie defensive tackle. What does that really mean when most of camp has been un-padded and McClellan’s contributions have come against his own teammates? If the Packers’ defense is going to rise to its full potential, the Packers are going to need McClellan to play well throughout this season, but especially early. With Micah Parsons on the mend, the Packers will need all the help they can get, and with the defensive line still vulnerable, an early push from McClellan could go a long way. title: Houston Texans Offensive Training Camp Standouts
summary: The Houston Texans are back at training camp and inching closer to the start of the regular season. The pads are finally on, which means there’s still plenty of time before Week one, but a few players have already stood out. WR Jayden Higgins Higgins put together a solid rookie season, but he’s clearly put […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 01: Lewis Bond #82 of the Houston Texans crosses the field during Houston Texans training camp at Houston Methodist Training Center on August 01, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans are back at training camp and inching closer to the start of the regular season. The pads are finally on, which means there’s still plenty of time before Week one, but a few players have already stood out. WR Jayden Higgins Higgins put together a solid rookie season, but he’s clearly put in the work this offseason to make that second-year leap, and it’s showing. Quarterback C.J. Stroud and Higgins weren’t always on the same page last season, but it’s safe to say that narrative is being put to rest with how locked in the two have looked throughout the early stages of training camp. The Texans need someone to emerge alongside Nico Collins, and Higgins is looking more and more like that player. OL Keylan Rutledge Rutledge was selected by Houston in the first round of this year’s draft, so expectations are understandably high. So far, he’s lived up to the hype during the opening days of camp. He brings a level of physicality and nastiness that this offense has desperately needed. If the offense can begin matching the intensity of the defense, the sky is truly the limit. The former Georgia Tech standout has held his own against Houston’s elite defensive front and hasn’t been afraid to mix it up. Expect him to see plenty of snaps in 2026. WR Lewis Bond Bond is another rookie making noise. The sixth-round pick out of Boston College knows how difficult it is for a late-round selection to earn a roster spot, but he has continued to turn heads in a talented wide receiver room. The Texans open the preseason on August 13, giving Bond another great opportunity to prove he belongs on an NFL roster. If he continues this trajectory, it wouldn’t be surprising to see him carve out a role during the regular season. It’s still early, but the regular season will be here before you know it.

title: Houston Texans 53-man roster prediction post-Clowney signing
summary: The third edition of the roster prediction series is here. Nick Caserio made multiple decisive additions to replenish the ranks after several injuries on defense. It is more difficult than ever to evaluate who is on the fringes of the roster due to a new team policy. I’ve cut through the clutter, scoured videos, and […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 27: Xavier Hutchinson #19 of the Houston Texans and Nico Collins #12 celebrate during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on December 27, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The third edition of the roster prediction series is here. Nick Caserio made multiple decisive additions to replenish the ranks after several injuries on defense. It is more difficult than ever to evaluate who is on the fringes of the roster due to a new team policy . I’ve cut through the clutter, scoured videos, and sourced my own knowledge to bring you the most up-to-date roster prediction on the market. Here’s a quick recap of everything that’s happened at Texans Training Camp: Injuries : Jaylin Noel (finger), M.J. Stewart (quad), Jake Hansen (ankle) Additions : DE Jadeveon Clowney, DT Mario Edwards Jr., LB Sione Takitaki Cuts : RB Evan Hull, OT Derrick Graham Here are the past 53-man roster predictions Rosterology 1.0 Rosterology 2.0 Note: Rookies are in bold and UDFAs are italicized Last Four In: British Brooks, RB/FB Alijah Huzzie, DB Naquan Jones, DT Sione Takitaki, LB First Four Out: Mario Edwards Jr., DT Tremon Smith, CB Cade Stover, TE Evan Brown – OC/OG Biggest Riser: Jake Andrews, OC By rule, a “riser” has to be on the roster before the previous Rosterology. Therefore, Mario Edwards Jr. and Jadeveon Clowney don’t fit. Though the Texans have tried to move on, Jake Andrews persists. Andrews practices with the starters more than Rutledge, and the coaching staff trusts him despite his athletic deficiencies. Honorable mention goes to WR Justin Watson, who went from “First Four Out” in the first two editions to squarely on the roster. Biggest Faller: Jake Hummel, LB Hummel’s absence from camp has been as mysterious as unfortunate. With the injuries to E.J. Speed and Jake Hansen, Hummel was a ‘First Four In” two weeks ago. Now, he’s nowhere to be found. The Texans signed Sione TakiTaki this weekend to fill in the gap. Honorable mention goes to DE Dominique Robinson, who dropped out of the 53 when Jadeveon Clowney came back into the fold. Offense (26) Quarterbacks: 3 C.J. Stroud, Davis Mills, Graham Mertz Analysis: Mertz moves from outside the bubble to on the roster after I sought further analysis into the Texans’ history. In the past five roster cut downs, they’ve alway kept three QBs on the roster. I cannot see the Texans switching things up anytime soon. Mertz has practiced exclusively on the third team, knows the offense well, and should make the team. This isn’t about the best 53, it’s about predicting the right 53. Running Backs: 4 David Montgomery, Woody Marks, British Brooks, Jawhar Jordan CUT: Noah Whittington, Josh Pitsenberger Analysis: I waxed poetic about British Brooks two weeks ago only to completely renege on my opinion. He is getting more run than Jordan at RB3, but I’m concerned about the team keeping four RBs given the depth at TE. Evan Hull (who I was going to start calling Evan of House Hull based on HBO’s House of the Dragon ), was cut to make way for veteran DE Mario Edwards Jr. The Texans brought in two top free agent options in Alexander Mattisson and Hassan Haskins but signed neither one. Still one of the weakest position groups despite UDFA Noah Whittington’s steady improvement. Wide Receivers: 6 Nico Collins, Tank Dell, Jayden Higgins, Justin Watson, Xavier Hutchinson, Lewis Bond CUT: Jared Wayne, Daniel Sobkowics, Jalen Walthall, Treyvhon Saunders, Jha’Quan Jackson, DJ Turner INJURED RESERVE: Jaylin Noel Analysis: Watson swaps in for Noel due to the lingering injury. If Noel is healthy, the offense will keep seven WRs. Watson is too integral to this offense to cut him loose. The staff lean on him more than fans consider. That will push a safety, RB, or DT off the roster in a future edition. Jared Wayne, the WR who collided with and fractured Tank Dell’s leg in 2024, is back and proving a point. He is working with the second team and is clearly a favorite in this offense. Potentially outplaying Lewis Bond for the last roster spot. Tight Ends: 4 Dalton Schultz, Marlin Klein , Foster Moreau, Brevin Jordan CUT: Cade Stover, Layne Pryor, Louis Hansen Analysis: “Sideline Klein” has impressed thusfar. He’s utilized as a blocker and rarely targeted in the passing game, but he’s in there with the starters. Stover is the clear odd one out. I wouldn’t be surprised if Houston trades him in the preseason for a late-round pick. Doubtful Houston can stash him on their practice squad. Offensive Lineman: 9 Aireontae Ersery, Braden Smith, Trent Brown, Wyatt Teller, Jake Andrews, Blake Fisher, Keylan Rutledge, Febechi Nwaiwu , Ed Ingram CUT: Evan Brown, Jarrett Patterson, Eli Cox, Jarrett Kingston, Sam Hagen, James Neal III Analysis: It’s being reported, even if the Texans PR department discourages it, that Jake Andrews is running with the starting offensive line. That pushes him back onto the Rosterology. He replaces Evan Brown, who has not been seen with the first team since Rutledge started rotating at center and guard. One thought: reports from camp indicate little improvement up front. Could the Texans make a big move and trade for a young, impact offensive lineman? Defense (24) Defensive Ends: 4 Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter, Dylan Horton, Jadeveon Clowney CUT: Dominique Robinson, Solomon Byrd, Ali Gaye, Sabastian Harsh Analysis: The addition of Clowney bolsters this group immensely. It also pushes Dominique Robinson off the roster entirely. Robinson has yet to show anything demonstrative in practice to earn a spot – hence the signing of Clowney. Could Robinson still make the roster as the fifth DE? Absolutely, but it’s yet to earn a spot through his on field play. Defensive Tackles: 5 Tommy Togiai, Sheldon Rankins, Kayden McDonald , Logan Hall, Naquan Jones CUT: Mario Edwards Jr., Junior Tafuna, Dominic Bailey, Kyonte Hamilton Analysis: The return of Mario Edwards Jr. throws a nasty curveball into this group and makes it much more interesting. However, he was one of the worst-graded DTs in the NFL last year and is 32. Jones looks formidable at practice and played well last year as the usurper to Edwards Jr. I don’t have Edwards cracking the roster just yet. I need to see him out-perform Jones. Linebackers: 6 Henry To’oTo’o, Azeez Al-Shaair, Wade Woodaz , Jamal Hill, Marte Mapu, Sione TakiTaki INJURED RESERVE: E.J. Speed, Jake Hansen CUT: K.C. Ossai, Aiden Fisher Analysis: This group has gone through a turbine. No Speed. No Hansen. Enter TakiTaki. It’s yet to be seen if he’s going to make an impact or not, but he’s a much needed veteran. Fisher has made plenty of plays at practice but can be an easy practice squad carryover. Cornerbacks: 4 Derek Stingley Jr. Kamari Lassiter, Jaylin Smith, Alijah Huzzie CUT: Tremon Smith, Ja’Marcus Ingram, Brandon Codrington, Stephen Hall , Collin Wright Analysis: The more I play around with the numbers, the more I think Tremon Smith is at jeopardy. His main role is a gunner on special teams, but that isn’t nearly enough to keep promising second-year CBs Jaylin Smith and Alijah Huzzie away. Especially with the need for depth at LB and DE, Tremon may be a roster casualty at 30 years old. Safeties: 5 Reed Blankenship, Calen Bullock, Jalen Pitre, Kamari Ramsey , Jaylen Reed CUT: Kevon Merriweather INJURED RESERVE: M.J. Stewart Analysis: The stress of picking who stays in this room stems from the fact that last season only three safeties made the initial roster. Ramsey and Reed are the depth and future. Special Teams Jack Stonehouse, Kai’mi Fiarbairn, Austin Brinkman CUT: P Kai Kroeger

title: Colts QB Daniel Jones Improves a Tier, But Still Below Average in The Athletic’s latest ranking
summary: The good news is that Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones ascended a tier in the Athletic’s latest quarterback rankings (subscription) and had the greatest improvement among his colleagues. However, the bad news is that he’s still ranked below average among all league starters—coming in at 21st overall: 21. Daniel Jones Jones made the largest […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) celebrates a touchdown with Blue on Sunday, Sept. 7, 2025, during the game at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis. The Indianapolis Colts defeated the Miami Dolphins, 33-8. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The good news is that Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones ascended a tier in the Athletic’s latest quarterback rankings (subscription) and had the greatest improvement among his colleagues . However, the bad news is that he’s still ranked below average among all league starters—coming in at 21st overall: 21. Daniel Jones Jones made the largest year-over-year jump in average vote (+1.1) while climbing eight spots in the rankings. He set career bests in yards per attempt, passer rating and EPA per pass play before suffering a torn right Achilles tendon in December. “I thought he looked broken in New York (with the Giants),” an offensive coordinator said. “I thought he looked functional in Indy. He looked like a 3.” Jones, who is practicing without limitations at training camp, received more Tier 2 votes (eight) than the rest of his career combined (six). Quite a few voters, including defensive coordinators who faced Indianapolis, credited Colts coach Shane Steichen for outstanding game plans. “Daniel Jones is interesting,” one defensive coordinator said. “I think he showed that when you are not protected and you do not have all the answers given to you, it is hard to operate at this level of football.” The implication was that Indy protected Jones, and Steichen gave him answers. “Indy was perfect for him,” another defensive coach said. “The best thing he ever could have done was get with Shane. Steichen has the best mix of tempo versus non-tempo, versus huddle calls, versus ‘Hey, listen, this one’s on two, this one’s on three.’ He tells his quarterback how to change the pace of a game, and he does it as well as anybody right now.” Jones proved he could execute that offense at a high level, although his production tapered later in the season, after defenses had more video to study. One exec thought Jones’ history of lower-body injuries could threaten his mobility longer term. “What Steichen wanted to do scheme-wise, he was not able to do with the guys he had before Daniel Jones,” said another defensive coordinator whose team faced the Colts. “From an intelligence standpoint, getting them in the right plays, going through the right key progressions, that is where Daniel Jones showed he got it.” The “glass half full” crowd will tell you that when fully healthy, in his first-year in Indianapolis with Colts head coach Shane Steichen, that Jones was in the midst of a career year—leading a historically elite league offense on a team that once sat 8-2. Unfortunately, a fractured fibula and season-ending Achilles limited his mobility regarding the former, and ultimately ended his season regarding the latter. It coincided with the Colts late season collapse, where Indianapolis would lose 7 straight games and fall out of playoff contention again. Despite missing the Colts last four games because of the Achilles, Jones was still named a Pro Bowl alternate. He completed 261 of 384 pass attempts (68.0%) for 3,101 total passing yards, 19 passing touchdowns, and 8 interceptions, as well as amassed 5 rushing touchdowns during his 13 starts this past season. The “glass half empty” will tell you that Jones had already shown some signs of regression before the lower leg injuries and is a ‘system quarterback’ under Steichen—heavily leaning on star workhorse Jonathan Taylor as the offense’s true focal point to open up his passing game after-the-fact. The hope has to be that Jones regains his prior first half form, but there may be some truth that he’s a system quarterback, but one could make the argument that so are other Pro Bowl quarterbacks such as Brock Purdy and Jared Goff—both of whom have had more consistent high level success under other talented offensive minds. In fact, each has even made a Super Bowl as a starting quarterback. To me, that’s not the same slam that it appeared to be just a few years ago. If there’s another silver lining for Colts fans, it’s that the other quarterbacks in the AFC South: Trevor Lawrence (16th), CJ Stroud (20th), and Cam Ward (25th) aren’t significantly better or in Ward’s case, still considered a bit worse. It doesn’t appear as this division is ruled by a Patrick Mahomes type quite yet.

title: If the Colts Corners are as advertised, what does it do to the ceiling of the squad?
summary: With Daniel Jones at least looking healthy enough to be the Colts starting QB when the season starts, it does eliminate the biggest question mark for the offense. There are others that include Pierce’s recovery time and the 3rd WR, but I’m allowing myself to feel good about the offense to this point. I also […]
full_text: With Daniel Jones at least looking healthy enough to be the Colts starting QB when the season starts, it does eliminate the biggest question mark for the offense. There are others that include Pierce’s recovery time and the 3rd WR, but I’m allowing myself to feel good about the offense to this point. I also see Westbrook-Ikhine showing as capable and Warren picking up right where he left off. We may also see a possible Robin to Taylor’s Batman in the backfield, as factors for the offense to click along at 28 points a game, even if they can’t match the “historic” run from last year’s first eight games. The defense comes into the season with their own question marks. Who gets most of the snaps opposite Latu? Do we have an NFL caliber LB on the squad? Can our cornerbacks stay healthy? We may not know the answers to the first two questions, but what we have seen or have been reported to have seen, is a tandem in Ward and Gardner that are drawing attention in a good way. We invested heavily, very heavily, into the combo. Mooney will account for nearly 20 million this year and we can have him for 24.7 next year, if things go well this year. Sauce will still be a very affordable 9.5 this year, before the bigger 21 million number next year and 26.2 in 2028. This doesn’t even add the investment of two first round picks into the mix. Both are proven alphas, with their only negative being last year’s injuries. Those injuries have been the source of most of the angst about the position group. But what if you allow yourself to see them as the Pro Bowl caliber players that they have been? Just how positively can they effect the defense? Most of us have witnessed defenses that have one of those “Shutdown Corners” that take away half of the field. I don’t recall many with two such players. One thing that I think we will see, is opponents trying to rely on timing routes. A QB is going to have trust his WR to be where he is supposed to be, at the time he is supposed to be there. If QBs are surveying the field, looking for the open target, they are not going to be risking throwing toward that combo as they will not appear to be open. Those extra beats that QBs have to hold the ball, will give our subpar pass rush a fighting chance, or hopefully a leg up. Two guys do not make a defense, but if our duo stays on the field and shows the same ability to lock up their man that they have shown throughout their careers and are currently showing in camp, it is going to have a trickle down effect that has to be a positive.
author: Clydesdales

title: Daniel Jones airs it out, shines as pocket passer on Day 6
summary: WESTFIELD, Ind. — Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was on point Tuesday morning with an impressive performance at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus, proving precisely why the franchise signed him to a two-year, $88 million extension in March with incentives that could reach up to $100M. Before Jones suffered a season-ending Achilles injury, he had […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones throws a pass during a training camp practice at Gand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, Ind. — August 10, 2025 | Thomas Butler-Guerrero WESTFIELD, Ind. — Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was on point Tuesday morning with an impressive performance at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus, proving precisely why the franchise signed him to a two-year, $88 million extension in March with incentives that could reach up to $100M. Before Jones suffered a season-ending Achilles injury, he had the Colts leading the NFL in both yards per play (6.3) and points per game (29.8). There’s no doubt the fans in the grandstands saw that Jones looks fully healthy, ready to play and command this offense. Day 6 of training camp featured the most explosive day for the starting offense as Jones stretched the field and delivered accurate throws. After officially sporting the pads on Monday in a practice dominated by physical football with an emphasis on the run game, Shane Steichen’s offense finally unleashed an aerial attack. The eight-year veteran quarterback completed 9-of-11 passes in team drills, layering perfectly placed throws to different receivers in each session. The fireworks started early after a competitive goal-line period as running back Jonathan Taylor punched in a pair of rushing touchdowns and receiver Josh Downs won on an out route for another short score. Then the starting offense flipped around to use the length of the field. With the offense backed up on its own 20-yard line, Jones recognized single-high coverage and never hesitated to sling it. On the very first play, Jones launched a perfectly placed deep post to receiver Laquon Treadwell, dropping the pass over the top of free safety Camryn Bynum for a 50-yard completion. It set the tone for the biggest offensive showing from the first-team offense, and he never cooled off. Jones followed with a 20-yard strike over the middle to tight end Tyler Warren before flashing another element of his skillset during the next team period. Off a play-action fake, Jones tucked the football and raced right to the far side of the field for a sizable gain, reminding everyone that his mobility remains a weapon within Steichen’s offense. Moments later, Jones dumped a slick screen to Taylor, who turned it into yet another explosive gain of 50-plus yards for the second straight practice behind strong blocking in open space. Receiver Alec Pierce remained sidelined on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list with a calf injury. If the first half of camp showcased Jones’ efficiency, the final team period Tuesday morning highlighted just how dangerous Indianapolis’ passing attack can become when its deep threat returns. Danny Dimes fired a laser 20 yards downfield to Warren, who elevated over Bynum to high-point the football and make the sensational catch near midfield. Two snaps later, Jones uncorked another immaculate deep throw and connected with receiver Ashton Dulin on a beautiful completion of 50 yards despite tight coverage from cornerback Charvarius Ward. dart from Dan & a grab from Dulin😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/mLDRGAYyTi — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 4, 2026 Jones finished his remarkable day by finding Warren and Will Mallory on crossing routes for consecutive 20-yard gains before being relieved by the second unit. It has become clear that Warren is carving out a significant role in the offense while entering his second NFL campaign. With Indianapolis expected to feature plenty of 12 personnel and two tight end sets this season, Warren continues developing more chemistry with Jones to often find space for chunk plays. Tuesday’s practice also marked the first extended receiver versus defensive back 1-on-1 drills of camp. Cornerback Justin Walley has been attached to the hip of Josh Downs in the slot, and that competitive battle was back on full display. Walley has more than stood his ground, but it was Downs hanging onto a throw from Jones to win the matchup this time around. With Sauce Gardner sidelined because of an illness, it was cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt who received additional work with the starting defense and earned reps as the Colts’ fourth cornerback in dime packages. Taylor-Britt was another standout Tuesday after breaking up multiple passes intended for receiver Nick Westbrook-Ikhene, who fetched four consecutive targets in the 7-on-7 session. The first three passes fell incomplete due to a couple of deflections by Ward and Taylor-Britt. Despite the secondary handling the receiving corps in the first half of camp, Tuesday ultimately looked different and belonged to the offensive skill group. The success could be attributed to the absence of Garnder, but it was Jones’ accuracy and willingness to let it rip that stole the show. After days of emphasizing the run game and physicality, the Colts opened the playbook and attacked vertically throughout a fast-paced, 90-minute practice. Nearly every team period began deep inside the offense’s own territory, yet Jones showed how often this offense can flip field position when in rhythm. The Colts host a night practice on Thursday from 8 to 10 p.m. at Grand Park, featuring a post-practice fireworks show.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Daniel Jones is impressing in his Colts return
summary: When Daniel Jones went down in Jacksonville against the Jaguars, it meant two things: the losing streak was about to continue, and it didn’t look good. Non-contact injuries are the worst possible types of injuries in sports. No one is around, yet the player falls in a heap on the ground. Indianapolis Colts fans’ worst […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) throws a pass during Indianapolis Colts Training Camp Family Day on Friday, July 31, 2026, at Grand Park in Westfield, Ind. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co When Daniel Jones went down in Jacksonville against the Jaguars, it meant two things: the losing streak was about to continue, and it didn’t look good. Non-contact injuries are the worst possible types of injuries in sports. No one is around, yet the player falls in a heap on the ground. Indianapolis Colts fans’ worst fears were realized as Jones suffered a torn Achilles, and the season was over for him and ultimately the team. Fast forward to training camp in Westfield and his devastating injury could have been just a dream. JJ Stankevitz of Colts.com captured a Jones that was running without issue , even punching in a touchdown on the ground. Does that sound like a player who isn’t ready to go? Mo Alie-Cox and Quentin Nelson were certainly impressed. “He looks like he never got hurt,” Alie-Cox said. “He’s throwing dimes left and right on the field, getting out the pocket, scrambling and different things like that.” “He’s been incredible. He’s back like he’s never left,” left guard Quenton Nelson said. “He worked so hard to get here. It’s been awesome to see.” Training camp is a time of myth, legend, and sometimes fairy tales. The best and the brightest in camp don’t always pan out. While that may be true, hearing that Jones is getting up to speed so quickly is incredibly encouraging and bodes well going into this season. The alternative was dark. Faults and all, Jones is the best quarterback on this team, and any hopes and dreams begin and end with him. Watching the rust fade away, his leg appearing to be fully healed, and having a full training camp to connect with his teammates is huge. Eight months is all it took for Daniel Jones to rejoin the Colts. Other quarterbacks have suffered similar injuries, but Jones relies on his mobility. Having that part of his game return so quickly is highly fortunate and puts the season back on the right track. A healthy Jones doesn’t solve everything, but an unhealthy Jones dissolves everything. The Colts need him to be healthy. For now, that certainly appears to be the case.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Is Colts’ Chris Ballard on ‘borrowed time’ serving as team’s longtime GM?
summary: Last week to kickoff team training camp, Indianapolis Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard indicated that if offered a contract extension, he won’t accept it because his built roster needs to win—entering ‘Year 10.’ Now chivalry may not in fact be dead, but on the other hand, there doesn’t appear to be any contract extension […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Westfield, IN, USA; Indianapolis Colts GM Chris Ballard is seen on day two of training camp at Grand Park Sports Campus. Mandatory Credit: Robert Goddin-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Last week to kickoff team training camp, Indianapolis Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard indicated that if offered a contract extension, he won’t accept it because his built roster needs to win—entering ‘Year 10.’ Now chivalry may not in fact be dead, but on the other hand, there doesn’t appear to be any contract extension forthcoming from Colts team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon. If there had been, despite the public posturing, Ballard would’ve already accepted a lucrative NFL general manager’s salary for the next few years. Ballard’s lengthy tenure as Colts general manager from 2017-2025 speaks for itself, overall win-loss record of 70-78-1, no division titles, and two playoff appearances with 1 win—and never advancing past the AFC Divisional Round approaching a decade on the job for Indianapolis. Despite proclaiming upon his arrival that it would never be about one guy, the Colts have struggled replacing and finding any sort of stability since former franchise quarterback Andrew Luck shockingly retired just ahead of the 2019 season—with the starting quarterback position continuing to be a turnstile. While a re-signed Daniel Jones may solidify the QB1 position, if he can regain his first half 2025 form, he still has to stay healthy for an entire season coming off a late year season-ending torn Achilles and even a lack of prior durability with the Giants. It figures to be ‘playoffs or pack your papers’ in Indianapolis, as the Colts have to obtain meaningful success in 2026—and that’s at least a playoff appearance one would reasonably think. The problem for Ballard and the Colts right now though is that it’s a fair question of whether Indianapolis is anymore than the 3rd best team in the AFC South, especially since current head coach Shane Steichen has gone a combined 2-10 against both the Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars over his first three seasons in Indy. The Colts’ top divisional rivals are only continuing to improve too, as the Texans just re-signed their former #1 overall pick, veteran edge Jadeveon Clowney, who had 8.5 sacks last year as a rotational defensive end to what’s already a loaded positional group and stacked Houston defense collectively. It’s a fair question of whether Clowney would be an upgrade to anyone the Colts could start opposite Laiatu Latu along their d-line right now. It’s not just at defensive end where the Colts surprisingly didn’t reinforce the position with more higher-end talent, as the wide receiver spot on the outside opposite currently hobbled Alec Pierce continues to be a major question mark: One week into Colts training camp and I STILL remain convinced they are living on the edge at WR. With Alec Pierce (ankle) still out, the depth chart is essentially 1) Josh Downs 2-4) Ashton Dulin, Laquon Treadwell, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine (in some order). Gotta make a move IMO. — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) August 3, 2026 It seems like every offseason, Colts fans have this same typical frustration with Ballard, where there’s at least a starting position or two that looks visibly weak on paper, but Indy had some flexibility to do more. It’s been at wide receiver, left tackle, cornerback, tight end, linebacker, and safety before in years past, and with the exception of safety (where Nick Cross did emerge two years ago to be fair), it seems to have worked out less often than it’s ultimately gone right on Ballard’s intuition and seemingly ‘liking his guys.’ Perhaps Arden Key will be a solidifying veteran edge or 2nd-year pro Jaylahn Tuimoloau will take a major leap forward, and Ashton Dulin will continue to work his tail off and ascend as a suitable WR2, but it seems like Ballard and Co. are taking a major gamble, with their margin of error being small at premium NFL positions. I’m not rooting for the Colts to lose by any means. I hope they win and win consistently at that—and snap their playoff drought of five seasons dating back to 2020—and finally win at Jacksonville, snapping another woeful franchise streak in the process. By winning games, the Colts are more fun to discuss and analyze, our viewership is better across the board, and it’s more fun to write exciting articles filled with hope and serious title aspirations than somber summaries. The hope has to be that with Jones fully healthy, the Colts can replicate their first half of 2025 form, especially with former All-Pro cornerback Sauce Gardner anchoring their secondary for a full season. That being said, looking at the Colts roster as a whole, particularly with the arguable remaining key deficiencies at both Edge2 and WR2, and I’m not sure how anyone can feel super confident that it stacks up better than either the Texans or Jaguars right now—and finishing 3rd place in the AFC South simply won’t cut it again. More than likely, that means the Colts winning 7-9 games, falling just short of the playoff sticks again, and without even a 2027 first round pick to make the Horseshoe faithful even feel slightly better about it with more favorable early draft positioning. That’s what we call staying in NFL purgatory. However, I’d love to be proven wrong, and in order to do so, Ballard must firmly silence his critics and meaningfully win again, because his continued job security (*and perhaps Steichen’s too) seemingly depends on it.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Trevor Lawrence ranked 16th among NFL quarterbacks by The Athletic’s anonymous league survey
summary: In an annual anonymous survey gathered by Mike Sando of The Athletic, 50 voters across the NFL — from head coaches to former general managers to offensive assistants to analytics/game management coaches — placed 35 veteran quarterbacks into five tiers. This year’s results saw Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence leap into Tier 2, marking just […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - JULY 29: Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence (16) talks with the media following training camp on July 29, 2026 at the Miller Electric Center in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In an annual anonymous survey gathered by Mike Sando of The Athletic , 50 voters across the NFL — from head coaches to former general managers to offensive assistants to analytics/game management coaches — placed 35 veteran quarterbacks into five tiers. This year’s results saw Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence leap into Tier 2, marking just his second career appearance in the category (2022). The percentage of Tier 2 votes he’s received started at 8% as a rookie, jumped to 66%, fell to 36%, continued dipping to 20%, and then shot back up again to 52% following last season. Here’s a breakdown of Lawrence’s votes this year. 1 vote for Tier 1: “Carries his team each week” 26 votes for Tier 2: “Carries his team sometimes” 23 votes for Tier 3: “Legit starter but needs a better run game or defense to win” No votes for Tier 4: “Unproven player or veteran who ideally would not be a full season starter” No votes for Tier 5: “Not a starter, period” It looks like readers are even less optimistic about Lawrence. According to the survey embedded into the article, 62% of The Athletic’s subscribers ranked Lawrence as a Tier 3 quarterback, compared to 30% for Tier 2 and just 2% for Tier 1. “Man, if there’s anybody that’s between a 2 and a 3, I would say him right now,” a former head coach told Sando. “If he does it again this year, I could see putting him as a standing 2.” “You are not in Year 2 anymore,” an offensive coordinator said. “This is just kind of who you are — streaky, up and down.” Is this blatant disrespect, or are fair points being made? Which “tier” would you place Lawrence into right now? Let us know in the comments below!

title: Defense outshines Trevor Lawrence on Day 6 of Jaguars training camp
summary: Day 6 of Jacksonville Jaguars training camp was ruled by the defense. Antonio Johnson, Jarrian Jones, and Eric Murray came down with interceptions. Jabbar Muhammad dominated at the catch point. Travon Walker, Zach Durfee, and Bryan Thomas Jr. (you read that right) all had would-be sacks of Trevor Lawrence. Branson Combs delivered the hit of […]
full_text: Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen directs practice near quarterback Trevor Lawrence (16) during the sixth day of NFL training camp at the Miller Electric Center on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Jacksonville, Fla. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Day 6 of Jacksonville Jaguars training camp was ruled by the defense. Antonio Johnson, Jarrian Jones, and Eric Murray came down with interceptions. Jabbar Muhammad dominated at the catch point. Travon Walker, Zach Durfee, and Bryan Thomas Jr. (you read that right) all had would-be sacks of Trevor Lawrence. Branson Combs delivered the hit of the day on a pass breakup at the goal line. The defense won six of nine reps during redzone drills. AJ DAY AJ DAY @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/Ud7LjXvjeH — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 4, 2026 The ascending Parker Washington continued to impress from an individual standpoint, as he was literally unguardable during 1-vs-1 drills and made a tough catch during redzone drills — but his feet were just barely out of bounds because he had to leave the ground to make the catch. On a deep crossing route during team drills, a pass from Lawrence went just past his fingertips. It wasn’t a complete disasterclass from the offense, but they clearly weren’t clicking. Lawrence never found anything close to a rhythm and the running game couldn’t get anything going between the tackles. “There’s definitely some meat on the bone there,” defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said after practice in regard to his top-ranked run defense from last year. “I thought today, for us defensively, was a little bit better than yesterday. But that’s what you’re trying to do, you’re trying to build a callous and, just honestly, entering blocks the right way, entering tackles the right way, all the fundamental things that are important to winning and playing good football.” With pads on for the second straight day, the Jaguars have more opportunities to become more physical as a team. “We just want that for everybody,” Campanile said. “We want that to be the culture of the room … [if] we’re not performing physically and we’re not violently finishing, trying to whoop the other guy’s ass on every play, it’s going to get called out. And if you are, it’s going to get celebrated. And I just think that’s a good culture to have, and hopefully we’re trending that way, but our players believe in that. From the defensive backs all the way down to the D-line, they all believe in that. And they’re great guys to coach, honestly, because of that. They’re great. We have great, great dudes here. Great dudes.” Notes & Quotes Campanile has been bringing a special guest to practice: legendary defensive line coach Pete Jenkins, who has nearly four decades of football coaching experience including 22 seasons in the SEC and three in the NFL. “He’s kind of been everywhere I’ve been since I was in Miami, and like, he’s the G.O.A.T.,” Campanile said. “So much of what I believe comes from Coach, and he’s honest. He comes in here, and he’s ripping my ass and ripping everybody—he’s just telling the truth. We got him in here kind of just watching everything, making sure we’re doing a great job with the drills and training the guys the right way. He’s done a pretty good job for all the teams in the SEC the last 10, what, 20 years, 30 years. So hopefully, having him here, I know it is going to help us.” When asked what he’s specifically looking to improve in his game this offseason, Travon Walker replied, “Obviously, I’m a big power player, I just feel like I need to start playing with my length a little bit more. If I play with my length a lot more, it’ll keep guys from getting on me so much and having to bench press and having to use my strength all the time. I just start off locked out, I feel like I’ll take advantage of a lot more of my reps.” Jacksonville’s pair of sixth-round rookie wideouts continued to flash. Josh Cameron had a strong sideline snag against Montaric Brown to move the chains during a two-minute period; CJ Williams went full extension while keeping his feet inbounds for a touchdown during a redzone period. All of a sudden, the team’s receiver room is as deep as it’s ever been. Ameer Abdullah looks good! Sporting three-quarters-length pants, the spry 33-year-old had consecutive long runs down the right sideline in 11-vs-11 team drills. The only other positive run I recall came from Bhayshul Tuten. Abdullah is competing with DeeJay Dallas and UDFA J’Mari Taylor to make the 53-man roster as RB4. Right ( maybe left? ) tackle Anton Harrison got knicked up during team drills, but it wasn’t bad enough to depart practice, and Lawrence was sporting an arm sleeve on his throwing shoulder (as he did last offseason) simply because he’s throwing so much. Arik Armstead and Chris Rodriguez Jr. had scheduled days off. Unfortunately, in more significant injury news, linebacker Jared Bartlett was carted off the field with an apparent right leg injury. Jaguars fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: The next wave: Chiefs’ young defensive backs embracing bigger roles
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs’ secondary is getting younger, but those players are ready to grow up. With veterans departing during the offseason, players who were once learning behind established leaders are now being asked to lead themselves. Few embody that transition more than safety Chamarri Conner and second-year cornerback Nohl Williams. For Conner, the change […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Nohl Williams #20, DeShon Singleton, Jaden Hicks #21 and Jason Canady #22 walk to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs’ secondary is getting younger, but those players are ready to grow up. With veterans departing during the offseason, players who were once learning behind established leaders are now being asked to lead themselves. Few embody that transition more than safety Chamarri Conner and second-year cornerback Nohl Williams. For Conner, the change has brought a new responsibility. “Definitely changed my mentality,” Conner said after Tuesday’s practice. “We’ve got a lot of younger guys that came in. We’ve got a lot of older veteran guys that are still learning. I’m kind of in that middle piece to help guys out, kind of bridge that gap.” That role fits where Conner finds himself entering his third NFL season. After spending much of his first two years moving between safety and the Nickel position, Conner expects to settle into a more defined role this season. “I’m very comfortable playing safety,” Conner said. “It’s exciting to be in one spot. I’m always ready to do whatever the team needs, but I’m excited for this year. I’m excited for this season.” While his responsibilities have become more focused on the field, they’ve expanded off of it. Conner now finds himself helping younger teammates navigate defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s defense, while still continuing to grow himself as an experienced player in the system. The result, he believes, is a defensive back room motivated to improve. “I think we’re a group full of guys that’s eager to learn, eager to get better every day and a group of hungry guys,” Conner said. “So, I’m excited.” Williams is experiencing a different kind of growth. Last summer, the rookie was trying to prove he belonged. This year, he knows what NFL training camp demands. “The best thing I have is experience,” Williams said. “I know what it’s supposed to look like. Just trying to stack days while I’m out here.” That experience extends well beyond understanding the playbook. Williams said his first NFL season taught him the physical toll that comes with playing meaningful defensive snaps. “Getting 20 snaps is way different than getting 40 snaps,” Williams said. “Even one play. It can just be one play, and something can happen. It is a 100 percent injury-rate game. You’ve got to take care of your body at all costs.” That lesson has changed how he prepares for his second season. “I do have a better understanding,” Williams said. “I am blessed to be in this position and to take it one day at a time.” Together, Conner and Williams represent two different stages of the Chiefs’ evolving secondary. Conner is stepping into a leadership role as one of the defense’s more experienced voices, while Williams is leaning on the lessons learned during his rookie season to take the next step in his development. For a defense replacing veteran leadership, those developments could prove just as important as any offseason addition. The Chiefs don’t simply need talented defensive backs. They need players ready to lead, players prepared for the grind of a 17-game season and players capable of helping the next wave develop behind them. Based on the early days of training camp, Conner and Williams appear ready to embrace those responsibilities.
author: Maurice Elston

title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 6: A perspective from Joe Bleymaier
summary: After Tuesday’s Kansas City Chiefs training camp practice, the sixth of camp involving the full team and the second with pads on, pass-game coordinator Joe Bleymaier — who has stepped up in the absence of offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy — answered questions from local media. He provided some further insight into camp, deeper thoughts than […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Andy Reid during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After Tuesday’s Kansas City Chiefs training camp practice, the sixth of camp involving the full team and the second with pads on, pass-game coordinator Joe Bleymaier — who has stepped up in the absence of offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy — answered questions from local media. He provided some further insight into camp, deeper thoughts than we typically get from the offensive coaching staff. Here were his most notable quotes from Tuesday, shaping the noteworthy observations from Arrowhead Pride’s in-person coverage of practice. The incredible Patrick Mahomes It’s hard to point out any restrictions on quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ game right now. During a goal-to-go situation in a full-team period Tuesday, the play call had Mahomes sprint right on an option play before tucking it and gliding into the end zone. If it looks like Mahomes is comfortable playing at 100%, Bleymaier has a hard time denying it. “He’s always pushing the limits physically, what he can do with the football and the recovery timetable from the injuries that he has had. I haven’t seen anything with the knee out there on the field that would lend itself to show any sort of hangover or any sort of setback from the season,” Bleymaier shared. “I hate to say I’m surprised by that, but it’s just nonexistent, any sort of knee issues.” “We’re not going to put any limitations on what Patrick can do,” Bleymaier said later on. “So rather than maybe emphasizing what we’re going to try and do more, we’re really trying to eliminate holding him back, or ‘let’s not put him in this certain situation.‘ Everything is open. From under center, to rolling left, to going right, the whole playbook.” “He plays the game with a style,” Bleymaier reminded reporters. “You never want to take that away from him.” Getting running backs in space When asked about starting running back Kenneth Walker, Bleymaier made it clear that the offense is ready to maximize the advantage it has with Walker as an open-field playmaker. “He’s going to be tough to tackle. He brings another element to the offense; I think it’s clear. Some of our screens so far this camp, a lot of our runs, and then the play actions after that, all of that kind of ties in together. Him with the offensive line, and how that opens up the rest of the field. It’s a credit to him; he has been tremendous.” Later on, Bleymaier talked about the whole group’s talent as a strength for the play calling. “You look at, specifically, our running backs and their skillsets. They’re tough to tackle in space,” Bleymaier reiterated. “Handing them the ball off or tossing them the ball is one way to get them out in space; then throwing them the ball is a similar way… sometimes, if everything is covered down the field and we got a running back one on one in space, that’s going to be a great matchup for us.” Development from the backup quarterbacks The performance of reserve quarterbacks Justin Fields and rookie Garrett Nussmeier has stood out in practice as more impressive than the backups at camp in recent seasons. Nussmeier makes some real, NFL-level anticipation throws, and Fields has been pinpoint accurate on some downfield throws. “I’ve been impressed mentally with those guys and they’re command of the offense as well,” Bleymaier said of Fields and Nussmeier. “You can tell Justin is a veteran in the league; everything comes naturally to him in terms of calling the play and running the huddle. Then out there physically, he’s very gifted. “Nuss, as a rookie, is continuing to learn and grow. He’s soaking in everything the vets are telling him. He’s playing fast.” Cyrus Allen There was no official injury update from the Chiefs after practice, but Bleymaier provided his opinion on the upstart camp of rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen, who is recovering from a bone bruise and is “day to day.” “Early on, he grasped the playbook and what we were asking him to do,” Bleymaier said of Allen. “He has a natural feel for space out there after the snap. “Sometimes, with young guys, when they’re learning the offense, where to line up, all the details… once the ball is snapped, natural ability gets shoved down a little bit. You could still see that he was playing with that natural ability. He’s got great physical traits; they were showing up after the snap, his mental stuff was good pre-snap, and you can build on that. That’s exciting.” Filling in for Eric Bieniemy Bleymaier has taken on the most added responsibility since Bieniemy left camp to tend to his wife Mia Bieniemy. He has done his best to fill one particular role of Bieniemy’s on the practice field, clearly. “I lost my voice already,” Bleymaier smiled. “So some of him has worn off on me.” Bleymaier has been with the Chiefs for 11 seasons, many of those accompanied by Bieniemy on staff. The two have been able to reconnect and talk football recently. “He keeps in touch; it was great to hear from him, just on a personal standpoint,” Bleymaier shared. “He’s been reaching out more and more lately with some of the football stuff. That has kind of brought a little bit of a sense of normalcy back to our routine, just hearing him and his thoughts on the football.” As Bleymaier reflects on his interim role each day, he thinks about how Bieniemy would hope the practices are going — and it’s not pretty. “The funny thing was that he would not want anything to be smooth here,” Bleymaier said. “He would want this to be challenging camp, the coaches to be challenging the guys, and for us to be getting better.” The Chiefs will be back on the practice field at 9:15 a.m. on Wednesday morning.

title: Chiefs’ George Karlaftis: ‘We can take this defense wherever we want’
summary: As Kansas City Chiefs’ defensive end George Karlaftis prepares for the start of his fifth season, he is seeing fewer familiar faces on the field. Only longtime Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones boasts a longer tenure in Kansas City than Karlaftis. Longtime veterans such as defensive end Mike Danna and defensive tackle Derrick Nnadi moved […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; Kansas City, MO, USA; Kansas City Chiefs defensive end George Karlaftis (56) walks down the hill to the fields prior to training camp at Missouri Western University. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect As Kansas City Chiefs ’ defensive end George Karlaftis prepares for the start of his fifth season, he is seeing fewer familiar faces on the field. Only longtime Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones boasts a longer tenure in Kansas City than Karlaftis. Longtime veterans such as defensive end Mike Danna and defensive tackle Derrick Nnadi moved on to new teams in the offseason. The Chiefs eyed younger talent by selecting Clemson defensive tackle Peter Woods in the first round of April’s draft before adding Oklahoma pass rusher R Mason Thomas in the second. Speaking Monday after the team’s training camp practice at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe, Karlaftis discussed his new role as a mentor to younger players. “There’s a whole lot of [new] guys,” Karlaftis remarked. “It’s funny after these practices, they will all go straight to the iPad. That’s what I used to do, so it’s funny looking back at that. But [they] go to the iPad and watch the tape. They will come up to me—come up to Chris like, ‘Okay, what do you think about this rep and what do you think I could do better?’ Those guys, they’re hungry. Hungry for knowledge, hungry to get better.” One Chiefs coaching move that largely went unnoticed was the return of Terry Bradden as the team’s assistant defensive line coach. Bradden previously spent eight seasons with Kansas City and was a part of three Super Bowl-winning coaching staffs. He spent one year coaching the defensive line at Nebraska before returning to the Chiefs. Karlaftis reports that Bradden has been a big part of working with the new talent. Peter Woods going 1-v-1 with the Vet Trey Smith. #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/LsH2Yk8swf — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) August 3, 2026 “We’ve developed a routine after practice with Coach Bradden of doing ‘these hands,’” he explained. “[We’re] doing them every single day, so we can stack and really do stuff that we can apply to our game. So, [we’re] doing that on the field, coupled up with all the conversations we’ll have in the meeting rooms, outside of the meeting rooms and stuff like that. All those guys are just so hungry, and they want to get better. They want to be great, and they love ball, so I love having those guys around. They’re all great additions.” In Karlaftis’ second season in 2023, he was part of a fearsome Super Bowl-winning defensive unit that produced 57 sacks. Having been to the top of the NFL hierarchy, he knows that diminished results such as the team’s 33 sacks a year ago are not good enough. He believes the new additions will help make Kansas City’s front seven feared again for stout run defense and for getting home on opposing quarterbacks. “This year is all about mindset and mentality for us,” Karlaftis explained. “We feel like it starts with our group. It starts upfront. We can take this defense wherever we want as a front. Stopping the run and helping the guys in the back. Really, it’s just starting with us and putting the focus on handling what we need to [do] to make it easier on the linebackers and the [defensive backs] so we can have the best season possible. We want to get back to the promised land. We want to get back to getting all those sacks. We want to stop the run as well as we can. We are as motivated as ever.”

(Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the big changes the Los Angeles Chargers are undergoing for the upcoming season is at the offensive coordinator spot on the coaching staff. Greg Roman is out, and Mike McDaniel is in after spending the last four years as the Miami Dolphins head coach. McDaniel was let go by the Dolphins after failing to get out of the first round of the playoffs, but that task is now something he will be looking at in his new position with the Chargers. Given where the team’s talents are compared to Miami, there’s a chance he might be able to be the missing piece Los Angeles needs. “It was time for a change after the Chargers scored 15 combined points in their last two wild-card exits. Jim Harbaugh fired offensive coordinator Greg Roman, a longtime collaborator, and replaced him with Mike McDaniel to hopefully supercharge the offense as the former Dolphins coach did in his first couple years with Miami,” NFL.com contributor Bobby Kownack wrote. “McDaniel’s arrival as a quarterback whisperer is good news for Justin Herbert, who already plays at a Pro Bowl level, but the impact of his high-octane system should be felt everywhere, from the promising tight end trio of Oronde Gadsden II, David Njoku and Charlie Kolar to Omarion Hampton in the backfield.” McDaniel’s new system should make the Chargers offense more explosive, but it remains to be seen. The Chargers will spend the duration of training camp putting their finishing touches on the offense before going into the season, where they will look to win the AFC West for the first time since 2009. BFTB community, how excited are you about the Chargers offense with McDaniel? Let us know in the comments section below.

title: 49ers injury bug continues to favor Rams
summary: The Los Angeles Rams know as well as anyone that an NFL season can be defined by health just as much as talent. While every team deals with bumps and bruises during training camp, the San Francisco 49ers are once again finding themselves battling an all-too-familiar storyline: mounting injuries before the regular season even begins. […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams know as well as anyone that an NFL season can be defined by health just as much as talent. While every team deals with bumps and bruises during training camp, the San Francisco 49ers are once again finding themselves battling an all-too-familiar storyline: mounting injuries before the regular season even begins. The 49ers have ranked among the NFL's 10 most-injured teams in 12 of the last 13 seasons After 5 training camp practices, the injuries are already adding up 🤕 pic.twitter.com/1dF7U8OsiL — Bleacher Report (@BleacherReport) August 3, 2026 Training camp is designed to build chemistry, evaluate young talent, and prepare for the grind of a 17-game season. Instead, much of the conversation surrounding Kyle Shanahan’s team has centered on players being sidelined. San Francisco has already seen several contributors miss practice with various ailments, while other players are facing longer recoveries that could impact the early portion of the season. Reports from camp indicate the injury list has continued to grow during the opening weeks, creating concerns about the club’s overall depth before preseason games even begin. Unfortunately for the 49ers, this isn’t a new development. Over the past several seasons, San Francisco has consistently been one of the NFL’s most injury-plagued organizations. Whether it has been season-ending injuries to stars like Nick Bosa and Fred Warner in 2025, previous losses involving key players such as Trent Williams, Christian McCaffrey, Deebo Samuel, Dre Greenlaw, Talanoa Hufanga, or numerous offensive linemen and defensive starters in earlier seasons, the franchise has rarely enjoyed extended stretches of good health. The result has often been constant lineup shuffling and younger players being forced into significant roles earlier than expected. To San Francisco’s credit, the organization has generally done an excellent job of developing depth. Shanahan’s coaching staff has routinely identified contributors late in the draft and through undrafted free agency, allowing the 49ers to remain competitive despite significant injury losses. That depth has helped keep the team in playoff contention on multiple occasions, even when several starters were unavailable. Still, there is a limit to how much attrition any roster can absorb. For Rams fans, the situation serves as another reminder that the NFC West remains one of football’s most physical divisions. Every matchup between Los Angeles and San Francisco is hard-fought, and both teams understand the importance of entering those contests as healthy as possible. While no one wants to see injuries derail any player’s season, the Rams certainly won’t complain if one of their biggest division rivals is forced to rely on inexperienced players throughout the year. The Rams will take on the 49ers in Week 1 in Melbourne, Australia. If the 49ers enter the game trying to recover from training camp injuries, they may not stand much of a chance against the Rams strong roster. The 49ers' injury bug is NOT new… Since Levi's Stadium was built next to an electrical substation, they've been the most injured team in the NFL 🤯 pic.twitter.com/qwxNS7L9xD — Bussin' With The Boys (@BussinWTB) August 3, 2026 As the preseason progresses, the biggest question surrounding the 49ers won’t necessarily be whether they have enough talent to compete—it will be whether they can finally break the cycle of injuries that has followed the franchise for much of the past decade. If the injury bug continues to linger, it could once again become one of the defining storylines of San Francisco’s season and potentially shift the balance of power in the NFC West.

title: Not every Rams fan thinks Aaron Donald is a good idea
summary: The most popular player at Rams training camp this year isn’t even on the Rams. It seems like every single day that a new report comes out about Aaron Donald’s return to the Rams, and every single reporter wants his day in the sun. Tuesday was Albert Breer’s turn, saying that he thinks Donald is […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - NOVEMBER 23: Former Los Angeles Rams Aaron Donald GOAT bobble head during the Tampa Bay Buccaneers vs Los Angeles Rams game on November 23, 2025, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Photo by Jevone Moore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The most popular player at Rams training camp this year isn’t even on the Rams. It seems like every single day that a new report comes out about Aaron Donald’s return to the Rams, and every single reporter wants his day in the sun. Tuesday was Albert Breer’s turn, saying that he thinks Donald is coming back and will play the entire season. Not even Matthew Stafford, Myles Garrett, or Puka Nacua is getting this much publicity. Albert Breer said that he thinks Aaron Donald is "coming back" and that he thinks he'll "play the whole season," via @dpshow . — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) August 4, 2026 Last week, I posted a training camp survey for Rams fans , asking them over a dozen questions about their opinions and expectations for the team in 2026. Continuing in posting the results of that survey, the name Aaron Donald came up once and the results were not that surprising, but the wording of the question was intentional. Should the Rams pay Aaron Donald $30 million for 1 season? Yes – 56.6% No – 31.1% I don’t know – 12.3% As JB Scott wrote last month, there is a “$30 million dilemma” lording over the potential return of Donald . Do the Rams want to continue the contract that he had when he retired, which owed Donald $30 million for one season, or will they only take him back at a discount? If Donald will only play for at least $30 million, should the Rams pay it? Over half of you—56.6%—said that they should, that $30 million was practically a bargain for Donald, even if he’s 35 and has taken the last two years off. 12.3% of you were brave enough to admit you didn’t know. But almost one-third of Rams fans said that the Rams should not pay Donald $30 million, if that’s the price. Two years ago, there was probably no limit to what fans would encourage the Rams to pay Donald if he wouldn’t retire, but times have changed. Now 31.1% say $30 million is too much. Of course, Donald can play for less. He doesn’t have to demand that much money, although it is his right to, and if he does want to un-retire, he probably doesn’t care about the money anyway. After all, he walked away from all $30 million two years ago. What does it matter to him if he plays for $20 million? It would be weird to walk away from $30 million and then suddenly require to have it all. However, that is what could happen. If it does, one-third of Rams fans think it’s a bad idea. But almost no Rams fans think trading for Garrett was a bad idea. Could the trade for Myles Garrett backfire? No – 74.6% Yes – 16.4% I don’t know – 9% I knew that there was little chance that people would think the Garrett trade could backfire, especially at the price. The Rams only gave up one guaranteed first-round pick and the Browns are forced to pick up the bulk of his tab. Garrett only has an $8 million cap hit in 2026, and $15 million in 2027. The biggest loss then was probably Jared Verse. How could the trade backfire? Well, what if Verse turns out to be even better than anticipated? Verse is five years younger than Garrett and the Rams would have also had that extra first-round pick in 2027. If Garrett declines in his 30s for any reason, surely Rams fans would agree that there is backfire potential. But they don’t. Almost 75% concurred that the trade could NOT backfire, not in any way, shape, or form. Fewer were sure about the Ty Simpson pick backfiring. Was Ty Simpson right pick at #13? Yes – 45.1% I don’t know – 20.5% No – 14.8% Should’ve been Makai Lemon – 10.7% Should’ve been Rueben Bain – 5.7% Should’ve been Kenyon Sadiq – 3.3% That’s 45.1% yes, but 34.4% who either said no or a different player, which is the same as all of them saying no. Lemon was the most-requested other pick, but it’s tough to say how he’s been progressing because Lemon has had a hamstring injury for most of the offseason. A potential big combo of injuries to monitor as both DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon have hamstring injuries Unclear as to the severity of each, but Lemon was already dealing with an injury (same?) during OTAs. https://t.co/DpeXXbDGKx — Jesse Morse, M.D. (@DrJesseMorse) August 4, 2026 In any case, only 45% of fans fully support the Ty Simpson draft pick. Imagine if Simpson was more highly regarded as a draft prospect, it’s hard to imagine that the number wouldn’t be much higher in that case. Because of his lack of experience, Simpson is slower to be moved up the depth chart than most top-15 picks . Given time, Simpson could prove to be an outstanding quarterback for the Rams. Just a few months into his career though, he still has a lot of skeptics. Both nationally and among Rams fans. Fear not, Ty. Some are even skeptical about a $30 million Aaron Donald.

title: Former Rams cornerback has retired after 9 seasons
summary: Former Los Angeles Rams cornerback Ahkello Witherspoon has decided to hang up his cleats after nine seasons in the NFL. Washington, who signed Witherspoon in free agency, placed the veteran CB on the reserve/retired list on Tuesday. Witherspoon joined the team this offseason after spending the last three seasons with the Rams. He also played […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - JANUARY 04: Ahkello Witherspoon #4 of the Los Angeles Rams reacts after an interception during the second quarter of the game against the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Los Angeles Rams cornerback Ahkello Witherspoon has decided to hang up his cleats after nine seasons in the NFL. View this post on Instagram Washington, who signed Witherspoon in free agency , placed the veteran CB on the reserve/retired list on Tuesday. Witherspoon joined the team this offseason after spending the last three seasons with the Rams. He also played three years with the 49ers and two with the Steelers. Even though his final NFL season ended with two stints on injured reserve, he was still an integral part of L.A.’s defense. Witherspoon started all 17 games and had a career year during his first season with the Rams in 2023. That season, he set career highs in combined tackles (52), tackles for loss (3), passes defensed (14), interceptions (3) and fumble recoveries (2). According to Pro Football Reference , he also allowed a 48.1 completion percentage and a 75.7 passer rating in coverage. It was a season that should’ve propelled him to Pro Bowl honors, but it kicked off the Rams’ ongoing playoff streak, so that’s what mattered most. He didn’t experience as much success the following season, as he started just five of 13 games played and recorded only a single interception. Despite that, his lone pick was perhaps the play of the year in a late-season win over the Cardinals. With Arizona driving for a last-second touchdown with 37 seconds to play, Witherspoon made an incredible diving interception on a deflected pass, securing the Rams’ 13-9 win. Deflected and PICKED in the end zone. What a grab by Witherspoon! 📺: #AZvsLAR on NFL Network 📱: Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/DCKepFjgoT — NFL (@NFL) December 29, 2024 The turnover sealed the team’s ninth win in 11 games and eventually won them the NFC West crown, their first since the 2021 campaign. Injuries significantly limited his final season. Witherspoon suffered a broken scapula in Week 2 against the Titans and rebroke it in the wild card win over the Panthers. Even though Witherspoon’s NFL career didn’t end on a high note or with Super Bowl glory, his time in Hollywood showcased his potential most. He made clutch plays when it mattered and provided stability at a position where the Rams had lacked depth for years. Witherspoon deserves praise for what he brought to the team in his brief time there and has earned retirement following a solid career.

title: What does Quay Walker need to prove during Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp?
summary: When Las Vegas Raiders star defensive end Maxx Crosby was asked about the team’s defensive offseason additions at the beginning of training camp, he mentioned one player by name: linebacker Quay Walker. “It was back in OTAs,” Crosby replied, “but I was out there doing a walkthrough, and I’m getting in a stance, and we’re […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Quay Walker #7 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates against the Washington Commanders at Lambeau Field on September 11, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Las Vegas Raiders star defensive end Maxx Crosby was asked about the team’s defensive offseason additions at the beginning of training camp , he mentioned one player by name: linebacker Quay Walker. “It was back in OTAs,” Crosby replied, “but I was out there doing a walkthrough, and I’m getting in a stance, and we’re in the indoor [facility], Quay gave me a call and I just looked back. I looked at him and started just laughing out loud, and I don’t even know why. He’s like, ‘What are you laughing at, bro?’ I’m like, ‘I’ve never seen a linebacker that big. I’ve never played with a linebacker that looks like the size of me.’” The 6-foot-5, 255-pound defensive lineman was rightfully impressed by the 6-foot-4, 240-pound linebacker’s size. According to MockDraftable , Walker’s measurements at the 2022 NFL Combine are in the 91st, 61st and 84th percentiles when it comes to height, weight and wingspan (nearly 80 inches), respectively, for the position. It’s worth noting that MockDraftable’s database goes back to 1999, when linebackers were heavier in the NFL, and 240-plus-pound second-level defenders are a rare breed in today’s game. That change is due to the rise of the passing game in the league, shifting the priority to athletic linebackers who can hold up in coverage. Despite what his size might suggest, the Georgia product is also an elite athlete for the position. He tested very well at the combine to earn a 9.63 out of 10 Relative Athletic Score , highlighted by a 4.52-second 40-yard dash (9.65 RAS), 6.89-second three-cone time (9.29) and 10-foot-2 broad jump (8.69). For good measure, he also showed off plenty of strength during the pre-draft process by hitting 23 reps on the bench press. Physically, there’s no reason why Walker isn’t a perennial Pro Bowler and/or All-Pro in the NFL. However, heading into his fifth season, the only postseason recognition the four-year veteran has received so far is a mention on the PFWA’s All-Rookie team in 2022. Walker’s perception around the league does seem to be trending up. He was named an “honorable mention” in Jeremy Fowler of ESPN’s column that polls NFL executives and coaches to rank the top off-ball linebackers, and the quote about the Raiders’ free-agent signing sheds some light on why he hasn’t been a Pro Bowler or All-Pro yet. “The light finally came on for him last year,” an NFC assistant coach told Fowler. “I thought he diagnosed the run game better than in the past. He has always been fast, long and can hit.” When diving into his film this offseason, Walker’s instincts have clearly held him back, especially in coverage. He’ll have a great rep on one play where the physical traits mentioned above stand out, but then turn around and have a mental lapse where it looks like he’s thinking too much and hesitates to give up a first down or worse. For context, Pro Football Focus credited Walker with six forced incompletions during the 2025 regular season, tied for the fourth-most among linebackers. However, PFF also had him on the hook for the second-most receiving touchdowns allowed (five) at the position. Walker’s instincts against the run are better and have improved over the years, as the quote above notes. But he still had moments of not being in the right spot that need to be cleaned up moving forward to reach his potential. So, what should the 26-year-old be focusing on during his first training camp in Las Vegas? The mental part of the game/position. Luckily, the former Bulldog will have a familiar face next to him in college teammate Nakobe Dean , who lacks size at 5-foot-11 and 230 pounds but has great instincts. The former Packer wore the green dot in Green Bay, making him responsible for getting the entire defense lined up correctly. However, in Las Vegas, Dean can take on those duties. That would allow Walker to hone in on his assignment and just play ball, so to speak, rather than having a lot on his plate mentally. In other words, reuniting the 2021 National Champions could help unlock the former first-round pick’s potential.
