title: Las Vegas Raiders Summer Scouting: DT Rankings
summary: I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders do have some […]
full_text: EUGENE, OREGON - NOVEMBER 22: A'Mauri Washington #52 of the Oregon Ducks on the line of scrimmage against the Southern California Trojans at Autzen Stadium on November 22, 2025 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Tom Hauck/Getty Images) | Getty Images I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders do have some talent on the interior OL, and I’d expect Las Vegas to add more in 2027 as John Spytek does. The Raiders defensive tackle room has been an issue for a while, they lack a ton of talent but they have also devoted resources to that position as well. Adam Butler is aging, and Thomas Booker is slated to be a free agent following the 2026 season. Additionally, the Raiders are likely banking on Tonka Hemingway to see a continued breakout in 2026, and if so you feel more confident in the room longterm but need to continue adding talent to the room to pair with those mentioned, JJ Pegues, Brandon Cleveland, and others. These rankings are extremely early, and they will evolve over not only the summer but the next 8-10 months throughout the season, and into draft season. Some lists will feature 10, 15, 20, or more ranked prospects but I’ll include others on the list below to note. A’Mauri Washington, Oregon – 6’3/330, Sr Washington could have declared during the 2026 class, and he’d have been a first rounder but I’d expect him to be a first rounder in 2027. Washington has exceptional strength, elite athleticism, and he does a phenomenal job working across the board. Washington’s frame gives him natural leverage and length advantages, which he utilizes extremely well to his advantage along with his natural core strength. Additionally the senior has an elite pass rush plan, Washington works well laterally, and he shows a ton of upside still despite being near the end of his collegiate career. Washington is best in the run game, but he has shown an ability to be a 4-6 sack defensive tackle in the NFL. David Stone, Oklahoma – 6’3/310, R-So Stone could very easily be the first defensive tackle off the board, he’s an exceptional athlete with elite length, and good strength. Stone plays across the Sooners DL, working a bit at NT, 3T, 2T, and some wide 4/5 technique but he’ll mainly stay on the interior at a 2/3 technique. Stone has a phenomenal bull rush, he converts speed to power well, engages his core & lower body strength through reps, and I like his hand combat skill as well. Stone plays extremely violent, but he relies on the power too often, and he needs to improve the pass rush technique. Stone has great length, but doesn’t utilize it as often as he needs to and there’s also some concerns in the run game where he’s not as much of a staple as he needs to be. AJ Holmes, Texas Tech – 6’3/305, Sr Texas Tech’s defense will follow up a strong season in 2025 with a possible better one in 2026. Holmes transferred to Tech from Houston and he recorded a career year in his first season with the Red Raiders with 38 tackles, 9 TFL, and 4.5 sacks. Holmes now steps into a fulltime starter role, and he has a ton of juice. Holmes plays violent, he has a good bit of lower body twitch, good length, and should take the role as a possible Skyler Gil-Howard replacement. Holmes works exceptionally well laterally, and he showed a good ability vs the run with an ability to dip, drive, and use his strength/speed profile to his advantage. Holmes needs to improve his hand strength, and his punches are inconsistent, but I also have a bit of concerns how well he handles double teams as the true starter. Mateen Ibirogba, Texas Tech – 6’3/295, R-Jr Ibirogba was the premier defensive tackle as a transfer from Wake Forest this portal cycle, and he could skyrocket into the first round despite just 22 tackles, 3.5 TFL, and 2 sacks in his career. Ibirogba transitioned to DT in 2024 from EDGE and he’s flashed brilliance as a pass rusher. Ibirogba is an exceptional athlete, with a ton of lower body agility, good bend, and fluid hips that allows him to push and cut through defenders well. He consistently fires off the ball, has an elite second step, and Ibirogba closes the pocket well while running a fluid loop. The Junior is extremely smart, understands rushing lanes, passing lanes, and blocking concepts which allow him to work through schemes and gaps to pair with his athleticism to beat blocks before they develop. He’ll need to improve in the run game, consistently getting moved around, and there’s a limited depth of pass rush moves with average strength and power. Ibirogba is in a phenomenal scheme at Texas Tech, that should help him develop into a possible top 10 pick. Ahmad Moten, Miami – 6’3/330, Jr The first true NT on this list (Washington is a bit interesting as a tweener 3T/NT). Moten has a stout frame, great length, and his lower body is extremely strong which allows him to push defenders back in the pass game while showing exceptional anchor in the run game. Moten also moves well laterally, showing an ability to slice through defenders more than you’d expect at 330 pounds. He has a quick first step, keeps his pads low, and understands natural leverage where he’ll get up and under offensive lineman. There’s issue in double teams, and Moten is an average pass rusher where he’ll really need to improve his ability to win with more diverse pass rush moves, but the pure run defense and upside is intriguing. Justin Scott, Miami – 6’4/298, R-So Scott is a possible DT1 candidate. He has true 3-Tech size, but plays a lot of 0/1 technique though I’d expect him to shift more into a pass rush focused role for the Hurricanes this year. Scott plays with great athletic ability, he has fluid hips/ankles, shows a good ability to stack and shed lineman, is aggressive at the point of attack, and there’s a lot of lateral flashes in his game. Additionally, I like Scott in the run game, where he’s violent, physical, and uses his athleticism to get into rushing lanes not relying on his strength profile either. There’s some issues with pass rush consistency, and Scott doesn’t always have a good plan outside speed to power, but the run game is exceptional. Scott has true three down potential, and paired with an elite motor he’ll rise. Will Echoles, Ole Miss – 6’3/318, R-So Echoles is young, but he’s both versatile and aggressive. Echoles plays with elite athleticsm, but despite his size I have concerns on the power profile. Echoles does have good natural size, his length is average, but he’s able to move way better than someone at 320 pounds usually will. Ole Miss moved him across the defensive line, he fires off the ball, has a quick second step, and his lower body is extremely athletic allowing him to be fluid and bend well to defeat blocks. I’d like to see him tap into the speed to power more often, and also utilize better pass rush technique, Echoles still logged 70 tackles, 12 TFL, and 5 sacks in his first season starting for the Rebels. Additionally he shows good pad level, an ability to utilize leverage extremely well, and Echoles is exceptionally smart at the position with diverse pass rush moves. The sky is the limit for him as a possible two gap defensive tackle in pass downs. Santana Hopper, Colorado – 6’2/275, Sr Hopper worked from a high school LB, to a standout defensive tackle while going from App State to Tulane, and now Colorado. An exceptional athlete, Hopper does lack some strength but he’s lighting in a bottle. Hopper has an elite first step, fluid hips, and powerful hands that allow him to drive defenders back. He’s an aggressive player, who enjoys the run game, and similar to others above his athleticism jumps off the screen with an innate ability to get into the backfield and slice through blocks. Hopper has a lack of length, but it doesn’t limit him, where…

title: What if Jack Bech doesn’t take next step?
summary: One of the many players the Las Vegas Raiders hope takes a big step forward this season is second-year wide receiver Jack Bech. He was a second-round pick last year. However, the TCU product, was slow to progress as a rookie and ended up not having much of an impact in 2025. He had just […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 14: Jack Bech #18 of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on December 14, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the many players the Las Vegas Raiders hope takes a big step forward this season is second-year wide receiver Jack Bech. He was a second-round pick last year. However, the TCU product, was slow to progress as a rookie and ended up not having much of an impact in 2025. He had just 20 catches for 224 yards as a rookie. He had just seven games with no receptions. So, the team wants to see legitimate progress made for an offense that needs young wide receivers to step up. Bech is a key player because of the draft capital investment the team made in him. So, the expectation is he needs to show immediate progress in the system of new coach Klint Kubiak. However, there are some rumblings that Bech may not exactly be a great fit for Kubiak’s system, so there are no guarantees he will quickly improve in 2026. So, what if the worst-case scenario unfolds and Bech doens’t improve and he isn’t ready to take on a bigger role in 2026? Well, it certainly would hurt the Raiders now and in the future. The team also has fellow 2025 draft pick, Dont’e Thornton. However, the 4th round pick failed to live up to the preseason hype last season and he too may be considered a tough fit for Kubiak’s offense. There is new hype in sixth-round ick Malik Benson and he could get some playing time, but he is a different player than Bech, so even if he develops the Raiders would be missing something that needed for Bech. So, yes, the pressure is on all involved (including general manager John Spytek who drafted Bech) to ensure that he develops in 2026.

title: Raiders news: Will Klint Kubiak become more aggressive on 4th down?
summary: Fourth-down aggression has gotten more common in the NFL among offensive playcallers in recent seasons. Still, some playcallers are more aggressive than others. It appears new Las Vegas Raiders head coach and offensive playcaller Klint Kubiak has been among the least aggresssie play callers on fourth down in recent years. Pro Football focus conducted a […]
full_text: SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 04: Offensive Coordinator Klint Kubiak of the Seattle Seahawks speaks to the media ahead of Super Bowl LX at the San Jose Convention Center on February 04, 2026 in San Jose, California. (Photo by Eakin Howard/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fourth-down aggression has gotten more common in the NFL among offensive playcallers in recent seasons. Still, some playcallers are more aggressive than others. It appears new Las Vegas Raiders head coach and offensive playcaller Klint Kubiak has been among the least aggresssie play callers on fourth down in recent years. Pro Football focus conducted a study of the most and the least aggressive teams on fourth down spanning the 2021-25 NFL seasons. The Seattle Seahawks and San Francisco 49ers went for it on fourth down the least amount of times in that time period. Also, the New Orleans Saints had the second fewest fourth-down conversions in that time span. Kubiak was with those three teams in the past three seasons. So, these stats are not all on Kubiak, but he is part of a trend. It’s not necessarily good or bad if a playcaller is overly aggressive or not. But it will be interesting to see Kubiak’s approach on fourth down as a head coach In other Raiders’ links: D-line rankings: Establish the Run ranks all 32 NFL defensive lines. title: Vikings Training Camp Notes: 8/4 Edition
summary: The Vikings held another training camp practice today, this one in shells. Overall it was a lighter practice- tomorrow’s practice is to be a longer, padded practice, so not as many things to report from this practice, but certainly some tidbids here and there. On the Quarterback Competition Other Notes Today’s Press Conferences That’s all […]
full_text: The Vikings held another training camp practice today, this one in shells. Overall it was a lighter practice- tomorrow’s practice is to be a longer, padded practice, so not as many things to report from this practice, but certainly some tidbids here and there. On the Quarterback Competition It was a decent day for both quarterbacks generally. Both had some mildly good throws between team and redzone drills and some inaccurate ones. Probably more par for the course rather than terribly concerning. No deep bombs again today. Mostly short stuff with some intermediate throws mixed in for both QBs. There was a lot of mixing and matching between 1s and 2s and even 3s today on both sides of the ball. Some of the team drills today looked more like a half-speed install. The offense was working against staff members while the defense was doing the same on the other field. However, it was noteworthy that in the last portion of full-speed team drills that Kyler Murray was exclusively with the first-team and J.J. McCarthy was exclusively with the second-team. Perhaps a sign of things to come. Other Notes I said it yesterday and I’ll say it again today: Charles Demmings looks like the real deal. He had multiple PBUs again today and plays with swagger. So far, he looks like the best draft pick of the bunch. He can be physical, and he may have to tone that down to some degree to avoid penalties, but he plays with confidence no matter which receiver he is up against- and its often either Jefferson, Addison, or Felton. He looked to be getting regular reps with the first-team defense today. Christian Darrisaw did not practice today, nor did Andrew Van Ginkel and I believe Blake Cashman. It was kind of a veteran’s day off today between two padded practices. Domonique Orange was in uniform today, but I didn’t see him participating in team drills. Still, probably a positive sign that he should return sooner rather than later. Demond Claiborne participated in team drills as well, although he had a drop in red zone drills. I watched most of the offensive line drills today and I don’t think there will be a serious challenge to either Blake Brandel or Michael Jurgens at center. Vershon Lee is more cross-training at center but still primarily a guard. I don’t see either Gavin Gerhardt or Walter Rouse making the team at this point, although they have a shot to change that- but probably not a big one. They are last in the pecking order and I’m not sure Rouse will have much of an opportunity to compete at guard. He’s not going to win a roster spot at tackle with Ryan Van Demark and Caleb Tiernan basically roster locks. Jauan Jennings is not a dynamic athlete compared to the other receivers on the roster. He has value as a blocker and can win contested catches with his size and physicality, but he’s not likely to create much separation as a route runner. Tai Felton could earn some reps this year on offense as a more dynamic third wide receiver. Caleb Banks had a few snaps with the first team, but that was it. That was the case yesterday too. They are slowly working him in and hopefully will begin to increase his snap count. Jake Golday had a couple nice plays in run defense- disrupting runs in the backfield Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins continues to work with the first-team and had a nice TFL on a run play. The third-string defensive tackles got more snaps today- this was a practice where backups got more reps generally- including Eric Johnson and Taki Taimani. TE Gavin Bartholomew continues to have a good training camp. He looks like he could end up as TE3. Toward the end of practice, the defense (mostly backups) hollering and trash talking the offense collectively, which prompted Josh Metellus to come on the field as a captain and told the defense to knock it off, in so many words. CB Charles Demmings and WR Jauan Jennings exchanged some shoves at the end of practice on a short reception by Jennings from Murray with Demmings in coverage. Today’s Press Conferences LIVE: Head Coach Kevin O’Connell talks to the media at training camp https://t.co/ZIgUor9fIu — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) August 4, 2026 LIVE: WR Jordan Addison talks to the media at training camp https://t.co/GtwEcLFTcP — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) August 4, 2026 That’s all I have for today. I’ll be back tomorrow. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

title: Jordan Addison Just Got Even More Expensive (Again)
summary: One of the questions that the Minnesota Vikings are going to have to come up with an answer for relatively soon is what to do with wide receiver Jordan Addison. They’ve already picked up the fifth-year option on his rookie contract, which would appear to be the precursor to a long-term extension with the purple, […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 9: Zay Flowers #4 of the Baltimore Ravens and Jordan Addison #3 of the Minnesota Vikings pose for a photo following an NFL football game at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 09, 2025 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the questions that the Minnesota Vikings are going to have to come up with an answer for relatively soon is what to do with wide receiver Jordan Addison. They’ve already picked up the fifth-year option on his rookie contract, which would appear to be the precursor to a long-term extension with the purple, and such an extension just continues to get more and more expensive. On Tuesday morning, the Baltimore Ravens announced that they had signed wide receiver Zay Flowers to a four-year, $140 million contract extension with $108 million in guaranteed money. Those terms are nearly identical to the extension that Justin Jefferson signed two years ago. Jefferson’s extension was also a four-year, $140 million pact with $110 million guaranteed. So, Zay Flowers is, officially, making “Justin Jefferson money.” Flowers and Addison went with back-to-back picks in the 2023 NFL Draft, with the Ravens taking Flowers at #22 overall and the Vikings selecting Addison at #23. Thus far in their careers, Flowers has the edge in receptions (237 to 175) and receiving yardage (3,128 to 2,396, with Flowers going over the 1,000-yard mark twice), while Addison has found the end zone more times than Flowers has (22 touchdowns to 14). Of course, Addison has had to compete with Jefferson for catches, which causes his numbers to take a bit of a hit. Flowers has led the Ravens in receptions in each of his three NFL seasons, while Addison has been the clear #2 wide receiver in the Minnesota offense. Them’s the breaks, I guess. Still, given this contract extension, its tough to imagine a contract extension for Addison coming in below this sort of level. That means the Vikings could, potentially, be paying two wide receivers “Justin Jefferson money,” with one of those receivers being the Justin Jefferson, who is still, arguably, the best wide receiver in football. I know that the Vikings still employ Rob Brzezinski, who is still one of the premiere cap guys in the business. Still, this could prove to be one of the first tests of Nolan Teasley’s priorities as GM of the Vikings. Handling this contract situation with Jordan Addison could prove to be tricky, and it will be interesting to see how the new front office handles it and, just as importantly, when they handle it. After all, I don’t think Addison is going to get any cheaper if the team puts it off or anything.

title: Vikings Training Camp Day 5: Defense Wins, Murray Leads QB Battle
summary: The Minnesota Vikings held their first padded training camp practice at TCO Performance Center, and The Real Forno Show‘s Tyler Forness was there live to break it all down. The headline: the defense dominated, Kyler Murray is outpacing J.J. McCarthy in the quarterback competition, and a fifth-round rookie cornerback may be stealing the show. Here’s […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 01: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during Training Camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 01, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings held their first padded training camp practice at TCO Performance Center, and The Real Forno Show ‘s Tyler Forness was there live to break it all down. The headline: the defense dominated, Kyler Murray is outpacing J.J. McCarthy in the quarterback competition, and a fifth-round rookie cornerback may be stealing the show. Here’s everything Vikings fans need to know from Day 5 of camp. QB Battle Update: Processing Speed Is the Defining Factor The quarterback competition is the story of this camp, and Tyler Forness laid out the clearest picture yet of where things stand. J.J. McCarthy showed improvement over his rough Saturday outing — completing his first three passes and flashing some nice throws — but the same persistent issue remains. “The consistency of the processing is, I think, gonna be the biggest differentiating factor between the two. Murray has it, and McCarthy is still too slow.” — Tyler Forness Forness was pointed about what McCarthy must fix to win the job: “He has to fix that because you watch the talent, he can throw a football. He can do a lot of things. He’s a good leader… But this consistency element and processing, those are two things he does not have, and if he is going to win this job, those are the two things that he needs to have.” Meanwhile, Kyler Murray impressed with his veteran intuition and decision-making, particularly in seven-on-seven drills. A standout moment: Murray cycled through his progressions, found Tai Felton breaking away from coverage, and delivered a perfectly placed ball to the pylon for one of the best catches of camp. “That’s more of, I think, veteran intuition where, ‘Okay, I have nowhere to go with this football, but I need to give my receiver a chance.’ That’s the perfect kind of ball.” — Tyler Forness Key Practice Takeaways — Vikings Training Camp Day 5 Defense won the day — Dallas Turner drew chips from the offensive line, and Ivan Pace was flying around making plays, including a notable pass breakup in 11-on-11 drills J.J. McCarthy recovered from a poor Saturday but processing speed remains the key gap vs. Murray Kyler Murray flashed veteran poise, layered deep over routes with consistency, but threw a concerning late ball to Jordan Addison Tai Felton made arguably the catch of camp, a leaping, one-handed, toe-tap grab at the pylon Myles Price looked noticeably quicker and shiftier, creating six yards of separation on an in-breaking route in one-on-ones Charles “Chuck” Demmings , a fifth-round pick out of Stephen F. Austin (FCS), shadowed Justin Jefferson stride-for-stride in coverage — Forness called him a potential steal Blake Cashman is out with an undisclosed injury; Kevin O’Connell is expected to speak with media soon Jadeveon Clowney signed with the Houston Texans, thinning an already slim edge rusher free agent market for Minnesota Defensive scheme: Forness flagged a developing 3-3-5 defensive look under Brian Flores, utilizing the linebacker trio of Golda, Cashman, and Wilson as key blitzers A Rookie Corner Turning Heads One of the most compelling stories from camp is fifth-round cornerback Charles Demmings. After holding up against Jordan Addison and Justin Jefferson in one-on-one drills, Demmings continued his strong camp by running step-for-step with Jauan Jennings on a seam route and blanketing Jefferson on a corner route. Forness was effusive: “I think Chuck Demmings is a good player. title: Jared Wilson all about getting comfortable in Year 2, from the playbook to his jersey number
summary: Jared Wilson knows that his first season in the NFL was anything but a walk in the park. The 2025 third-round draft pick may have started 17 games as the New England Patriots’ left guard, but he went through his fair share of rookie growing pains as well. Now in his second season, however, Wilson […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 4: New England Patriots center Jared Wilson talks to reporters during training camp at Gillette Stadium on August 4, 2025. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Jared Wilson knows that his first season in the NFL was anything but a walk in the park. The 2025 third-round draft pick may have started 17 games as the New England Patriots’ left guard, but he went through his fair share of rookie growing pains as well. Now in his second season, however, Wilson is in a different position — both figuratively and literally. It all contributed to him being more comfortable than he was a year ago. “I definitely had my struggles, for sure. The learning curve, it was a lot,” Wilson admitted after Tuesday’s training camp practice at Gillette Stadium. That learning curve has begun to flatten now, particularly when it comes to the playbook. “The big thing was just the playbook,” he said. “Anybody who’s questioning themselves during a play is automatically going to slow down during the play. That was definitely the biggest learning curve, the playbook.” Better understanding the playbook is a big part of Wilson making strides in Year 2. The same is true for being able to purposefully watch film. “Learning to watch film better,” he said about positive changes to his preparatory process. “Not just watching plays, seeing the play, skip, seeing the play, skip — but actually looking at stuff like stances, how leveraged the linebackers are, if they’re bumped to they’re backside, if they’re bumped frontside. Just honing in on the little things that give away the big things.” The little things proved to be a challenge for Wilson in 2025, partially because he was learning a new position. This year, the circumstances are different. Despite being inserted as the Patriots’ left guard and holding the job throughout the season, Wilson changed positions this spring. With Garrett Bradbury getting traded to Chicago, the road was clear for him to move back to his college position at center. While that means a return to familiar territory for the 23-year-old, it also means he has to build a rapport with Drake Maye quickly. “Reps, that’s literally what it is,” Wilson said about establishing the center-quarterback connection. “As many times as you can do it, the better it’s going to get. Just reps and communication.” Wilson sounded optimistic about his chemistry with Maye, and about going back to center in general. Helping him with that move was another seemingly far less consequential change: after wearing No. 58 on his jersey as a rookie, he has now gone back to the No. 55 he donned at the University of Georgia. It’s all part of the process. “I just wanted to go back to 55,” he explained. “I was talking to my wife about it and she thought it was a good idea. I thought it was a good idea, too. Just getting back to being comfortable.”

title: What claiming Tejhaun Palmer, waiving Jeremiah Franklin means for the Patriots
summary: The New England Patriots stay busy tweaking the back-end of their roster. On Tuesday, they made a pair of transactions: wide receiver Tejhaun Palmer was claimed off waivers following his release from the Arizona Cardinals, while tight end Jeremiah Franklin was let go in a corresponding move. Let’s find out what all of that means […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tight end Jeremiah Franklin (80) does a drill during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots stay busy tweaking the back-end of their roster. On Tuesday, they made a pair of transactions : wide receiver Tejhaun Palmer was claimed off waivers following his release from the Arizona Cardinals, while tight end Jeremiah Franklin was let go in a corresponding move. Let’s find out what all of that means for Mike Vrabel’s team. Reactionary move? Among the “other” wide receivers on the Patriots’ roster, Cameron Dorner had arguably been the best so far this summer. The potential practice squad candidate was among the absentees from Tuesday’s practice , however, which might have prompted New England to take action. Time will tell whether or not the two situations are related, but with Dorner absent New England had only three non-roster candidate wideouts available in practice. Fact also is that the two are both similar players in terms of positional usage — both are outside receivers first — and size. With both now on the roster, the wide receiver group looks as follows: Wide receiver (12): A.J. Brown (1), Romeo Doubs (87), DeMario Douglas (3), Kayshon Boutte (9), Mack Hollins (13), Kyle Williams (18), Efton Chism III (86), Cameron Dorner (88), Kyle Dixon (83), Nick DeGennaro (23), Kobe Prentice (19), Tejhaun Palmer (—) IR (2): Jimmy Kibble, Jeremiah Webb The first seven names on that list are realistically fighting for spots on the 53-man roster. The rest, which now includes Palmer, will be competing for a limited number of practice squad opportunities. Another high-end athlete Even though it would never say so and instead go with the old “we’re looking for good football players” adage, there is no denying New England’s current regime has a type: it wants to improve the roster’s athleticism through its acquisitions, and Palmer very much fits the bill. Like Monday free agency signing Casey Rogers , the newest Patriot is a high-end athlete. A look at the newest Patriot through the eyes of @mathbomb.bsky.social's Relative Athletic Score.What stands out about Tejhaun Palmer? His speed. — Bernd Buchmasser (@berndbuchmasser.bsky.social) 2026-08-04T21:55:58.875Z Entering the third season of his NFL career, Palmer has not yet been able to take full advantage of his size/speed combination. The 2024 sixth-round draft pick has played just six non-preseason snaps in his lone in-game appearance over the last two years, and has no statistics to his name. Whether his fortunes will change in Foxborough can be questioned, but that does not mean he has no skill especially athletically. Tight end picture clearing up The second shoe to drop on Tuesday was the release of backup tight end Jeremiah Franklin, an undrafted rookie tight end out of Boston College who just joined the team ahead of training camp. With Franklin out of the picture, the Patriots are now down to six tight ends. Tight end (6): Hunter Henry (85), Eli Raridon (82), Tanner Arkin (84), Jack Westover (37), C.J. Dippre (81), Mitch Van Vooren (46) After nine training camp practices, there appears to be a clear pecking order at the position. Hunter Henry is the undisputed TE1, as he has been since arriving in 2021; third-round rookie Eli Raridon is the second option and a potential heir apparent to Henry; undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin, one of the surprises of camp, is the current TE3 due to his abilities as a blocker. Outside of those three, the group has been quiet this summer. In fact, on Tuesday, only one of that depth trio — Mitch Van Vooren — was even present at practice: C.J. Dippre remains on the physically unable to perform list, while TE/FB hybrid Jack Westover did not participate. No cap changes Releasing Franklin creates no sudden cap charge for the Patriots, and neither does claiming Palmer off waivers. The former was on a minimum deal for a player of his experience, as was the latter. And with no guarantees embedded into either pact, the moves involving those do not leave a trace on New England’s salary cap. Just like on Monday, cap expert Miguel Benzan has the Patriots $33.7 million under the salary cap .
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 7 performances of note from the Patriots’ ninth training camp practice
summary: After one day without an audience, the New England Patriots returned to the fields behind Gillette Stadium on Tuesday for their ninth practice of training camp. The fans were treated to an entertaining session. To recap it, please visit our Patriots training camp notebook. In the meantime, here is who caught our eye during the […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 30: New England Patriots wide receivers A.J. Brown and Kayshon Boutte at training camp on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images After one day without an audience, the New England Patriots returned to the fields behind Gillette Stadium on Tuesday for their ninth practice of training camp. The fans were treated to an entertaining session. To recap it, please visit our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eye during the two-hour session. Standout of the day The deep passing game: Kayshon Boutte, A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins, the biggest top-level receivers on New England’s roster, made several big plays on Tuesday. Their stat lines show how involved they were: Boutte caught a team-leading five passes in team drills, followed by Brown and Hollins hauling in four receptions each. Boutte did most of his damage against the second-string defense, and remains the factual WR4 behind Brown, Romeo Doubs and DeMario Douglas, but it is clear just how much trust both Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito have in him. He rewarded that trust with multiple downfield receptions on Tuesday — including in both QB’s two-minute drill situations. The same was true for Hollins, whose most notable play was a deep sideline shot from DeVito for what would have been a 40-plus-yard touchdown in a true game setting. Overall, the veteran has been productive the last two days and continues to be a key target in select situations. Brown, meanwhile, showed no signs of limitation from his dislocated thumb. In fact, the offseason trade pickup looked no less impressive than he had after suffering the injury on Monday. He did not have the same highlight-reel plays that Boutte and Hollins produced, but he still caught all four of his targets, including three on slants from Maye. Other performances of note RB Terrell Jennings: Outside of what was roughly a 15-yard run, Jennings did not have any true standout moments on Monday. What qualifies him for this here list is something else: in his second practice back from the non-football injury list, he was part of the top punt team and the first running back up with the second-stringers. This meant that he took the spot in the rotation previously held by Lan Larison, who himself remains ahead of Jam Miller. There is a long way to go still, but that appears to be the current pecking order in the team’s eyes. ED Dre’Mont Jones and ED Elijah Ponder: New England’s top pass rush duo had a productive day on Tuesday. Dre’Mont Jones, who lined up all over the defensive line, registered a pair of would-be sacks and another pressure against Drake Maye, while Ponder brought consistent pressure from the edge as well and in addition broke up a Maye pass intended for Hunter Henry. CB Channing Canada: The Patriots’ depth cornerback competition is one of the most intriguing on the roster, with nobody yet to truly elevate himself to earn a fifth and potential sixth spot behind Christian Gonzalez, Carlton Davis, Marcus Jones and Charles Woods. One of the issues is consistency, and Channing Canada fell victim to it on Tuesday. The undrafted free agent gave up big catches to both Mack Hollins and Kayshon Boutte as part of the second-string defense. Coming off a strong practice on Monday, it was a step back. CB Kobee Minor: While he did give up a handful of catches including to Kayshon Boutte and A.J. Brown, Minor had a positive day overall Tuesday — a step in the right direction after a handful of challenging practices. He was competitive in coverage even on those receptions and also broke up a Behren Morton pass intended for Kyle Dixon. He later got his revenge on Boutte by forcing an incompletion on a curl route, and registered what would be a run stuff in a game situation. He also saw reps with the starter defense as well as the third-stringers. K Andy Borregales: New England’s kicker continued his good training camp on Tuesday, splitting the uprights on all seven of his field goal attempts. He had five regular tries of up to 52 yards and later also a pair of “pressure” kicks in two-minute situations — one from 49 and the other from 54 yards. He was perfect on both and we now have the second-year kicker with 28 successful kicks this summer on 30 attempts. Other players worth mentioning include linebackers Chad Muma and Khalil Jacobs. The former remains the third off-ball linebacker, while the latter appears to have overtaken veteran free agency pickup K.J. Britt in the race for the LB4 role. In front of them, second-year DT Joshua Farmer had arguably his most impactful practice of the summer. The Patriots will hold their tenth practice of training camp on Wednesday, which is expected to be a walkthrough. Practice is scheduled to kick off at 10:00 a.m. ET.

title: Patriots claim former Cardinals wideout Tejhaun Palmer, waive rookie tight end
summary: The New England Patriots circled back to the wire after the ninth practice of training camp. The organization officially claimed wide receiver Tejhaun Palmer off waivers from the Arizona Cardinals on Tuesday afternoon. In a corresponding 91-man roster move, tight end Jeremiah Franklin was placed on waivers. Palmer, 26, entered the NFL in the sixth […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - AUGUST 9: Wide receiver Tejhaun Palmer #83 of the Arizona Cardinals raises his arms towards the fans during the pregame warmups before the NFL Preseason 2025 game between Kansas City Chiefs and Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on August 9, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Bruce Yeung/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots circled back to the wire after the ninth practice of training camp. The organization officially claimed wide receiver Tejhaun Palmer off waivers from the Arizona Cardinals on Tuesday afternoon. In a corresponding 91-man roster move, tight end Jeremiah Franklin was placed on waivers. Palmer, 26, entered the NFL in the sixth round of the 2024 draft at No. 191 overall. The 6-foot-2, 210-pound wide receiver by way of Snow College and UAB spent the majority of his initial two regular seasons on the Cardinals’ practice squad. Ahead of Arizona’s finale last January, Palmer was promoted to the 53-man roster. He saw four snaps on offense to go with two snaps on special teams in his debut and was waived on Monday. Franklin, 22, had signed in Foxborough as an undrafted free agent leading up to training camp in July. The 6-foot-3, 244-pound tight end out of Boston College did so after participating in the Patriots’ local pro day as well as rookie minicamp on a tryout basis. During his tenure in Chestnut Hill, Franklin appeared in 44 games, including 30 starts, on the way to catching 93 passes for 1,010 yards and six touchdowns. The Patriots move further into August with 12 wide receivers on the active depth chart. And after losing veteran Julian Hill to injured reserve in June, the tight end room stands at six, including C.J. Dippre on the physically unable to perform list. A closed walkthrough practice is scheduled for 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday.

title: Patriots training camp recap: Big receivers shine in late-game situations
summary: The New England Patriots donned full pads for their fifth straight practice as work moved back outside of the red zone and outside on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. Here’s what went down throughout the two-hour session. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton Davis, TE Jack Westover (new), FB Reggie Gilliam (rest), OG Caedan Wallace, WR […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 01: New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown (1) and New England Patriots wide receiver Mack Hollins (13) warms up during training camp on August 1, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. (Photo by M. Anthony Nesmith/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots donned full pads for their fifth straight practice as work moved back outside of the red zone and outside on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. Here’s what went down throughout the two-hour session. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton Davis, TE Jack Westover (new), FB Reggie Gilliam (rest), OG Caedan Wallace, WR Cameron Dorner (new) Returnee: WR Kyle Williams, DT David Blay Jr. Limited: OT Morgan Moses (rest), DL Christian Barmore (rest) PUP/NFI: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler The Patriots continued to manage several veterans’ workloads, while Kyle Williams was upgraded to a full participant after arriving late and observing practice on Monday. Tight end Jack Westover and wide receiver Cameron Dorner were then a pair of new absences on the offensive side of the football. Takeaways Two-minute: For the first-time this summer, the Patriots repped an end-of-half situation with the ball on the 20-yard line and 1:05 on the clock. After missing a first-down throw over the middle to Romeo Doubs, Drake Maye found two short completions before getting the needed chunk play to Mack Hollins over the middle of the field. A short slant to A.J. Brown worked the unit into field goal range as they let the clock tick down to :04. Andy Borregales then connected on a 54-yard field goal. Tommy DeVito’s second group found similar success, again with Mack Hollins providing a pair of chunk plays — in addition to a reception from Kayshon Boutte while working the sideline — to reach field goal range. Borregales then knocked through a 49-yard attempt. Automatic A.J.: Despite dislocating his thumb on Monday, wide receiver A.J. Brown was a full participant on Tuesday appearing to wear just a small bandage under his gloves. “I think he’s going to be okay,“ Mike Vrabel said. ”I told him the linemen do that every other snap, and it’s not a national story when a lineman pops his finger back in place. But we had a little bit of fun with that.“ After a slow start from Drake Maye that included connecting on just one his first five throws — including a miscommunication with Brown — the QB ended the day strong going 8-of-9 (excluding two spikes). That included connecting with Brown four times as they remained automatic on slants (three catches) in addition to a back shoulder ball to Kayshon Boutte, who finished his day with five receptions (two from Maye). Splitting the uprights: Sophomore kicker Andy Borregales continued his strong summer connecting on all five of his field goal attempts with a max distance of 52 yards. Borregales then tacked on two “pressure” kicks from distance to conclude the aforementioned two-minute drives. Our tracking now has Borregales as 28-of-30 this training camp. “He’s made the majority of his field goals, a high majority,” Vrabel said before practice. “I think that that’s something that’s a fine balance of where you want your kicker to be. If you feel good about the competition or the job that he did last year, then I’ll just try to evaluate that each week. I think he’s continuing to work with Tom [Quinn] on his steps, the consistency and everything else.” Edge pressure: New England’s top two edge rushers — Dre’Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder — were active in the fully padded practice. Early in competitive periods, Ponder recorded a pass breakup dropping out in coverage before appearing to beat Morgan Moses around the edge. The veteran Jones then ended the day strong appearing to get home for potentially two would-be sacks. Behind them, rookie Gabe Jacas saw his workload slightly increase again in his third practice of the summer. “These situations he has to just understand, and it’s good to see him get acclimated to the special team stuff. So, I think it’s going well,” Vrabel said of Jacas. “I think we’re off to a good start, and hopefully he can continue to keep adding things and figure out where he can help us defensively and really, special teams.” Other notes: In Kyle Williams’ return, he caught his lone target from Tommy DeVito and was open downfield for a potential walk-in touchdown during two-minute but was overthrown. Fellow second-year receiver Efton Chism caught two passes from DeVito and continued to be sprinkled in with the top offense. UDFA wide receiver Nick DeGennaro made a nice downfield adjustment to connect with Behren Morton on a deep ball. Back off the NFI list, Terrell Jennings received the first reps with the second-team offense before Lan Larison worked in. After dropping his lone full-team target on Monday, it was another quiet day for Eli Raridon without a target on Tuesday. The Patriots run game continued to not find much success against the defensive front. Joshua Farmer was in the backfield on one instance to blow up a Rhamondre Stevenson run. Chad Muma continued to serve as the Patriots third linebacker in base defense and again found himself around the football multiple times. After a competitive practice on Monday, UDFA cornerback Channing Canada was on the wrong side of multiple completions. Kobee Minor gave up multiple catches as well but also broke up a pass intended for Kyle Dixon. Rookie cornerback Karon Prunty worked through a block to blow up a screen to Lan Larison. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Wednesday for a walkthrough, which is set to begin at 10:00 a.m. ET.

title: Patriots training camp primer: Day 9 practice preview, schedule, more
summary: The New England Patriots are in the middle of a challenging training camp stretch, with Tuesday’s session the second in a string of five straight. The expectation is that the team will once again be in full pads, which suggests that the level of competition and physicality will remain high. With that said, here is […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 1: New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas runs during training camp at Gillette Stadium on August 1, 2026. (Photo by Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots are in the middle of a challenging training camp stretch, with Tuesday’s session the second in a string of five straight. The expectation is that the team will once again be in full pads, which suggests that the level of competition and physicality will remain high. With that said, here is what you need to know about camp practice No. 9. Schedule After Monday’s session was moved indoors due to inclement weather, practice will be taking place on the fields behind Gillette Stadium on Tuesday. This, in turn, means that fans will be able to attend the session again. 9:30 a.m. ET: Mike Vrabel press conference 10:15 a.m. ET: Practice ca. 12:15 p.m. ET: Player availability (RB TreVeyon Henderson, WR DeMario Douglas, C Jared Wilson, ED Dre’Mont Jones, ED Gabe Jacas, LB Namdi Obiazor) As always, of course, the schedule is tentative and subject to change. For more information, please visit our Pats Pulpit Training Camp Guide . Story of the day How is A.J. Brown looking one day after dislocating his thumb ? The Patriots’ star offseason addition admitted after Monday’s session that he hurt his thumb, but that it was popped back in. He finished practice with four catches, including three during 11-on-11s, and no visible limitations. However, it remains to be seen whether or not his status changes heading into another fully-padded practice. Injuries to monitor NFI: S Brenden Schooler PUP: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III Practice absentees: OL Caedan Wallace, DT David Blay Jr, CB Carlton Davis III New injuries: WR A.J. Brown Monday’s practice saw running back Terrell Jennings return from the non-football injury list, adding a new dimension to the competition for the third running back spot. In the meantime, Carlton Davis has now missed a week’s worth of practices, with Caedan Wallace also out after getting banged up on Saturday. David Blay Jr’s absence could be related to the signing of fellow defensive tackle Casey Rogers , who took his jersey number in what might be an ominous sign for the undrafted rookie. Players to watch OL James Hudson III: A reserve offensive tackle entering camp, Hudson saw some action at guard on Monday. For the offseason signing, who has had his issues throughout the summer, adding a second position might be the difference between a spot on the roster or practice squad and being cut for good. ED Gabe Jacas: The Patriots’ second-round draft pick managed to up his participation level on Monday, but he remains limited. Will Tuesday see him further add to his workload? And if so, will he begin challenging Elijah Ponder for starter reps on the edge? LB Chad Muma: The linebacker depth chart behind Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss remains unsettled, but Muma looks like the current frontrunner for the third spot. He spent some time with the starters on Monday and looked good particularly as a run defender. Him playing a similar role again on Tuesday might be a sign that he has taken the lead in the LB3 competition. The backup cornerbacks: Speaking of competitions, the one for the fifth and possible sixth cornerback spots is heating up. On Monday, rookies Channing Canada and Karon Prunty were among the standout performers , while Marcella Dial Jr. also remains part of the mix. Kindle Vildor and Kobee Minor, meanwhile, have seemingly slipped over the last few sessions. Pats Pulpit will have you covered throughout the day, so please make sure to regularly check back to patspulpit.com for all the latest news from camp. Credentialed Patriots beat writers Brian Hines ( @iambrianhines ), Andrew Guindon ( @NestPgs ) and Taylor Kyles ( @tkyles39 ) will bring you live updates from camp on their Twitter/X feeds, so please make sure to give them a follow.

title: Patriots secondary emphasizing takeaways as practice intensity heats up
summary: The New England Patriots’ secondary is looking to generate more takeaways during training camp. After Monday’s practice moved indoors due to heavy rainfall, increased verbal banter from both the offense and defense fuels friendly competition between the two sides. New England’s third-year safety Dell Pettus helped spark that competitive energy for the defensive backs after […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JUNE 02: Dell Pettus #24 of the New England Patriots walks on to the field during New England Patriots OTA on June 2, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ secondary is looking to generate more takeaways during training camp. After Monday’s practice moved indoors due to heavy rainfall, increased verbal banter from both the offense and defense fuels friendly competition between the two sides. New England’s third-year safety Dell Pettus helped spark that competitive energy for the defensive backs after picking off a Drake Maye deep pass on Saturday . That turnover marked just the defense’s second interception this summer through the first seven sessions. “It was definitely a great feeling,” Pettus said of the pick following Monday’s practice. “Just trusting the process, the scheme and the technique. It’s something that we talk about all the time — it’s just like, do your job. You can do your job one million times, be in a good spot, and never get the ball your way. But we have a really good quarterback, so he rarely makes bad decisions.” After the play concluded, Pettus ran toward the end zone and punted the ball over the fence in celebration of securing the first defensive takeaway since day two of summer camp. That energy stems from a conversation the safeties had before that practice. “In that situation, I just think I was able to be in a good spot, get rewarded and make a good play,” Pettus added. “The defense needed that. We were talking about getting more takeaways at practice and getting more turnovers. And I think [the pick] was just like an energizer at practice.” Veteran Kevin Byard led that conversation. The Patriots’ free-agency signing spent six seasons with the Tennessee Titans under Mike Vrabel, and he’s carrying the same edge and competitive mindset as his head coach does in the safety’s first year in New England. “After those first few practices, [Byard] brought us up, and he was like, ‘We need takeaways today,’” Pettus shared. “Before we went to any competitive team activity, he said, ‘We need more takeaways; we’re going to go out here and go get the football. Forget what everybody else is talking about; forget what the coaches talk about. This is our team. This is our defensive backfield.’ And like, it’s up to us to go get it, because the coaches can’t play for us. And I told him I thought that was great to hear just because he set the tone for us that day.” Byard acknowledged that the intensity in training camp is “heating up,” and that’s what this time of the offseason is for. A frequent matchup this summer has been between A.J. Brown and Christian Gonzalez. Brown secured a pass from Maye under smothering coverage from Gonzalez during Monday’s seven-on-seven period and turned to the cornerback with friendly banter. “I think it was competitive. You know, a heavy emphasis on [the] red zone,” Byard said about Monday’s session. “We got some really competitive periods, whether it was one-on-ones or team … Obviously it’s still early in training camp, so it’s a lot of back and forth. But it’s been fun. I think it’s just the competitive spirit of this team at every position and level. Offense and defense [are] just trying to get better, and I think we’re pushing each other.” Entering his 11th year in the NFL, Byard is coming off a First-Team All-Pro selection, leading the league with seven interceptions for a new career total of 36. Adding a ball hawk like Byard not only elevates outcomes on the field for New England in 2026 but also impacts the development of the safety corps. “How to get the football,” Pettus said of what he’s learned from Byard thus far. “He’s such an impressive guy … But he came in week one, and he’s asking our coaches and challenging them about why we’re doing things and how that’s going to help us get the football. As a young defensive back, you always want the football, but hearing that’s his process no matter what he’s doing, it’s, ‘How am I going to get the football? What can I do to get myself in a better position to get the football?’ “I took a step back, and I was like, I don’t think I ever really thought like that … He’s really breaking it down in a science-type of way of where am I going to be and how am I putting myself in a position to get the football? Because if I can’t get the football, I’m not doing my job. You can tell he’s a veteran and why he led this league in interceptions last season. I look forward to working with him this season because I feel like all he’s going to do is help me and everybody around him be a better player.”
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Drake Maye breaks down the Patriots wide receiver room
summary: The New England Patriots wide receiver room is one of the deepest position groups on the roster. Following the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason, New England’s top seven now features Brown, Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kayshon Boutte, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. Rather than viewing the room as crowded, […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 28: New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and wide receiver Mack Hollins shake hands at training camp on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots wide receiver room is one of the deepest position groups on the roster. Following the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason, New England’s top seven now features Brown, Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kayshon Boutte, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. Rather than viewing the room as crowded, Drake Maye sees it as competitive. Appearing on SiriusXM NFL Radio on Monday, the quarterback broke down the group, starting with his two newest targets. “Start off the bat with A.J., having him coming in and kind of set the tone for the room. I think him and Romeo — the guys in there, they’ve really enjoyed the competitive drive in that room. People say it’s a crowded room but, as you know as receivers go, you’re going to need everybody. “With A.J., the ability for him to not only make me look good, but go out there and make plays and catch the football; we were watching some of his ‘target tape’ the other day, and him being able to take a slant, take an under, and take it to the house. But at the same time he has route craft and he knows you can’t just win everything physically. At some point, you have to use routes, use his technique, and he does a great job. “I think Romeo has done a great job coming in here and learning the offense. He hasn’t been in an offense like this that has some decision-making [for receivers]. I think he’s getting better and better as he’s gotten through OTAs and even in camp, he’s making some great plays for us. He’s kind of shifty and has a little wiggle to him that I didn’t really expect throwing to him in camp.” Through eight training camp practices, Maye’s chemistry with both Brown and Doubs has progressed nicely. When the offense breaks the huddle in 11 personnel, those two are stapled on Maye’s sides. In the slot, however, has primarily been DeMario Douglas. “Next up, we have Pop in the slot,” Maye said. “I think Pop’s the one from last year that’s just continuing to get better and better. You see it every year. From my rookie year being with him to Year 3 now, just kind of the connection and knowing how he runs routes. I think he does a great job in man; it’s hard to cover him. So he’s going to be a big piece of what we do when we’re in ‘11’ personnel. I’m looking forward to seeing how he continues to grow and make more plays this year. I think he definitely will.” Last season, veteran free agent addition Mack Hollins led all Patriots wide receivers playing 68 percent of the offensive snaps. Hollins turned in a productive season catching 46 passes for 550 yards while being a strong veteran presence in the locker room. “Mack is kind of the Swiss-Army knife. He does it all,” Maye explained. “He’s obviously big in the run game, but I think Coach [McDaniels] rewards him with play-action off it. So he always says, ‘Just throw it to me on the in-cuts.’ He loves [that]. He’s big and has that demeanor to him that people feed off, that energy about him.” New England’s wide receiver room then features a pair of second-year players in Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III, who are both pushing for larger roles this season. “Kyle, last year, was kind of a big-play guy,” Maye said. “I think he’s worked hard to be able to [run] different routes and be able to build his route-arsenal coming into his second year. I’m looking forward to seeing how that goes. And obviously he’s a deep threat, he’s fast, can run by people – which is always something the defense has to think about. “Then Chis, you can’t forget about Efton Chism. He kind of became one of those guys late in the season when Mack got hurt, he had a role where we tried to replace what Mack does. I think the biggest thing with Chis is he’s just doing the right things and making a lot of plays. He was a big preseason guy last year and so he’ll probably continue to make plays.” Last but not least, Maye mentioned wide receiver Kayshon Boutte. The twos chemistry has been apparent over their two seasons together, but the 24-year old has been in the middle of trade talks this offseason as he enters the last year of his rookie contract and has been pushed down the depth chart. “Probably the last one is Boutte,” Maye said. “He’s a comforting receiver to throw to. You get to know him – same thing as Pop, this is my third year with Boutte and I was throwing to him on scout team when I was a rookie. Now we’re making plays; I threw my first touchdown to him. He’s just one of those guys that is quiet, does everything the right way, cares about his teammates, and he just puts his head down and works. There’s a lot of talk about whatever you want to say with Boutte, but he just continues to make plays. He’s going to be in the right spot and make a play on the football.” Whether there is any significance to Maye mentioning Boutte last is unknown. It is notable, however, that the quarterback also did not mention Boutte when discussing his pass catchers last week, instead highlighting Brown, Doubs, Douglas, tight end Hunter Henry, and running backs Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. How the logjam at wide receiver resolves itself is a question that will be answered later this summer. But for now, it is a good problem to have with all seven off to a strong start this training camp.

title: Saints kick off their 2026 season with 50/50 Raffle to benefit local organizations
summary: Earlier today, the New Orleans Saints announced their 2026 50/50 Raffle initiative beneficiaries. Now entering its 11th season, the 50/50 Raffle has become a cornerstone of the Saints’ philanthropic efforts, supporting a diverse array of charitable causes and nonprofit organizations throughout the region. During the 2026 season, proceeds from the 50/50 Raffle will benefit more […]
full_text: Earlier today, the New Orleans Saints announced their 2026 50/50 Raffle initiative beneficiaries. Now entering its 11th season, the 50/50 Raffle has become a cornerstone of the Saints’ philanthropic efforts, supporting a diverse array of charitable causes and nonprofit organizations throughout the region. During the 2026 season, proceeds from the 50/50 Raffle will benefit more than 19 nonprofit organizations across Louisiana, each of which plays a vital role in serving local communities. title: Jonas Sanker on developing at the Star position
summary: During his media availability after Monday’s training camp, New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker was asked about watching players like Jalen Ramsey play in the slot. It was a great question because Ramsey played the position while Brandon Staley was his defensive coordinator with the Los Angeles Rams. Sanker went on to explain that Ramsey […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 30: Jonas Sanker #33 of the New Orleans Saints participates in drills during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 30, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images During his media availability after Monday’s training camp, New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker was asked about watching players like Jalen Ramsey play in the slot. It was a great question because Ramsey played the position while Brandon Staley was his defensive coordinator with the Los Angeles Rams. Sanker went on to explain that Ramsey wasn’t the only player he has studied because Ramsey possesses such a unique skill set that you can’t, and really shouldn’t, try to play exactly like him. Instead, Sanker said he has leaned on the resources available to him within the building. Justin Reid, Julian Blackmon, and Terrell Burgess have all played in the slot as well. Burgess, specifically, played the position under Staley, making him a valuable resource. You can already see the growth Sanker is making early in camp. The extra work and veteran leadership appear to be paying off, as he has consistently been making plays throughout camp. Sanker also praised Blackmon, mentioning how he has been able to make plays for the defense as well. Sanker was also asked if his experience playing safety has helped him now that he’s lining up closer to the line of scrimmage. He said that his background at safety has definitely benefited him. At safety, you’re taught to be patient because if you make a mistake, the other safety has to clean it up and make you right. Now that he’s playing closer to the line, he understands exactly what the safeties behind him are seeing because he has played that position himself. That experience allows him to fit his assignments properly and avoid putting the safety in a position where they have to compensate for his mistakes. Sanker appears to have a firm grasp on the star position and is showing early signs of success.

title: Julian Blackmon embracing fresh start after injury-shortened first season with Saints
summary: After signing with the New Orleans Saints as a free agent last offseason, veteran safety Julian Blackmon appeared in just one game before suffering a season-ending shoulder injury that sidelined him for the remaining 16 games. Now healthy, Blackmon says the experience has changed the way he approaches football. “I feel like that’s exactly how […]
full_text: After signing with the New Orleans Saints as a free agent last offseason, veteran safety Julian Blackmon appeared in just one game before suffering a season-ending shoulder injury that sidelined him for the remaining 16 games. Now healthy, Blackmon says the experience has changed the way he approaches football. “I feel like that’s exactly how I approached the offseason—just humbly,” Blackmon said after practice. “Because something that’s given to you can be just as quickly taken away.” Blackmon’s 2025 season came to a disappointing end in the Saints’ season opening loss to the Arizona Cardinals. Despite suffering what was later diagnosed as a posterior labrum tear in his right shoulder, he finished the game, playing every defensive snap while recording seven tackles and a pass breakup. It wasn’t until the following day that the severity of the injury became clear, ultimately landing him on injured reserve for the rest of the season. Looking back, Blackmon said the setback was a reality check of just how quickly things can change in the NFL. “For me, obviously, my career has been trials and errors. A lot of hardships, but at the same time, a lot of gratitude,” he said. “So just being out there with my guys again, remembering what it feels like to be in pads again, it’s a blessing. That’s how I approached the offseason and how I approach the season coming up.” Although his regular season lasted just one game, Blackmon believes he left enough of an impression during last year’s training camp to earn the coaching staff’s confidence heading into 2026. “I felt like I was doing really well in training camp last year,” Blackmon said. “The coaches felt like I did enough and they saw enough to know that if I came back and was able to get a full season, things would be really good. It’d benefit the whole team.” That confidence has only fueled his excitement entering his second year in The Big Easy. “We like to say, ‘Together we eat,’ and I’m excited for my opportunity this year because I feel like we can do that with me on the field,” he said. Blackmon is also optimistic about what the Saints’ safety tandem can become alongside veteran Justin Reid. With both players entering their second season under defensive coordinator Brandon Staley, the Blackmon believes their familiarity with the system has put them in position to take a significant step forward. “It’s a possibility,” Blackmon said when asked if he and Reid can become one of the league’s top safety duos. “I feel like both of us have a good understanding of what we want to get done. Year two under Staley helps a lot. We feel a lot more comfortable.” Blackmon added that communication has been one of the biggest reasons for their growing chemistry during their time in New Orleans. “There’s a lot of different caveats that we have in each coverage, but because we are very communicative with each other, it makes it a lot easier,” he said. “That’s something that I don’t see too out of reach for us to go for.” After losing almost an entire season to injury, Blackmon is no longer taking the opportunity to play for granted. If he can stay healthy, the Saints believe they’ll finally get the player they signed a year ago.

title: Isaiah Likely wants to show Giants made ‘right choice’ by signing him
summary: It wasn’t a surprise when John Harbaugh started bringing players he coached with the Baltimore Ravens to the New York Giants in free agency. After all, while Harbaugh believed that the Giants’ roster was close to competing, he still wanted players who were steeped in his culture to help him build a winning culture in […]
full_text: New York Giants tight end Isaiah Likely during practice. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It wasn’t a surprise when John Harbaugh started bringing players he coached with the Baltimore Ravens to the New York Giants in free agency. After all, while Harbaugh believed that the Giants’ roster was close to competing, he still wanted players who were steeped in his culture to help him build a winning culture in New York. The crown jewel of that free agent class is tight end Isaiah Likely , who the Baltimore Ravens drafted out of Coastal Carolina University in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL Draft. Likely spent the next four years as Baltimore’s second tight end, living in the shadow of All-Pro tight end Mark Andrews. But while he never quite got enough of an opportunity to establish himself as a star, he did earn Harbaugh’s admiration — enough so that the Giants made Likely one of the highest-paid tight ends in the NFL despite never eclipsing 45 receptions or 480 yards in a season. “I sure hope he’s a big weapon,” Harbaugh said. “I hope he’s a guy that makes a bunch of plays for us. That’s why we brought him here.” Likely gave props to Andrews for helping him develop. “He’s taught me a lot since I’ve come in the league,” Likely said following Tuesday’s practice. “Being able to just understand zones, to be able to just go out there, run freely and just let my talent shine. So, I feel like Mark’s brought me to the point now where I feel like being myself, being a star caliber tight end that I see myself being.” Likely was never a particularly productive tight end for the Ravens, but he did develop a good chemistry with quarterback Lamar Jackson and the two routinely hooked up when the play went off-script. That experience should help Likely establish a rapport with Giants’ quarterback Jaxson Dart, who likewise embraces chaos. “They’re both dogs,” Likely said. “And I’d say, with Jax [Dart], it’s really just having him understand the defense, really just letting his talent shine and showing that he’s really a capable franchise quarterback to be able to play against any defense if necessary.” In addition to his experience with an athletic quarterback who loves to freelance, Likely has plenty of experience with the type of offenses that Harbaugh likes to see his teams run. In particular, Likely’s rookie season was with Greg Roman calling the plays. Roman has rejoined John Harbaugh in New York after spending the last two seasons with Jim Harbaugh as the Los Angeles Chargers. Roman is now a senior offensive assistant for the Giants and seems to be in charge of designing the Giants’ run game. “I’d say there’s similarities in the run game,” Likely said of what Roman schemed in 2022. “Obviously, G-Ro’s a wizard, best of the best when it comes to the run.” That year the Ravens had one of the best running games in the NFL, ranking second in total yardage, yards per game, and yards per attempt, as well as fourth in rushing EPA while being seventh in rushing attempts. But, Likely continues, the offense won’t be just Roman’s work. Rather it will be a complex confection that draws on elements from across the Giants’ offensive coaching staff — a staff that features four former offensive coordinators. Matt Nagy is in charge of the offense, but part of his job is being the mixologist who balances the input of his assistants. As Likely says, the Giants offense is, “Just taking the flavors of just coaching from Coach Nagy [offensive coordinator Matt Nagy], Coach TK [tight ends coach Tim Kelly], [quarterbacks] Coach [Brian] Callahan, Coach Greg Roman as well. And then all just trying to make it our offense.” It’s a (potentially) heady mix of philosophies and perspectives that could yield a relatively unique offense in New York. The goal, Likely says, is to make every play look identical and give opposing defenses as few clues as to their intentions as possible. After all, if defenses aren’t sure what’s coming, they play slower and are less able to stop it. “Whether it’s running, pass, making everything look alike and putting the best players in situations to win,” Likely said. “Obviously trying to keep everything as simple as possible so you don’t have to think a lot when you’re out there. But dressing [the offense] up to the defense to make it look like exotic, creativity and be able to put the best players in the best situation to win.” Running back Tyrone Tracy says that Matt Nagy calls the concept “Elegant Simplicity.” Unfortunately, the offense hasn’t found much traction just yet in practice. That could be viewed as a concern regarding the offense, or a good sign for the Giants’ defense. The Giants’ defensive front has been consistently dominant in practice, and the secondary has been disruptive on the back end. “I feel like no matter who you put out there, they have a job to do,” Likely said. “And Coach Dennard [defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson] out there, he’s telling them every day to compete. Nobody has a guaranteed spot every day. I mean, every day is a new day. “And they know that when they’re out there, when they see nine [Likely’s number], when they see anybody out there, I’m going to give you the best look that you can get. So, I feel like that’s the competing aspect of training camp. And that’s going to help us during the season.” Ultimately, Likely understands that while he might be the crown jewel of the Giants’ free agent class, he’s just one part of the team, one of 11 players on the field. He believes that if he does his job to the best of his ability, he’ll prove the Giants’ faith in him. “I come out every day telling myself just win your one-eleventh every play, and whether it has run or pass matchups, whether it’s zone or man. And I feel like, if I win my one-eleventh, whether it’s I got to go against safety, linebacker, the end, corner, just giving Jax the best possibility to throw the ball or running back to be able to run in space.” The end result? “Going out there every day and [showing] everybody that when the Giants got me, they [made] the right choice.”
