title: NY Giants training camp, practice No. 6: Winners, losers, takeaways
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — At the end of practice, head coach John Harbaugh likes to put the New York Giants in “win or lose the game” situations. Tuesday’s situation had the offense trailing by six points, :42 left on the clock, and the ball at roughly the opponent’s 20-yard line. The offense had just […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart | Getty Images WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — At the end of practice, head coach John Harbaugh likes to put the New York Giants in “win or lose the game” situations. Tuesday’s situation had the offense trailing by six points, :42 left on the clock, and the ball at roughly the opponent’s 20-yard line. The offense had just gone through a difficult red zone period where the first team had three possessions from the 10-yard line or inside that. They ran 11 plays and failed to score. In this situation, on third-and-goal from the 3-yard line, Jaxson Dart waited, waited, and waited some more. He finally scrambled in for a touchdown. That led to some jawing, and to Dart throwing the ball at cornerback Greg Newsome. That resulted in a 15-yard penalty that forced Ben Sauls to kick the “game-winning” field goal, which he made, from 48 yards. Harbaugh issued a controlled response when asked about the play, but was clearly not pleased. “I think it’s a 15-yard penalty for taunting, so we backed up the extra point and had to do it again. Did you see that? That’s how we handled it,” Harbaugh said. The coach didn’t say much to Dart on the field. “I think he understands that for the game-winning extra point, we don’t want it to be a 50-yard extra point,” Harbaugh said. “Do you think I need to say anything in that case? Pretty clear cut, right?” Winners Jarrod Gray — Surprised to see the Aussie rugby star signed by the Giants through the International Pathway Program mentioned here? So, here is why I had to mention him. I looked over to a corner of the field at one point and Gray, who has little football experience, was working one-on-one with a coach, learning NFL blocking techniques. A peek through my binoculars revealed that coach to be former Giant star Chris Snee, now part of the team’s front office. Any day an offensive lineman can get solo instruction from Snee makes that a winnng day. Colton Hood — The rookie cornerback made a pair of excellent plays on Wednesday. In run support, Hood stepped to a wide run to his side and stopped Eric Gray for what appeared to be a short loss. In pass defense, Hood denied Beaux Collins a touchdown on a red zone fade, ripping away a throw from Jameis Winston for an incompletion. Ben Sauls — The second-year kicker did push two kicks to the left, which was his bug-a-boo during spring practices, but he made 10 of 12 kicks overall. That’s a pretty good day. Jermaine Eluemunor — The Giants did 1-on-1 pass blocking drills for the first time in this camp. Eluemunor took two reps. He guided Abdul Carter around the pocket on one rep. On his next rep, he accepted a power rush from Brian Burns and stoned him. That was a pretty good day’s work. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Losers Jameis Winston — I am not trying to count passes attempted and completed during this camp. I have always felt that was pretty much pointless, and this time around I am not bothering with it. Still, Winston had a terrible day on Monday. He followed that on Tuesday with another day where he was largely off-target. His worst throw of the day was probably a ball that was picked off in the end zone, I believe by Jason Pinnock. Winston threw the ball right to him. Some boxed lunch recipients — The Greenbrier is providing media with boxed lunches prior to practice. Well, my apologies to any of my media cohorts who grabbed a boxed lunch expecting there to be chocolate chip cookies inside only to find them missing. I won’t name names, but a certain reporter known for “quirky” eating habits raided several of the boxes and took away the cookies. So, sorry. Education of a rookie During those 1-on-1 passing drills, rookie right guard Sisi Mauigoa lined up against Abdul Carter on back-to-back snaps. On the first, Carter tried to bully Mauigoa and got stopped in his tracks. Players never go back-to-back in this drill, so I suspect Carter asked for the do-over. On the second rep, Carter faked to the outside, swiped across Mauigoa, and blasted past the helpless rookie. Injury updates Malik Nabers continued his routine of working briefly at the start of practice. As usual, he participated in position drills, caught some passes, then called it a day. Wide receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster missed practice with what Harbaugh called “a little knee swelling.” Remaining Greenbrier practice schedule Wednesday, August 5 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Thursday, August 6 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Friday, August 7 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Saturday, August 8 — 10 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.

full_text: John Harbaugh watches Monday’s practice. | Getty Images WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants will be on the field for their sixth practice of training camp on Tuesday afternoon. Head coach John Harbaugh said on Monday that this second week is “ the big week of camp .” It is the week when the Giants will be in pads for practice more often than at any other time this season. Veteran defensive tackle D.J. Reader , in his 11th NFL training camp, understands the importance of the physical work padded practices allow. “You’ve got to callous the body. The thing that’s important in football is callousing the body to be ready to take on those blows throughout the season, because you’re going to get chinks in your armor, and if you didn’t build your armor up enough to be able to withstand those hits, those dents, those little scratches you’ll take in your armor, then shame on you,” Reader said. “I think it’s important to be able to callous the body. Do it with intent. Be smart about it, but you have to callous the body to go out there and play this game. You’re not just going to roll out there, roll out of bed, and be able to go out there on Sundays and get it done.” Updates #NyGiants Odell Beckham had a MAJOR uptick in first team reps today. title: QB tiers: NY Giants’ Jaxson Dart ranked No. 24 by coaches, executives
summary: The New York Giants are at something of crossroads in 2026. They’re hoping that the combination of quarterback Jaxson Dart and head coach John Harbaugh can lift the team back to competitiveness. The rest of the NFL seems to be taking a “wait and see” approach, particularly with respect to Dart. The Athletic released itsannual […]
full_text: ﻿NY Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart throwing in training camp. | Getty Images The New York Giants are at something of crossroads in 2026. They’re hoping that the combination of quarterback Jaxson Dart and head coach John Harbaugh can lift the team back to competitiveness. The rest of the NFL seems to be taking a “wait and see” approach, particularly with respect to Dart. The Athletic released itsannual Quarterback Tiers lis t on Tuesday, ranking the all 35 veteran quarterbacks expected to play significant snaps in 2026. Dart ranked 24th on the list, just below names like Daniel Jones, Bryce Young, and Kyler Murray. The Athletic constructed the list by polling 50 coaches and executives from around the NFL, keeping their responses anonymous. The panel this year consisted of eight general managers, five assistant GMs, five former GMs and three other executives, plus nine head coaches, 10 defensive coordinators, five offensive coordinators, two offensive assistants, one defensive assistant and two coaches specializing in analytics/game management. That’s 21 execs and 29 coaches overall. The voters are asked to divide the 35 quarterbacks into five tiers, ranging from the elite quarterbacks who carry their team on a week-to-week basis, to Tier 5 quarterbacks, who probably shouldn’t see the field. There were five “newcomers” who hadn’t been included in a “Tiers” list before, Cam Ward, Jaxson Dart, Tyler Shough, Shedeur Sanders, and Malik Willis. Due to insufficient data — four of them were rookies and Willis hadn’t played enough — they were grouped in the third tier. And of those newcomers, Dart is the most highly-regarded by coaches and executives around the NFL. Dart was ranked an average 3.24 by the voters, ahead of Cam Ward (3.34) and Tyler Shough (3.42). And while Dart didn’t get as many “Tier 2” votes as Ward or Shough (two for Dart while the others got four each), he also got far fewer “Tier 4” votes than his fellow rookies. The third tier is defined as: Legit starter but needs better running game or defense to win Lower-volume dropback passing offense suits him best Interestingly, and perhaps predictably, defensive coordinators have a more favorable view of Dart than do offensive coaches or executives. Running quarterbacks and explosive playmakers are the bane of defensive coordinators’ existences, and we’ve seen defenses shift radically to account for those skill sets over the last five or six years. And from that perspective, it makes sense that defensive minds would respect Dart. “It’s more athleticism, playmaking ability, splash plays than consistency,” a defensive coach said. Dart was one of the best running quarterbacks in the NFL, putting up rushing numbers that deserve to be talked about in the same conversation as Cam Newton, Josh Allen, and Lamar Jackson. But at the same time, Dart was a very “boom or bust” player. He thrived in chaos and producied big plays when pressured, but was also one of the NFL’s least-efficient quarterbacks on a down-to-down basis when pressured. That lack of efficiency and consistency has offensive coaches skeptical. Conversely, offensive minds were much more favorable in their view of Shough, who was very consistent from down to down in Kellen Moore’s offense. Former quarterback and NFL scout Nate Tice said in his review of the rookie quarterbacks that Shough is “very Tua coded” in his play. In other words, he’s dedicated to staying on time and on schedule, and consistently throws the ball away when pressured, rather than attempt to take a risk and create a big play as Dart does. Executives, meanwhile, question whether Dart’s play style makes him a long-term risk. “I’m going to give Jaxson a nudge and give him a 3, arrow up,” a GM said. “But he is not going to change his style of play, so that is where I’m like, ‘I don’t know if this guy is going to last.’” Quarterback picks need to pay off long term, because quarterback consistency is what makes offensive play predictive of future success. If a quarterback can’t be available, then the team as a whole won’t be consistent, which has a way of costing executives their jobs. However, the responses do seem to be positive overall regarding Dart’s future. That same defensive coach from above said, “That is one where if (offensive coordinator) Matt (Nagy) does a good job, he can get back in the head-coaching mix.” “I do like Dart,” a defensive coordinator said. “He can throw it. He’s athletic, and he has a little moxie about him. I like that s—.” The Giants like that [expletive deleted] as well, but like the offensive minds and unnamed GM, they’re also hoping that Dart can improve his consistency and cut down on the risky plays. If he can, he could find himself following in the footsteps of Drake Maye and Caleb Williams and making the leap for Tier 3 to Tier 2 next year.

title: The Giants’ salary cap situation for 2026 and beyond
summary: During training camp, most of what we as fans think about is which players are going to start or provide valuable backup and what that suggests about the team’s chances of success in the upcoming season. I’m pretty sure, though, that the New York Giants’ brain trust is also thinking about the team through a […]
full_text: During training camp, most of what we as fans think about is which players are going to start or provide valuable backup and what that suggests about the team’s chances of success in the upcoming season. I’m pretty sure, though, that the New York Giants’ brain trust is also thinking about the team through a financial lens. That means three things: How much flexibility the team’s current financial situation gives them to make moves during camp if a dire need arises, whether because of a major injury (heaven forbid) or underperformance of the players at a specific position. Which players with significant contracts may be “on the block” in head coach John Harbaugh’s mind as targets to be cut, or to be traded in-season if the team does not perform well. Which players might be targets for contract extensions during the season to lock them up for additional years while creating 2027 cap space. Let’s look at the Giants’ financial situation from each of these perspectives. Current cap space The Giants at the moment have $10.1 million in cap space, ninth-lowest in the NFL, per Over The Cap . That’s not a good look for a team coming off a 4-13 season. The teams in worse cap position were all either playoff teams (Steelers, Packers, Bears, Jaguars, Bills) or playoff wannabees who didn’t get there (Chiefs, Cowboys, Buccaneers). In other respects the Giants’ cap situation looks better. The Giants are middle of the pack in active cap spending (i.e., top 51 players on the roster) at $262.9M. It’s not more because the Giants carry $28.6M in dead money into the 2026 season. If that sounds bad, consider the Dolphins ($179.2M dead money), the Browns ($116.8M), the Saints ($112.1M), and the Jets ($111.5M). Miami is only spending $112.6 million on players actually on the roster and only has $16.1 million in cap space left to add more. Half the Giants’ dead money is from the unavoidable Dexter Lawrence breakup, $5 million more from the release of Bobby Okereke, which I think everyone agrees was the right move, and the rest from the releases of (in decreasing order of cost) James Hudson, Jamie Gillan, Chris Board, Graham Gano, Jason Sanders, and Cam Jones. Veterans at risk The Giants whose cap hits are the highest for the 2026 season are: Paulson Adebo ($24.2M) Brian Burns ($21.4M) Jevon Holland ($18.5M) Darius Slayton ($15.9M) Kayvon Thibodeaux ($14.5M) Andrew Thomas ($13.0M) Jon Runyan Jr. ($11.8M) Abdul Carter ($10.3M) Arvell Reese ($8.7M) Greg Newsome II ($8M) Malik Nabers ($8.0M) Chauncey Golston ($6.9M) Of those, Burns, Thomas, Carter, Reese, and Nabers are surely not going anywhere, strictly from the standpoint of value to the team. As for the rest, from the financial standpoint, all of them would incur a significant dead money hit in 2027 if released this season. The only ones who would actually save money against the 2026 cap if released are Runyan ($9.25M) and Newsome ($5M). Runyan and Newsome are also the players in the group above with the smallest dead money hits in 2027 if cut ($2.5M and $3.0M respectively). Thus, these two seem to be the players most at risk of being released if they do not perform up to Harbaugh’s standards in camp, or if they are simply beaten out by other players. Creating cap space with contract extensions As I have complained several times on these pages, general manager Joe Schoen doesn’t like to use void years to create cap space. He has been one of only a few GMs not to take advantage of the void year loophole to add talent. That said, what Schoen does like to do – a lot – is to convert salary to a signing bonus whose cap accounting is spread out over the life of the contract. It’s the equivalent of tiptoeing right up to the void year line but not crossing it. The player doesn’t care because the signing bonus cash is paid up front. Among current Giants: Andrew Thomas signed a five-year, $117.5 million contract extension in 2023. Thus far his contract has incurred cap charges of only $9.3M, $19.9M, and $9.3M in 2023, 2024, and 2025 because the cap charge for his $15 million signing bonus was spread over several years. This year, for the third consecutive season, Schoen converted part of Thomas’ salary ($14.8M) into a signing bonus to free up $11.0 million in cap space. The good news is that Thomas’ 2026 cap hit is now only $13 million. The bad news is that by deferring the cap hits, Thomas’ cap hits for 2027-2029 will now be $29.95M, $29.95M, and $29.62M. Schoen is paying those amounts in cheaper dollars since the NFL salary cap has risen every year except after the pandemic, but the you-know-what will hit the fan starting next season. That’s the price Schoen pays for eschewing void years. Thomas has had a troubling injury history, having played in only 10, 6, and 13 games the past three seasons. When healthy, though, he is one of the top few left tackles in the NFL. He’s also still only 27 years old. Don’t be surprised if Schoen tries to sign Thomas to a contract extension in mid-season to alleviate those $29M+ cap hits that are coming via further signing bonus cap sleight-of-hand. Brian Burns’ story is almost identical to Thomas’. Burns signed a 5-year, $141 million contract with the Giants as part of the trade that brought him here. He incurred cap hits of only $15.5M and $17.8M his first two seasons as a Giant. In 2025, though, Schoen converted $16 million of Burns’ salary into a prorated signing bonus to free up up $12 million of cap space. In 2026, once again Schoen played the same game, converting $22.75M of salary into a signing bonus for cap purposes. The bad news is that in 2027 and 2028, Burns’ cap hit will now be $44.1 million. That type of cap hit can’t be swallowed easily. Burns isn’t quite at Thomas’ level of excellence, but he is probably in no worse than the second tier of edge defenders behind players such as Myles Garrtt, Micah Parsons, Maxx Crosby, etc. Thus, look for Schoen to also try to sign Burns to a contract extension during the season and use the same signing bonus strategy to lessen those $44.1 million cap hits. Adebo’s contract is tied for 14th-highest among NFL cornerbacks. It’s only for three years, but it carries the largest cap hit of any Giant ($24.2 million) this season, and next season’s $20.3 million cap hit is nothing to sneeze at. Unlike Thomas and Burns, Adebo has really only had one excellent NFL season (2023). He was all right as the Giants’ CB1 last year, but with one interception and five pass breakups, he wasn’t an impact player. There is little the Giants can do with his contract situation this year. His play has not earned him an extension, and the Giants would lose $5.7M by cutting him while incurring $29.9M of dead money. The Giants just have to hope that Adebo returns to his 2023 form in Dennard Wilson’s defense, which might convince them to offer a contract extension. If not, then the Giants will probably swallow $6.3 million of dead money in 2027 to release him and save $14 million of cap space. Jevon Holland is in a somewhat similar situation. He had two elite seasons in Miami but two mediocre ones as well, and his first Giants season was also nondescript. He carries an $18.5 million cap hit this year and $18.9 million next year, and the Giants can save $13.8 million by cutting him in 2027, swallowing $5 million in dead money to do so. But if he bounces back, an extension is a possibility. Darius Slayton is probably in the most precarious future situation of anyone on the list. His $15.9 million 2026 cap hit is unavoidable, because almost all of it would be dead money if he is released. In 2027 the Giants could save $10 million against the cap, with only $3M in dead money, by releasing him. Add to that the plethora of wide receivers in training camp this summer. If Slayton falls on the depth chart and sees much less playing time, he’s surely a goner in 2027. On the other hand, if his recently revealed 2025 sports hernia is fully healed and he becomes entrenched as WR2, an…

title: Eli Apple is a cautionary tale for NY Giants CB Deonte Banks
summary: Former New York Giants cornerback Eli Apple was released by the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. It is possibe that will be the end of the NFL line for Apple, who has played just six games the past two seasons. That, in and of itself, is probably only a mild curiosity for Giants fans. After […]
full_text: New York Giants cornerback Deonte Banks | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Former New York Giants cornerback Eli Apple was released by the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. It is possibe that will be the end of the NFL line for Apple, who has played just six games the past two seasons. That, in and of itself, is probably only a mild curiosity for Giants fans. After all, it’s been about seven years since the former first round pick played for the Giants, and many Giants fans likely forgot Apple was even in the NFL. The Giants traded Apple to the New Orleans Saints after five games in 2018, and he has since played for the Carolina Panthers, Cincinnati Bengals, Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers, and then the 49ers. It remains to be seen if this is where Apple’s story in the NFL ends, but it still serves as a cautionary tale for the Giants and their 2023 first-round pick, Deonte Banks. There are a somewhat uncomfortable number of parallels between Banks and Apple. Both are former first-round picks who were heralded for an elite blend of size and athleticism coming out of college. Both flashed the potential to be good, perhaps even great, press man coverage specialists early in their careers. And both regressed over the following years as questions mounted. Some in the Giants’ fandom and media are ready to move on from Banks as well, tossing him in the dustbin of history as yet another bust. That said, Apple and Banks are two different men and their paths can absolutely diverge. As of this writing, Banks remains on the Giants, and was recently moved into the “lock” category to make the roster in Ed’s recent 53-man roster forecast. And at the very least, Banks may have secured his continued roster spot by emerging as a great kick returner. If that’s all he’s able to be, it’s a disappointing outcome for a former first-round cornerback, but still a useful piece for the Giants. The new kick-off rules are confusing and frustrating, but they do accomplish the goal of making the play matter in a way it didn’t until recently. A great kick returner can change the complexion of a game, and the Giants would certainly enjoy having their own Devin Hester. That said, if the Giants and Banks want to avoid his career path mirroring Apple’s, it falls to Addison Lynch and Dennard Wilson to help him realize his potential. And so far there has been more than, perhaps, a glimmer of hope over the course of spring and summer practices. Banks started out as a second team corner, but has worked his way into meaningful snaps with the starters. In fact, Banks has reportedly looked good enough in his opportunities that he’s counted among the pleasant surprises in the first week of camp. He has, reportedly, been sticky in coverage and has gotten his hands on passes – though he still struggles to haul them in for interceptions. Witness the bad drop Banks had on Monday. Athletic ability has never been a question for Banks, rather he’s struggled with consistency. “We tried to show him that his consistency was his deal,” defensive backs coach Addison Lynch said of Banks earlier in the off-season. “He just wasn’t consistent getting lined up fast, wasn’t consistent with his feet. He’s improved his consistency, so now his play is improved, now his confidence is up and he can just roll into the season.” For his part, Dennard Wilson (likely) wants to run a defense that uses man-match coverage, an aggressive variation of Cover 4 that uses post-snap coverage rules to transform a zone defense into a physical man coverage scheme. It’s a versatile scheme that deals with modern offenses well and is used by many defensive minds in the “Ravens 2.0” school. It would also play to Banks’ strengths in man coverage, but the versatile nature stresses defenders’ processing. That’s been an issue for Banks over the last two years under Shane Bowen, but Lynch may have reached Banks in a way that coaches were never able to with Apple. “I love how he’s handling it,” Lynch said. “Right now, he’s being an absolute pro. He’s doing the extra work, he’s in his book, he’s doing everything we ask him. He’s making plays on the ball and he’s doing a really good job handling himself play in and play out. He’s made major improvements that when he’s tired, he relies on his technique and he’s getting more technically sound, so everything with him is trending in the right direction.” Ultimately, while some may be done with Banks or believe he’s soon to be another former Giant, the Giants themselves should want him to blossom under Wilson and Lynch. He has rare athletic traits and if teams want to build through the draft, they need to develop the players they draft. Apple was never able to realize his potential with the Giants (or anyone else, for that matter), but that doesn’t mean Banks has to follow the same path. There’s still time for him to become the player the Giants hoped they were getting in 2023.

title: NY Giants RB Tyrone Tracy not worried about being overshadowed by Cam Skattebo
summary: Cam Skattebo is the New York Giants running back who gets all of the attention from fans and media. It is Tyrone Tracy, though, who is coming off back-to-back seasons of 1,000 or more yards from scrimmage.Does Tracy ever feel overlooked? “Not really,” Tracy said on Monday. “When you say he gets all the attention, […]
full_text: Tyrone Tracy | Getty Images Cam Skattebo is the New York Giants running back who gets all of the attention from fans and media. It is Tyrone Tracy, though, who is coming off back-to-back seasons of 1,000 or more yards from scrimmage. Does Tracy ever feel overlooked? “Not really,” Tracy said on Monday. “When you say he gets all the attention, I really don’t care about that, to be honest. I’m about football. About what I do on the field, how I carry myself on the field and off the field as well. But at the same time, I’m going to go out there and do what I need to do at the end of the day.” A fifth-round pick by the Giants in 2024, Tracy had 1,123 scrimmage yards as a rookie and 1,028 last season. He did not begin either of those seasons as the team’s No. 1 running back. What the Giants actually have at running back is a 1a and 1b with Skattebo and Tracy, whichever order you put them in. Tyrone Tracy says he does not feel overlooked because of the attention paid to fellow #NYG RB Cam Skattebo. pic.twitter.com/WMbG2lTa7q — Big Blue View (@bigblueview) August 4, 2026 Head coach John Harbaugh said Tracy will have “a big role” for the Giants. “Both those guys are going to be together back there playing a lot of football,” Harbaugh said. “You can’t play with one back anyway, and they’re both competing for everything at this point in time. Against themselves, against each other, against the opponent, against the defense. Both those guys are going to play a lot.” Tracy understands the assignment. “Iron sharpens iron, so he’s going to push me, I’m going to push him,” Tracy said. “And, obviously, we are two different running backs, so I think we complement each other really well. So, it’s not necessarily like me against him, but best believe that I’m going to push him to be the best that he can be, and he’s going to push me to be the best that I can be each and every day. Whether it’s running the ball, passing, blocking, being a good teammate. “Obviously, Skatt’s really loud. He’s loud. He’s a great leader, so that’s allowing me to be – pushing me to be a great leader as well. Each and every thing that we’re doing, I’m trying to challenge him, and he’s going to challenge me. So, I think we complement each other really well.” Tracy said all of the Giants’ running backs understand that Harbaugh wants an offense that leans on the run game. “We want to run the ball. I think if you look at Harbaugh and where he’s been, and all the running backs that he’s used really his whole career, they’ve all been successful,” Tracy said. “So, when he came here, we were all excited. You’ve got a running coach that’s coming to you, so as a running back room, we’re excited for him to be here, to be honest.” The mastermind behind the Giants’ run game is senior offensive assistant Greg Roman, a four-time offensive coordinator with a reputation for designing run concepts. “I think he has his schemes, to be honest. His schemes are so different. I’m sitting there in awe, really, each and every time he gets up to talk. He’s very detailed. He knows exactly what he’s talking about,” Tracy said. “If he says it’s going to be this way versus a certain look, I promise you, you go out there, and that look is going to end up exactly what he says. So, he’s been around the game. He’s been around winning teams. College level, too. When he was at Stanford, I think he said he ran the ball; one guy had like 40 carries one game for 200, 300 yards. He’s been around the game a long time. He has the stats to back it up, and he’s very knowledgeable. “So, Coach Ro, I mean, you can’t really say enough about him. He’s a good coach. Great coach with a lot of knowledge.” Tracy explained a little more about the run scheme. “There’s really no gray area, and it’s not just one way to run the ball,” Tracy said. “He’s calling the same run, but out of different formations, different motions, different pullers. There’s a whole bunch of different stuff going on, but again, he’s making it very simple and easy for us to learn.” Tracy said offensive coordinator Matt Nagy wants the offense to “look complicated to the defense, but simple to us as an offense.” “We want to be explosive,” Tracy said. “We want to move the ball down the field, and I think the way we’re doing that is being simple but also making the defense think a little bit.” Tracy, even if he doesn’t get much attention, will be a big part of it.

title: Scouting Jets wide receiver Cam Camper
summary: The Jets recently signed wide receiver Cam Camper to replace the injured Gee Scott. Today, we break Camper down in detail. full_text: WASHINGTON, DC - MAY 31: Cam Camper #16 of the Orlando Storm runs for a touchdown against the DC Defenders during the second half of the UFL game at Audi Field on May 31, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets recently signed wide receiver Cam Camper to replace the injured Gee Scott. Today, we break Camper down in detail. The 24-year old Camper is listed at 6’3” and 198 pounds and was an all-Mountain West Conference honorable mention in 2024 after posting over 900 receiving yards at Boise State. He also played for Indiana but was undrafted last season. Background Camper was just 5’9” as a high school senior, so he was unranked as a high school recruit and initially tried to walk on at Sam Houston State. When that didn’t work out, he went down the junior college route by enrolling at Trinity Valley Community College. In two years there, he was productive when he played, catching 22 passes for 353 yards and a touchdown in 2020 and 28 for 505 and three touchdowns in 2021. However, he missed time due to injuries in both seasons. By this time, Camper had grown a lot, and was on plenty of radars. He eventually ended up at Indiana, where he made an immediate impact with 11 catches for 156 yards in his debut. Things continued to go well from there, as he had another 100-yard game with 10 catches a few weeks later. However, he suffered a serious injury in the middle of of the season, limiting him to seven starts. He ended up with 46 catches for 569 yards and two touchdowns. He was ready to return in the middle of the 2023 season and started seven of the last eight games. While he had a 100-yard game against Akron, his overall production was down with 17 receptions for 285 yards and a touchdown. Having graduated, Camper opted to transfer to Boise State in 2024 and finally remained healthy all year as he started six of 14 games and racked up 903 yards and four scores on 58 receptions. This earned him an all-Mountain West Conference honorable mention. Coming out of college, Camper went undrafted and signed for the Jaguars ahead of training camp. He caught one pass for them in preseason but did not make their roster. Over the spring, Camper was drafted by the UFL’s Orlando Storm and he ended up fourth in the league with a 14.8 yards per catch average as he caught 23 passes for 340 yards and three touchdowns. He was 14th in the league for receiving yards, but only played seven regular season games; the lowest of anyone in the top-15. The Storm lost in the semi-finals with Camper held to two catches for 26 yards, so he set about trying to find an NFL team to sign him up. Camper was signed by the Jets early on in training camp, following an injury to Scott. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Scott brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism After his growth spurt during his JUCO days, Camper has good height but his catch radius still falls short of recent Jets signing Quincy Skinner, despite Skinner being over an inch shorter. Camper’s pro day numbers were about average across the board, but he ran a solid-for-his-size 4.52 in the 40-yard dash. He did not participate in the bench press at his pro day. Usage Camper primarily played on the outside during NFL preseason and UFL action, as well as during his college career. He did line up in the slot sometimes, including almost 20 percent of the time in college. He has not carried the ball as a rusher at any level. Deep threat Camper has had some good success on downfield routes in college and at the UFL level, although he’s more of a guy you would throw it up to than someone who is likely to get behind the defense. He can track the ball well over his shoulder though. His longest play at Indiana was just 41 yards but he did have plays of 45, 52 and 53 yards at Boise State. Hands In his two seasons at Indiana, Camper’s catch rate fell short of 60 percent each time. However, he improved that to 67 percent at Boise and 71 percent in the UFL. He only caught one of five targets in preseason NFL action though. His drop rate was low throughout his college career, although six of his 11 drops came in 2024. Camper showcases an impressive ability to lay out and make catches at full extension. He does not always catch the ball cleanly but shows good concentration in terms of his ability to maintain control and prevent the ball from hitting the turf. Routes Camper displays some good base fundamentals as a route runner, with well-executed releases and an ability to disguise his break by leaning inside to create leverage. He has shown some ability to use his body to box out, which may be something he needs to rely on if he can’t generate separation against NFL-level cornerbacks. Red zone Camper hasn’t exactly put up outstanding red zone numbers, as he has never had five touchdown catches in a season at any level post-high school. However, he has shown on a few occasions that he can be a good option to throw it up to near the goal line. He also scored on one two-point conversion in his college career. After the catch Camper’s numbers after the catch are nothing special, but he will fight for yardage even though he doesn’t break many tackles. He had one good highlight in this area during the UFL season, breaking this play for an 74-yard touchdown. He hasn’t been much of an option in the screen game, averaging less than six yards per play when targeted on those during his college career. He had one fumble during his college career, back in 2022. Run Blocking Camper was a solid blocker in college, who uses his size well on the outside. His performance grades for run blocking in the UFL were poor according to Pro Football Focus, but that’s often a sign that more is being asked of a receiver when compared to someone who might just get basic assignments and post an average grade. He had two blocking penalties in 2024, both in the same game. One was for holding and the other one was an illegal block in the back. Physicality Camper caught a lot of contested catches during his college career and a few more in the UFL. His size is an asset against smaller defensive backs. He was called for offensive pass interference once at Boise State. Special Teams Camper barely played any special teams in college or during his NFL preseason appearances, but he was used extensively on kick and punt coverage in the UFL and took to the role impressively as he had nine tackles, including seven in his last four games. He did not line up as a gunner on punts, instead playing on the wing. He has taken some snaps as a vice though, as well as rushing punts. He fielded one kickoff in college but did not return it. Instincts and Intelligence Camper shows some ability to read coverages and find open areas when plays are extended. He had one pre-snap penalty in 2024, for a false start. Attitude Camper has shown good determination to make it to the NFL having previously been unable to earn a college scholarship. No doubt he has had discipline instilled in him by his mother, who has a military background. On-field discipline was not an issue for Camper, who had eight offensive penalties in three years during his college career and one at the UFL level. There was one play in his college career where he was jawing with an opponent and induced a shove, enabling him to earn a flag with an over-exaggerated flop. Injuries Injuries have been a concern for Camper in the past, but he’s steered clear of them for the past few seasons. Having seen both of his JUCO seasons cut short due to undisclosed injuries, he tore his ACL in his first season at Indiana and then suffered another knee injury in his second game back. Although he showed toughness to get back into the line-up for the following game, Camper was obviously limited as he eventually had to have another surgery on his repaired knee. He also missed one game in college due to illness. Scheme Fit Camper will…

title: Nick Sirianni has been impressed with new Eagles assistant coaches
summary: The Eagles are nearly a week into training camp, and head coach Nick Sirianni gave some updates about how OC Sean Mannion is leading the offense, how new OL coach Chris Kuper is acclimating, and about rookies Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers. Here’s what the head coach had to say: On Sean Mannion’s leadership Sirianni […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 01: Philadelphia Eagles offensive line coach Chris Kuper speaks with Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 1st, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles are nearly a week into training camp, and head coach Nick Sirianni gave some updates about how OC Sean Mannion is leading the offense, how new OL coach Chris Kuper is acclimating, and about rookies Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers. Here’s what the head coach had to say: On Sean Mannion’s leadership Sirianni said that despite many of the changes to the coaching staff, meetings are still structured the same way. When asked if new run-game coordinator Ryan Mahaffey was leading the run-game portion of meetings, Sirianni revealed that OC Sean Mannion has actually lead most of the meetings up to this point. “What Sean [Mannion] just shows, is a very good overall view of the offense. When he comes up here, he has everybody’s attention and is able to talk to every position. I’ve been very impressed by that — obviously, one of the reasons we hired him as far as just his expertise. And, I think the guys have been really impressed by that.” The head coach went on to explain that it makes sense as they’re learning a newer system that Mannion is the vocal one in meetings, and then the group splits up and hears from their position coaches. Sirianni complimented his new OC with how he’s done speaking to the group, keeping everyone on the same page, and showing his expertise at every position. On training camp success Sirianni was asked what a successful training camp looked like to him, and he explained that it’s about looking at each particular day individually, because there’s going to be back and forth between the offense and defense, and different position groups. “When we come in here and we watch as a team, are we getting better at the little things? Are we getting better at our fundamentals? Are we taking steps? Are we taking steps with our things that require no talent, our ball security? When I say require no talent, just everybody being on the same page at all times. You’re looking for little progressions each and every day. It’s a marathon. Some days, it’s going to look like this, and some days, it’s going to look like this. It’s never just a true line. “ He admitted that as coaches, they’d all like it to be so simple, but progression ebbs and flows, and they’re ultimately just trying to get a little better each day. On new OL coach Chris Kuper “I hired him for a reason. We were really impressed by him, and we know he’s a phenomenal coach, and he’s doing a good job of building relationships with his players. He’s doing a good job of teaching his players. Obviously, I talk to guys all the time, and I know those guys think very highly of him and have been really impressed early on here in camp and through the OTAs. Building trust is the most important thing. You build trust by your daily habits, you build trust by consistently doing the right things. Those are the things that he’s been doing.” On rookie performances Sirianni said that it’s all about getting better everyday for rookies like Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers, but he really likes the skillset they have and how it will continue to develop. Specifically, the head coach said he loves the way Lemon goes about his business, and that the WR’s effort in the run game is awesome. He also pointed out Lemon’s quickness, which maybe isn’t on display with every catch, but is all over the film. Sirianni also spoke about Stowers and how his athletic ability with help him in third-down situations. “I think Eli has a really good feel for the zone, of where to sit in zones, and how to get open versus different types of zone coverage. We know that his athletic ability will [help him] shake free on third down when it is man coverage because he’s quick, he’s fast, he’s explosive. But what I’ve been impressed with him is just his ability to kind of read defenses and find the areas of the zone where he needs to sit and be at the right spot at the right time.” Other notables When asked about Landon Dickerson revealing he returned from injury too soon last season , Sirianni said that their organizational approach is to put player safety at the forefront. He explained that they work closely with the medical staff and are always thinking about the long-term health of the players. Sirianni addressed more pass plays to the running backs in the early days of training camp, saying that it all just depends on the style of offense they’re running at any particular time, and they’re always looking to utilize the skillset of their players. They don’t want to stop a guy like Saquon Barkley from running the ball, and they know the RBs have the ability to affect the game in other ways, too. The head coach explained his approach to getting QB4 Cole Payton reps during camp, and said that his job is to provide enough reps throughout practice to allow guys to develop. He noted that it can be especially easy in training camp to get locked into reps for the ones and twos, but Sirianni said the team has done a good job finding ways to work the developmental guys.

title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Offense out of sync as DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon miss time
summary: Today marked the fifth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: The Eagles practice again tomorrow starting at 10:00 AM Eastern. We’ll hear from Vic Fangio prior to practice around 9:40 AM.
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JUNE 2: DeVonta Smith #6 and Makai Lemon #9 of the Philadelphia Eagles look on during OTA offseason workouts at Jefferson Health Training Complex on June 2, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today marked the fifth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES Leading with injury news today since those developments were relevant to the on-field performance. EAGLES INJURY UPDATES: DID NOT PARTICIPATE: OT Lane Johnson (excused absence/not injury related) Johnson has missed three straight practices. WR DeVonta Smith (hamstring) Smith’s injury isn’t considered serious. WR Makai Lemon (hamstring) Lemon’s injury also isn’t considered serious. But the rookie wide receiver previously missed at least four of the Eagles’ eight spring practices due to a hamstring injury (currently unclear if it’s the same one or a new one). And now he’s missed full team drills in two of their five training camp practices thus far. Doesn’t seem ideal if he’s out for extended period of time. OG Micah Morris (shoulder) S Cole Wisniewski (hamstring) EDGE Keyshawn James-Newby (ankle) OG Jaedan Roberts (calf contusion) INJURED DURING PRACTICE DB Cooper DeJean (left arm) got banged up and finished practice watching action from the sideline. WR Britain Covey walked off the field with trainers. With Smith, Lemon, and Covey hurt, the Eagles are down to the following healthy receivers: Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, Darius Cooper, Elijah Moore, Johnny Wilson, Quez Watkins, Danny Gray, Samori Toure, and Erik Ezukanma. JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Whereas the Eagles looked really good on offense during Monday’s practice , that same unit was out of sync on Tuesday. Missing Lane, DeVonta, and Lemon probably didn’t help. It was also unusual to see some periods where Hurts was working behind an offensive line that mostly consisted of backups. Very much an extenuating circumstances kind of practice. That much acknowledged, I’m here to tell you what I saw, and it often wasn’t pretty. Hurts wasn’t shy to throw deep today but the attempts weren’t fruitful. Not all of them were his fault. A diving Quez Watkins failed to track one such throw. Michael Carter II intercepted Hurts (while bobbling the ball but ultimately preventing the ball from hitting the ground) on a play where it looked like Hollywood Brown wasn’t expecting the pass to come his way. Brown was initially jogging before he looked up and started to sprint once he saw the ball in the air. Hurts targeted Brown downfield again and the ball was placed on the receiver’s hands but the catch was not made. Cooper DeJean had tight coverage in a trail position to contest Brown. A deep attempt to Elijah Moore was overthrown as the ball lacked a tight spiral. Will Shipley was wiiiiiiiiide open on the wheel route … and he dropped the ball. Brutal. Would’ve been an easy catch-and-run touchdown if he simply caught it. The offense was plagued by penalties in this practice. There were stretches where it felt like there was a flag on every single rep. One such infraction wiped out a Hurts to Hollywood goal-to-go touchdown due to an illegal shift. Hurts overthrew Darius Cooper in the end zone. SportsRadio 94WIP’s Eliot Shorr-Parks charted Hurts as 6/19 on the day. Dontayvion Wicks has seemed to earn Hurts’ trust. Hurts had a good completion to him in 11-on-11 where Mitchell closed on the defender while trying to knock the ball down but the pass was zipped in for a catch. Hurts connected with Wicks again on a play where the receiver was ruled down just shy of the goal line despite his insistence otherwise. Hurts made a good throw into the end zone where Wicks failed to make a leaping catch in traffic. I wouldn’t say that Wicks looks like a star but he does look like a solid starting-caliber receiver. My guy Darius Cooper continues to make plays. Today it was Dalton hitting him for a one-handed toe-tapping touchdown snag along the back of the end zone with DeJean in coverage. I originally thought it might be incomplete but the back judge signaled touchdown. BACKUP QUARTERBACK COMPETITION: Tanner McKee was first up with the second-team offense in 11-on-11 today. He continues to hold the ball longer than you’d like to see but he made solid throws, including one anticipation pass to Samori Toure along the left sideline. Andy Dalton found Grant Calcaterra on play-action pass where the defense bit on the run to the left side to leave the tight end open on the right for an easy completion. Markel Bell, not Fred Johnson, took first-team right tackle reps with Lane missing practice once again. Zack Baun broke up a short Hurts pass to Dallas Goedert. ONE-ON-ONE ACTION: WR vs. DB: Cooper DeJean deflected a downfield Hurts pass to Elijah Moore … but the wide receiver was able to track the batted ball and tap his toes to make a catch along the right sideline. Nice play. Quinyon Mitchell had good downfield coverage on Dontayvion Wicks to prevent a catch. Tanner McKee overthrew Darius Cooper deep. The wide receiver had a step on his defender. LB vs. RB: Jihaad Campbell allowed a short catch to Will Shipley. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. knocked down a pass intended for Tank Bigsby. Later, Bigsby shook Trot Jr. by stutter stepping left before cutting right for a wide open catch. Chance Campbell did a nice job of chucking Carson Steele at the line of scrimmage to knock the running back off his route and force an incompletion. Campbell uses his size to his advantage. OL vs. DL: Didn’t get to see as much of this as I would’ve liked; it’s difficult to watch three fields at once. But I did notice Gabe Hall beast Michael Jordan by running through him. Many are understandably excited about Uar Bernard’s developmental potential. But his fellow rookie, Josh Weru, has flashed more thus far. The Kenyan rugby player notched a “sack” late in practice. He also did fall for a hard count to get flagged for a neutral zone infraction … as did Bernard at one point. Jake Elliott attempted six kicks and made all of them. The distances: 33, 38, 42, 44, 44, 50, and 52 yards. He’s 13/14 overall in training camp so far. 76ers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey attended today’s practice. Even Howie Roseman is jealous of his offseason. (For all of your Sixers and LeBron James coverage, check out Liberty Ballers .) UP NEXT: The Eagles practice again tomorrow starting at 10:00 AM Eastern. We’ll hear from Vic Fangio prior to practice around 9:40 AM.

title: Eagles News: Moro Ojomo was asked about his contract outlook
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … ‘I can’t be thinking about that:’ Moro Ojomo opens up on his contract and future – NBCSPMoro Ojomo couldn’t be happier for his fellow defensive linemen, Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter, for getting huge new contracts. Even though deep down we all know what it […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Moro Ojomo #97 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … ‘I can’t be thinking about that:’ Moro Ojomo opens up on his contract and future – NBCSP Moro Ojomo couldn’t be happier for his fellow defensive linemen, Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter, for getting huge new contracts. Even though deep down we all know what it means. It means Ojomo most likely won’t be here next year. Because nobody – even Howie Roseman – can pay big money to three interior linemen. And the way he’s been going, Ojomo is on track for pretty hefty payday. Ojomo said after practice Monday he can’t afford to think about his future. Because if he does, that means he’s not focused on what’s really important. “I think that when you get into those thoughts that it can be a rabbit hole,” he said. “So I’d rather kind of steer clean from them. At the end of the day, we’ve got a football season to play. I’ve got an agent and he’s hired for a reason, so he needs to do his job and (I’ll) do my job and we’ll see what happens.” As a 7th-round pick, Ojomo got a four-year rookie contract worth just $923,362 per year, which ranks outside the 250 highest-paid interior linemen in the NFL. Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Jalen Hurts strikes back – BGN JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Monday was a bounce back performance from Hurts and the offense after they were bested by Vic Fangio’s defense in the previous two practices. Encouraging to see. Mailbag: What simple improvements can the Eagles’ offense make? – PhillyVoice Question from @irisheagles (from Bluesky): Based on your limited viewing thus far, most likely UDFA to make the team. (Not named Rocco Underwood) My guy so far is S Maximus Pulley. Pulley had 85 tackles and 5 INTs (including two pick-sixes) for Wofford in 2025. He posted some All-22 of his highlights on YouTube. That’s a fun watch. Pulley reads quarterbacks’ eyes and makes big plays on the football against the pass, and he loves triggering downhill hunting tackles for loss in the run game. Fun player. In camp so far, he’s been around the football a lot when he has gotten reps, and he’s looked fearless playing the run. (Also, I don’t love what I have seen from Underwood so far. He has had some high snaps on punts, and as we pointed out in our Day 4 notes, the spin on his field goal snaps is imprecise.) Camp Notes – Good Day for Offense – Iggles Blitz We have talked about how deep this group is. They are going to make final cuts tough on Howie Roseman and the coaching staff. There are three locks. DeVonta Smith, Makai Lemon, Dontayvion Wicks. Hollywood Brown is a notch below that. He’s likely to make the roster, but does have to earn it. I’m guessing Cooper is in the lead for the number five spot now. There is a case for Wilson and Moore. Wilson has unique size at 6-6, 228 and is a good blocker. He’s willing to do the dirty work. Moore has good experience and has been a workhorse receiver in the past. Cooper seems to be playing the best for now and that has him in the lead. Lemon missed the team portion of practice today. Jeff McLane reported that it was due to an injury, but isn’t anything too serious. Eagles training camp diary: Jalen Hurts shines while rain moves practice indoors – The Athletic 10:52 a.m.: This is the play of the day and the best pass I’ve seen Hurts make all summer. He throws a dart to Moore deep down the middle of the field, placing the ball in a perfect spot over defenders for Moore to make the catch with nobody in front of him for a touchdown. The throw was probably 30-plus yards, and it hit Moore in stride. Hurts knew he threw a dime. He celebrated the pass in a way that’s atypical for the quarterback in a practice session. If he makes that pass in a game, talk radio spends the entire week on it, as opposed to his lack of touchdowns early in camp, which had been a topic over the weekend. A quick aside on that: The reason you haven’t read about the lack of touchdowns in camp so far in this space is that the context is required. They’ve only had one red-zone period before Monday’s session, and they’ve mostly been working on early-down installs from the middle of the field or his own territory. Unless Hurts throws deep balls, it’s not going to be a touchdown. Conversely, if they’re working in the red zone, you’ll see more touchdowns. title: Steelers training camp: Max Iheanachor highlights physical day of practice
summary: LATROBE – For a team that isn’t having any live tackling in training camp, the Pittsburgh Steelers certainly walked a very fine line today. full_text: Aug 03, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers offensive tackle Max Iheanachor (71) blocks linebacker T.J. Watt (90.)during a practice session at Training camp at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect LATROBE – For a team that isn’t having any live tackling in training camp, the Pittsburgh Steelers certainly walked a very fine line today. It was easily the most physical practice of camp, where we really gained some serious insight into the Steelers’ running game and how it could take shape over the course of the season. From rookie first rounder Max Iheanachor showing out, inside linebackers stepping up, and a wide receiver continuing to put together a strong start to camp, here is everything you need to know from day 6 of training camp. Max Iheanchor puts on a show The Steelers’ rookie first-rounder will very likely begin the season as a backup, but today showed exactly why the Steelers see a future with him. Iheanachor’s best play of the day came during 11-on-11’s on a toss play to Kaleb Johnson. Iheanachor won his rep and created a lane for the second-year back to pick up nearly 20 yards before being touched. Iheanachor also held his own, at the very least, in one on one blocking drills against each of the Steelers’ three best pass rushers in T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith, and Nick Herbig. It was by all accounts the best camp practice so far for the rookie who is showing serious promise already. Running backs finally get a chance to shine The practice felt much more physical in large part due to the fact that the Steelers were clearly emphasizing the run game today. It was still Rico Dowdle and Jaylen Warren leading the way with the first team. It’s still hard to decipher what exactly the plan is with the RB3 role. The Steelers have thrown Kaleb Johnson, Eli Heidenreich, and even Lew Nichols into those reps pretty evenly throughout camp thus far. Today, Kaleb Johnson had the best single run of any of the aforementioned backs. Ultimately, the Steelers will have some tough decisions to make in the running back room, but fans should feel more than confident in what the duo or Warren and Dowdle can accomplish. Roman Wilson continues to impress Wilson has consistently been running with the first team offense throughout camp, and he has made the most of those opportunities. Wilson beat Jamel Dean on a dig route for a wide open touchdown in red zone drills on a pass from Aaron Rodgers. That wouldn’t be the only time Rodgers found Wilson in the end zone, as the two connected on a slant route to end practice with a touchdown for the offense during their two-minute drill opportunity. Wilson continues to be one of Rodgers’ favorite targets in Latrobe. Payton Wilson and Cole Holcomb made impact plays While the running backs had their moment to shine today, so did the inside linebackers. While the offense was trying out run plays with all different running backs, Payton Wilson and Cole Holcomb seemed to always be in the backfield making plays. Wilson in particular saved what would have been a big gain for Jaylen Warren on one particular rep as he got in the backfield in a hurry. If Wilson and Holcomb improve at playing downhill, the Pittsburgh run defense could look a lot better than it did last season. Other notes It was a mixed bag from Jamel Dean today. Dean was beat by Roman Wilson and DK Metcalf for touchdowns on consecutive plays during red zone drills. He then ended his day with a diving pass breakup on a pass intended for Wilson during two-minute drills. Jaquan Brisker dropped what should have been an interception on a tipped ball over the middle during two-minute drills. This marks the second consecutive practice that Brisker has almost come down with a splash play. The jet sweep is back. Kaden Wetjen took a jet sweep from Will Howard during practice and gained about 10 yards, which got a big reaction from the crowd. Ben Skrownek got involved as a receiver, catching a touchdown from Mason Rudolph in red zone drills. Kaden Wetjen and Eli Heidenreich lined up as first-team kickoff returners, while Roman Wilson and Kaleb Johnson lined up as second-team returners. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Steelers stock report after Day Five of training camp
summary: LATROBE- There were plenty of reactions from people when it was reported that the Pittsburgh Steelers would not be having live tackling in camp this year. However, when the pads went on for the first time this season in Latrobe today, you could hear plenty of popping and the defense showing their physicality. Let’s take […]
full_text: Aug 03, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers safety Jaquan Brisker (3) participates in a practice session at Training camp at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect LATROBE- There were plenty of reactions from people when it was reported that the Pittsburgh Steelers would not be having live tackling in camp this year. However, when the pads went on for the first time this season in Latrobe today, you could hear plenty of popping and the defense showing their physicality. Let’s take a look at who did well and who didn’t in the Steelers’ fifth training camp practice, in stock-up and stock-down style. Stock Up: S Jaquan Brisker No defender benefited from having pads on and being able to be more physical today than Jaquan Brisker. Brisker had a huge pass breakup during the 11-0n-11 team period. Later in that same period, Brisker came screaming off the edge on a safety blitz and had Mason Rudolph dead to rights for what would have been a huge sack if they were allowed to tackle. Jaquan Brisker just came screaming off the edge on a blitz that would have ended up being a sack in a game. Brisker is having his best practice of camp today. — Joey Bray (@byjoeybray) August 3, 2026 The Steelers are particularly thin at the free safety spot, so Brisker will have to shoulder the majority of those responsibilities early in the season. It was easily the best performance that Brisker has put together so far this camp. CB Doneiko Slaughter If you are looking for a sleeper in the Steelers defensive back room, look no further than Doneiko Slaughter. With how well his fellow corner Asante Samuel Jr. has been playing, something that hasn’t been talked about enough is how well Slaughter has been playing this camp. Slaughter was around the ball a lot today and made several huge plays, including a pass breakup and intercepting a Will Howard downfield shot. Will Howard airs it out downfield but it’s picked off by Doneiko Slaughter who is having a really nice camp. — Joey Bray (@byjoeybray) August 3, 2026 The 2025 undrafted free agent out of Arkansas is having a phenomenal start to camp and is standing out in what figures to be a loaded cornerback room. If he continues this kind of play into the preseason, the Steelers will have a big decision to make on how many corners to keep. QB Drew Allar No quarterback has had more “wow” throws this camp than third-round pick Drew Allar, and today was no exception. Allar set his feet and threw a beauty of a deep ball to Cole Burgess in stride for a 50+ yard touchdown. Allar is still very much a work in progress, and Mike McCarthy has been working with Allar and Will Howard more than the other quarterbacks on the roster. However, it’s impossible to deny the impact plays we are seeing Allar make. For someone who isn’t expected to do much, if anything, this season, there have been plenty of reasons to get excited about Allar, and today was no exception. Drew Allar steps back and launches a perfect 60-yard bomb to Cole Burgess. Beautiful throw by Allar. — Joey Bray (@byjoeybray) August 3, 2026 Stock Down: OT Troy Fautanu It was a rough go for Fautanu today. The starting tackle had two false starts during 11-on-11 team periods that resulted in him ultimately getting pulled from the drill for a few plays. TJ Watt also seemed to be getting the best of Fautanu in blocking drills. All of this is no reason to sound the alarm or hit the panic button. Fautanu is one of the Steelers’ most talented and promising young players who just had a tough day. QB Will Howard It was not a day to remember for Will Howard. He had his moments in team periods connecting with Brandon Smith several times but also had moments where his accuracy and timing seemed to be off. Howard was also granted the opportunity to lead the offense down the field on a two-minute drill to end practice. It was an opportunity for him to end practice on a high note, but the drive was ultimately unsuccessful as the defense dominated in both two-minute drills to end practice. It will more than likely come down to performance in the preseason for Will Howard as he continues to compete with veteran Mason Rudolph for the backup quarterback job. title: Seahawks 2026 training camp, Day 9: News, notes, and updates from a hazy day in Renton
summary: It was another day of Seattle Seahawks training camp in Renton, albeit not in the best of conditions. The terrifying and deadly wildfires in Spokane have impacted and will impact the Seattle area throughout the week. Winds have blown the wildfire smoke in a westerly direction, which has decreased the air quality through thick throughout […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JULY 25: Devon Witherspoon #21 of the Seattle Seahawks reacts during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on July 25, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was another day of Seattle Seahawks training camp in Renton, albeit not in the best of conditions. The terrifying and deadly wildfires in Spokane have impacted and will impact the Seattle area throughout the week. Winds have blown the wildfire smoke in a westerly direction, which has decreased the air quality through thick throughout Western Washington on an otherwise very warm Tuesday. With Wednesday’s forecast set to be worse in terms of air quality, there is a chance that practice could be held indoors, but we’ll see how it goes. As I type this from my hotel room in Renton, the air quality index (AQI) is a moderate 99, but that’s borderline unhealthy. Our thoughts and condolences go out to everyone affected in the Spokane region. Here are the news and notes from Day 9 of camp. Seahawks training camp news and notes The defense barks back If you’ve read previous recaps and just watched the season premiere of ‘Hard Knocks’ , you would think the Seahawks offense was making the Seahawks defense look like it was 2023 all over again. And while there’s perhaps a kernel of truth there given Mike Macdonald’s palpable dissatisfaction with the defensive performances in practice (including the first padded one), the NFL’s best defense was not going to just roll over. From the Seattle Times’ Bob Condotta : The Seahawks were in full pads for the third time in camp Tuesday, and near the end conducted a few series of scrimmage sessions between the No. 1 offense and defense. The defense stopped the offense three-and-out on the first series when Sam Darnold couldn’t connect with Rashid Shaheed down the sidelines on third and long, with Nehemiah Pritchett, who appears to be winning the battle for the third corner spot, providing tight coverage. That line re Pritchett is definitely interesting and would be a continuation of his improvement from his second season. Here’s more from Seahawks.com’s John Boyle : During one portion of practice that operated like a modified scrimmage the No. 1 offense was twice stopped by the starting defense without scoring, and the No. 2 defense also was stymied by the No. 2 defense. There were also fewer big plays in general from the offense, and plenty of plays that stood out on defense, from multiple pass breakups by Ty Okada to an impressive run stop in the backfield by Ernest Jones IV, to Uchenna Nwosu releasing from the tackle blocking him to leap and bat down a Darnold pass. Ty Okada with the advantage over Bud Clark in the safety competition Also from Bob Condotta: While rookie safety Bud Clark has gotten some work with the No. 1 defense the past few practices, Ty Okada continues to work most consistently with the top defense alongside Love. Okada and Love got all the snaps as the deep safeties with the starters during the scrimmage sessions Tuesday, with Clark subbing in for a few plays as a third safety and working as a deep safety with the backup units. This is not a big surprise. If Okada starts over Clark it doesn’t mean Clark will be some sort of afterthought on defense. He’s been given a lot of responsibilities over the first couple of weeks of camp, and even the best rookies in history don’t just ascend that easily. Okada played very well in the absence of Coby Bryant and Julian Love last year, so I think this isn’t revelatory. We can still see Clark in a three-safety look, for example. And there’s still plenty of time for developments in the competition. Brian Fleury critiques the run game The new Seahawks offensive coordinator doesn’t sound like he’s too satisfied with how the new-look running game is performing. Of course, Zach Charbonnet is out due to injury but this may speak to more of the overall picture of blocking and making the right reads from the running back perspective. “I want us to be better. We are moving in the right direction. We have been efficient in practice, but I see things through a different lens. It’s not the success of the play on the practice field. I’m looking at everyone’s alignment and technique and there’s a lot of room for growth there. Not to say that we’re doing poorly but I expect that to be an extremely reliable portion of our game and it’s not there yet.” Tory Horton keeps on practicing This may seem like a nothing story, but given Horton’s recovery from a cracked tibia , it’s worth monitoring how much he’s practicing in camp. He had one maintenance day in the first week of camp and that seems to be it. Horton has ramped up nicely and is getting his work in with Sam Darnold. Last year he was a camp star, this year it’s about knocking off the rust and making that second-year leap after a promising (albeit truncated) rookie campaign. Sam Darnold to Tory Horton, who continues his return from the cracked shin that ended his rookie season last Nov. Ninth practice of #Seahawks training camp. Horton continuing to stack days, a good sign for Seattle’s offense. @thenewstribune pic.twitter.com/NdAZaMDWqa — Gregg Bell (@gbellseattle) August 4, 2026 Could the Jalen Milroe package return, new and improved? By most accounts, the second-year quarterback has had a positive training camp performance. After scarcely playing as a rookie and then not again after an ill-fated option play in Week 5 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, there is some wonder as to what’s next for Milroe in his development. Brian Fleury praised Milroe for being statistically efficient passing the ball during camp, and left the door open for his involvement in the offense this season. “Potentially. If he’s going to be active on gamedays, we’re going to have ways to use his skills to our advantage and surprise defenses with that. The decision about that is going to be based on how well he plays quarterback. We have to get over that hurdle first.” Jay Harbaugh press conference video Aden Durde press conference video Brian Fleury press conference video And now that I’m in Renton after briefly wondering if I’d have to fly from Portland to Seattle at the last minute … Field Gulls live at Seahawks training camp this week! That’s right. Field Gulls is already here in Renton and will be at VMAC and Lumen Fiel for three training camp practices! I will be going alongside Bryce Coutts (up from Canada) and Josh Hite (who’s local to the area) to the sessions on Aug. 5, 7, and 8. On those days, we will not have a news and notes summary of camp, but we will have our reactions and observations for you to read and watch. The Seahawks Syndicate crew consisting of myself, Bryce Coutts, Dan Viens, and Brandon Cain (who will be joining our podcasts from his California home) are also back for more training camp podcasts! Our three live shows will broadcast from our special recording area at Fast Fashion Brewing in SoDo! Emerald City Spectrum ’s Corbin Smith will be a special guest on Wednesday, Aug. 5 at 7:30 pm PT . You’re all invited to all three recordings, but we really want to see you at our Town Hall style show on Aug. 7 at 7:30 pm, in which there will be a ticket giveaway by Dan for the Seahawks-Cowboys preseason game. Get your questions in, come grab a beer, eat some pizza, and talk ‘Hawks! Our last show is 2:30 pm PT before Fan Fest on Saturday. Come hang with us at Fast Fashion and/or meet us at the berm on those two VMAC days.

Watch the first episode of Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks now on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/63MggvOQb6 — NFL (@NFL) August 5, 2026 The attention shifts to Sam Darnold, the man “who’s seen just about everything, maybe because he’s played just about everywhere,” says the dulcet voice of Liev Schreiber. “I’m not going around town being like, ‘yeah I won the Super Bowl,’” Darnold says in his interview. He really carries himself exceptionally well in a way that’s endearing to fans. Man, the offense appears to be kicking the defense’s ass in the early stages of training camp. Mike Macdonald tells Darnold this is “not where we want to be on defense.” He says they look really frustrated because the offense is making fast decisions. “They’re all on tilt now.” Devon Witherspoon: “Oh we look fried out here today.” DAMN! Beautiful pick over the middle by Patrick O’Connell on a Sam Darnold throw for Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Ernest Jones said “we need a pick right now” and he got it. Witherspoon is going to be a ‘Hard Knocks’ star. I can just feel it. Sam Darnold tells the rookies in the huddle they have to sign autographs, everyone who feels like signing autographs should also sign. It’s a clear theme in the organization given Macdonald instructs rookies to sign autographs. John Schneider checks in, addressing the Devon Witherspoon contract situation and Ian Rapoport’s report that Seattle was looking to make him the highest paid corner . “I called Ian and was like, ’Hey you need to call the agent and tell them that’s not f—king coming from us.” Everything is smoothed over after Spoon seemingly caught wind of the story. Witherspoon said, “My mind is go win football games, bro” and that the negotiations are not really on his mind right now. Julian Love mentioned in his press conference that Mike Macdonald talked to the team about the 1990s Chicago Bulls dynasty and how Michael Jordan couldn’t get over the hump. But there’s a greater point to it all besides Macdonald knowing so much ball. Why can’t the Seahawks have that perfect flow state of football? Mike Macdonald gave the Seahawks a history lesson on the 90s Bulls 🏀 Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks premieres tonight at 9pm ET on @HBOMax pic.twitter.com/o3aAeQwFio — NFL (@NFL) August 5, 2026 Speaking of basketball, we get the deep thoughts of Sam Darnold and Cooper Kupp on LeBron James signing with the Philadelphia 76ers. This might be too much NBA talk on Field Gulls without the SuperSonics back yet, so I’ll pause there. Can anyone link me to the article that said the Seahawks have the 32nd ranked running back room in the NFL? “WHO GIVES A F—K?!” says running backs coach, Thomas Hammock. If you can handle the profanity, this is a must-watch. . @Seahawks RB coach Thomas Hammock will have you ready to run through a brick wall 😤 Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks premieres tonight at 9pm ET on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/8s69vNv93B — NFL (@NFL) August 4, 2026 The Jadarian Price hype might be real. He looks so decisive and fast out there and this isn’t even the padded portion of practice yet. During the coaches’ meeting, you get a montage of assistants talking about who’s struggling and/or really need to step up when the pads come on. Thomas Hammock had a good review of Jadarian Price, the only player named in that segment. The July 30 practice was the first padded one of camp, so the crew wasted no time including that in the premiere. “God I love under-center seven-step drops.” – Sam Darnold. He also says it takes him back to “Joe Montana and the 49ers” but I think he jokingly pronounced it like the actor Joe Mantegna . A woman in the crowd got an autograph from Sam and said “you won my heart last year.” It was said in such an endearing, grandmotherly way. CONFIRMED: Sam Darnold went to the Travis Kelce/Taylor Swift wedding. You can see why the Seahawks signed Cooper Kupp. He might not be 2021 Kupp, but JSN said he’s like another coach out there. “Another explosive run because we can’t keep an edge!” Mike is NOT happy with the run defense in this padded practice. We get a close-up of a helmetless Connor O’Toole squaring up with Bobby Hart during practice. Macdonald has no time for such antics. “This is bullshit!” A little bit of shoving between Bryce Cabeldue and Tyrice Knight. A really needless Derick Hall chokeslam of Cabeldue that Macdonald is noticeably upset about. He’s speaking to Aden Durde about that incident. Eventually, Hall hugs it out after practice. That’s a wrap for the first episode! Good start, nothing too revealing about certain players, I imagine things will ramp up in the coming weeks as padded practices are more common and we start to see an increased roster churn. In my opinion, Mike Macdonald is going to come out of this series as a revelation to the rest of the NFL, and maybe to some Seahawks fans who aren’t as tuned into the team as we are. The cornerback signed a one-year deal with Washington in […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 14: Cornerback Ahkello Witherspoon #2 of the Seattle Seahawks runs off the field after a preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on August 14, 2021 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The Raiders defeated the Seahawks 20-7. (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images A one-time member of the Seattle Seahawks is calling it a career. Ahkello Witherspoon, who was in camp with former Seahawks defensive coordinator Dan Quinn and the Washington Commanders, was placed on the reserved/retired list on Tuesday, signaling the end of the line for the 31-year-old. The cornerback signed a one-year deal with Washington in March, after three seasons with the Los Angeles Rams. Originally a third-round pick of the San Francisco 49ers in 2017, Witherspoon signed a one-year, $4 million deal with the Seahawks at the end of his rookie deal in 2021. An explosive athlete with long, 33-inch arms, he figured to be a natural fit in then-defensive coordinator Ken Norton Jr.’s secondary. But, after he failed to win a job in training camp, he was traded to the Pittsburgh Steelers ahead of the regular season in exchange for a 2023 fifth-round pick . That selection was used on defensive end — and champion — Mike Morris, who played in every game during last season’s march to the Super Bowl. Across a nine-year career, Witherspoon started 64 games and notched 13 interceptions for the 49ers, Steelers, and Rams.
