To make room for Nelson’s addition, rookie UDFA wide receiver Kyre Duplessis was waived just a week after he himself joined the team. Since going undrafted, Nelson has spent time with the Miami Dolphins, Cincinnati Bengals, Denver Broncos, and New Orleans Saints, with his second stint in Denver taking him through most of the 2025 season before he was waived in May, though he is yet to appear in a regular season game. In four seasons at Nebraska, the 6-foot-3, 240-pound pass rusher registered 12 sacks and 26 TFLs. Duplessis, waived after a short stint in Seattle, had previously spent time with the Detroit Lions this offseason.

title: HBO ‘Hard Knocks’ director Pat Harris: Mike Macdonald ‘has embraced us being here’
summary: HBO’s critically acclaimed ‘Hard Knocks’ series premiered 25 years ago, when the defending Super Bowl champion Baltimore Ravens were chronicled throughout training camp and preseason. It was a groundbreaking behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of an NFL locker room, the off-field lives of coaches, players, and other staff, the tough world of roster cuts, […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JUNE 12: A sign at the entrance to the Seattle Seahawks headquarters and training facility at the Virginia Mason Athletic Center on June 12, 2024, in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Kirby Lee/Getty Images) | Getty Images HBO’s critically acclaimed ‘Hard Knocks’ series premiered 25 years ago, when the defending Super Bowl champion Baltimore Ravens were chronicled throughout training camp and preseason. It was a groundbreaking behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of an NFL locker room, the off-field lives of coaches, players, and other staff, the tough world of roster cuts, and countless other aspects of the sport the average fan previously had limited or no access to. At long last, after previous resistance over a decade ago , the Seattle Seahawks are finally on board. Furthermore, they’re the first reigning Super Bowl champion since the Ravens to be ‘Hard Knocks’ headliners. On Monday, Field Gulls had the opportunity to interview Pat Harris, lead director of ‘Hard Knocks’, who provided some insight into the filming process and how the Seahawks have taken to their first appearance. A former high school quarterback, Harris has been with the program in some capacity for over a decade, and this year he’s tasked with directing a season centered around the Super Bowl champions. This was a 20-minute interview, so some questions were omitted for length reasons and may be used another article, while some answers were condensed for clarity. You’ve been around ‘Hard Knocks’ for over a decade, but this is your second season as the lead director, last year you got to chronicle your childhood team, the Buffalo Bills? Looking back on it now, what was that experience like for you personally? Pat Harris : “It’s very surreal even hearing you say that I’ve been doing this a decade, uh, is still kind of crazy to me. I don’t really see myself as having been doing it that long, but that is factually correct. Last year was surreal. I think even getting to see some of those random phone memories that pop up, even knowing I got to spend time with my family during the month of July and August, which, unfortunately I have not been able to do in the last decade. I think those are just cool memories that I’ll always have with me and always kind of cherish. So I’m very happy to just [have] good memories.” Did you have any standout moments from last season? I know Buffalo Joe, Joe Andressen, him making the roster again last year was great just for the local rooting interest. Harris: “Yeah, so I actually personally love the Josh Allen, [biometric expert] Chris Hess stuff we did . That was a piece, actually, tried to… I read some stuff on Chris Hess years prior and pitched a piece at NFL Films, and it didn’t ever come together. So then it was kind of a full circle moment when we found out Chris was going to be coming to camp. I got to do some of the biometric stuff and the super high speed throwing mechanic stuff. So that was kind of a cool, personal project, getting to see how that all came together and then, kind of letting our camera people,flex their muscles a little bit. That’s always a cool one that still sticks out in my head.” This is the first time a reigning Super Bowl champion has been featured in a traditional training camp Hard Knocks since the very first edition 25 years ago with the Baltimore Ravens. Do you think, in a way, that this actually can garner even more general viewer interest knowing you’re chronicling the champs? Harris: “I would hope so. I think that’s our plan. You know, it was kind of similar to the Bills last year, picking some of the best teams in the league and trying to showcase the stories a little different than it might be with a team coming off the first overall pick, like we’ve done in the past. So I think the hope is that, yeah, we want to obviously showcase the Seahawks more, if those East Coast fans just don’t know as much about this team. We want to be able to take this opportunity to do that, but I’m hoping that, yeah, I mean, it doesn’t get any better than the Super Bowl champs.” “ I think [Mike Macdonald] has just been incredible. He has welcomed us with open arms. He’s embraced us being here.” HBO Hard Knocks director Pat Harris It’s interesting you bring that up with the East Coasters because it seems like the Seahawks have generally been perceived as this sort of afterthought champion, just like those Ravens were, kind of like an out of nowhere team to win it all. Do you see this as also an opportunity for non-Seahawks fans not just to get to know the team better, but some of the players and their personalities and also just help viewers get a better sense of ‘Ah, this is why Seattle was able to win the Super Bowl’ ? Harris : “No question. I think that was kind of our thought coming in and it’s exceeded expectations, I think, since we’ve been here, starting with Coach [Mike] Macdonald. I think he’s just been incredible. He has welcomed us with open arms. He’s embraced us being here. And then there’s just so many personalities. I think it’s fun to see the players getting comfortable with us after a couple days and really just trying to, you know, being able to showcase their true selves, they’re not nervous, having us around or anything. So I’m hoping that that’s kind of the two-pronged effect that obviously makes for great TV, but then the random fans can just kind of fall in love with players and people and ideally an organization.” If you could take a time machine and go back to, say, the 2013-2014 era, back when the Seahawks actually turned down hard knock, do you think it would have been an amazing experience to have ‘Hard Knocks’ be there during the Legion of Boom years? Harris : “From what everybody’s told us here, yes, they said that was like the cliche ‘made for TV’ team. I think it would have almost been too perfect looking back. You know, I wish we could have. It’s been fun seeing some of those guys pop around training camp, even the clip we posted with Richard Sherman coming by [to see Bud Clark]. So I think it’s fun to see them show up, but I think that would have been probably a pretty iconic one as well to document that team.” . @Seahawks rookie safety Bud Clark was so psyched to meet @RSherman_25 💚 Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks premieres Aug 4 on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/TqkiAVmjxq — NFL (@NFL) July 31, 2026 Some teams kind of run away from ‘Hard Knocks,’ some teams welcome with open arms. So what can you say so far about how the Seahawks organization has taken to the ‘Hard Knocks’ crew being there and just being a part of this whole process for the first time? Harris: “They’ve embraced it right off the bat, I think we had a very good first conversation. We came down here when the Seahawks were first announced. Met with [Mike Macdonald], GM [John Schneider], front office, and it was amazing to see their—I think they were excited for this opportunity from the beginning and that’s held true all throughout. “And I think that’s, you know, kind of been a trickle-down effect for all players and staff and coaches and the fact that everyone’s embraced it, has been great for us. Our crew, you know, we say countlessly, that everyone top to bottom has been so friendly and really welcomed us here. So I think it’s been great for that perspective. And I think the players just feel comfortable knowing their coach is being himself. They’re not seeing anything change. I think they’re just operating the exact same way.” And it also has helped that the weather has just been lovely at this time of year. It dispels the myth that it rains in Seattle all the time. Harris: “It’s amazing. I think a lot of smiles from our crew—we’re definitely used to camp, you know, usually being pretty hot and humid and uncomfortable and that has been far from it. We preemptively had to get crew sweatshirts this year for the first time because thought it might be a little chilly in the mornings, which it might be to…

title: 49ers News: Opening the injury report today with my hands over my eyes
summary: How a friendly 49ers competition produced training camp’s most pleasant surprise so far (paywall)“Jack and I have had a lot of conversations,” Green said. “He’s a real savvy football player, and Jack has real good ball skills. He has a very aggressive playing style when it comes to playing the ball, and I try and […]
full_text: A Silicon Valley Power substation in Santa Clara, California, US, on Monday, Nov. 3, 2025. Two of the world's biggest data center developers have projects in Nvidia Corp.'s hometown that may sit empty for years because the local utility isn't ready to supply electricity. Photographer: Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images | Bloomberg via Getty Images How a friendly 49ers competition produced training camp’s most pleasant surprise so far (paywall) “Jack and I have had a lot of conversations,” Green said. “He’s a real savvy football player, and Jack has real good ball skills. He has a very aggressive playing style when it comes to playing the ball, and I try and pick that up. “You should try to learn from who you can because we’re all in this together, basically.” …“He’s a great corner,” Jones said of Green. “I think he has the potential to be one of the true lockdown corners in the league, you know what I’m saying? As far as from me to him, I’ve just been trying to really tell him to go get that ball. Focus on the ball and not just PBUs. “That’s what I am preaching. … We’re all making each other better. A guy makes a play, and that gives you an energy boost.” Raheem Morris has been a big part of that, and Green is really enjoying his third defensive coordinator in three years. You get the sense that the 2024 second-round pick is not just saying that because it’s what people want to hear. “It’s easier to play faster, and I feel like he’s more detailed with just, like, realistic things, and there’s a lot less thinking,” Green said. “I’ve been able to get attached to guys and contest catches, make plays. That’s what he wants, and that fits us.” …“People don’t just wake up with that ability to go get the ball,” Jones said. “It comes with film study, it comes with practice and repetition. Sometimes you got to take a million reps just to get it right one time. “I played receiver too growing up. But I didn’t want to get thrown the ball. I wanted to go take it.” Source: Details of Deebo Samuel’s 49ers contract tied to usage, playoffs “Samuel will receive a $200,000 bonus if his combined rushing and receiving yards are 600 to 802 on the season. He will receive $450,000 if he achieves 803 scrimmage yards or more. He will earn double those amounts if the 49ers make the playoffs. Samuel will make an additional $200,000 if he scores five or six touchdowns in the regular season. If he scores seven or more touchdowns, he’ll receive a $450,000 incentive. Again, those figures will be doubled if the 49ers make the playoffs. Samuel will receive a $250,000 bonus for the season if he ranks 10th or better in average yards per kick return (minimum 20 returns). He’ll receive another $250,000 if he meets that incentive and the 49ers make the postseason. Samuel also is scheduled to make $250,000 if he plays 68 percent or more of the 49ers’ offensive snaps.” How 49ers’ offense, defense can benefit from Raheem Morris’ schematic changes “The 49ers’ changes on defense include expanded usage of five defensive linemen and a simplified set of coverage assignments designed to enable the cornerbacks and safeties to play fast without being required to make too many split-second adjustments.” Kawakami: ‘We know who we are’ — Brock Purdy on QB play and the 49ers’ 2026 vision (paywall) “The most visible proof came toward the end of last season, after Purdy came back from his injury and looked in complete command of every part of the Shanahan offense. Purdy “canned” plays — Shanahan terminology for switching to an alternate call — swiftly and with confidence and just seemed to run things like he knew most of the answers before the questions were asked.” 49ers’ Eddy Piñeiro gets kick out of finally finding job security in NFL (paywall) “That’s why I think it’s so hard for rookies when they come in,” said Piñeiro, who finally found some stability with the Panthers from 2022-24. “It’s just such a short leash they have with kickers. You miss kicks, you’re gone. It’s just part of the process, and I wish I would have known that faster in my career. I’m like, ‘Oh, I miss one, I’m gonna be OK.’ No, you’re not gonna be OK.” 49ers training camp Week 3: Full practice schedule, media availability, and key dates “ Wednesday, August 5 10:15 a.m. – Practice Following practice – Chris Foerster press conference Following Foerster – Player availability Thursday, August 6 10:15 a.m. – Practice Following practice – Raheem Morris press conference Following Morris – Player availability Friday, August 7 Walk-through – No media availability Saturday, August 8 9:15 a.m. – Klay Kubiak press conference 10:15 a.m. – Practice Following practice – Player availability” 49ers rookie De’Zhaun Stribling reveals what he’s learning from Mike Evans, veteran teammates “We kind of weren’t even ready for the whole thing,” Stribling admitted during a conversation with Matt Maiocco of NBC Sports Bay Area. “Everyone was still parking cars and trying to get set up. And got the call from a San Jose area code.” 49ers rookie Jaden Dugger… the pass rusher? “Dugger went from practicing with the off-ball linebackers to doing the same individual drills as Osa Odighizuwa in a matter of a week. Dugger may need to beef up. He’s 240 pounds. That’s not somebody who is going to hold up on a down-to-down basis. However, he’s 6’5” with a 7’ wingspan. Dugger’s 35” arms should allow him to stay clean, but it’s going to take some time to learn the trades of a pass rusher. The flashes are happening. During Monday’s practice, Dugger beat Trent Williams on a rep. That’s right, one of the best left tackles in the game. That’s where Dugger’s athleticism shows. A 10-foot-6 inch broad jump translates to a quick first step that would give any tackle, even Williams, problems. title: Deebo Samuel ‘in phenomenal shape’ as teammates fired up for his return
summary: The San Francisco 49ers had a reunion with Dre Greenlaw earlier this offseason, signing him to a one-year deal after his one year away. Now, the same has happened with Deebo Samuel, who returned on a one-year deal after spending the 2025 season with the Washington Commanders. Samuel was one of the veteran wide receivers […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Jacory Croskey-Merritt #22 of the Washington Commanders celebrates with Deebo Samuel #1 after scoring a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys in the third quarter of a game at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers had a reunion with Dre Greenlaw earlier this offseason, signing him to a one-year deal after his one year away. Now, the same has happened with Deebo Samuel, who returned on a one-year deal after spending the 2025 season with the Washington Commanders. Samuel was one of the veteran wide receivers still unsigned as training camp began, and the fit made sense with San Francisco after Ricky Pearsall experienced knee soreness that will now cost him the entire 2026 season. Samuel slots into that No. 2 wide receiver role for San Francisco, who also has Mike Evans out with a quad injury, and will look to make an immediate impact in training camp fitting back in with his old teammates. And it’s safe to say they’re excited for his return. “Oh, I’m so fired up, man,” running back Christian McCaffrey said of Samuel’s return. “Yeah, Deebo, he has such a presence on the field. When he’s in the game, you have to account for him in so many different ways. And, you know, I look at like a guy like Dre Greenlaw on defense. When you get him back, it’s just something about that gives you a little bit of confidence. And it’s the same with Deebo. He gives us all so much confidence. You know when he’s in the game, he’s got your back. He’s such a fun dude to play with and a game breaker.” Samuel’s versatility had been a huge part of his game in San Francisco, where he was utilized as a runner and a receiver. The rushing element wasn’t tapped into much last year in Washington, and it’s unclear how much of a role he’ll see there for the 49ers this year. But he is being used as a kick returner, adding to his versatility. That sentiment was echoed by fullback Kyle Juszczyk, who added that Samuel looks in great shape early on in camp. “Deebo is the best,” Juzczyk said. “He is such an incredible teammate, he’s such a good friend. He’s an incredible football player, so we are really happy to have him in the locker room just because he brings the best vibes and positivity. But we are also happy to have him on the field because he’s still got juice and he can still go out there and make good plays.” “He came in and he looks like he’s in phenomenal shape. And first day in pads, he’s making an impact right away. Looked like the old Deebo. I can’t say enough positive things about how excited we are to have him.” Samuel and Trent Williams have also maintained a close relationship, and the left tackle believes the wideout will bounce back in 2026 after dealing with some adversity this offseason. “Since he left, we still remain super, super close,” Williams said of Samuel. “We talk at least once a week, sometimes more. Seen him a lot in person. So honestly, I’m happy because I know that we’re going to get the best version of Deebo that the NFL has seen. He’s coming from a situation where he’s kind of been doubted a little bit. “And, you know, I think that may be the first piece of adversity he’s ran into as a football player because he’s been uber talented on every level. Every time he touched the ball, he’s exciting to see. And that’s the crazy thing about the NFL. You go somewhere and the team don’t do as good, and then everybody kind of writes you off. I love it though. That’s one of the things that adversity that every player needs, that gas in the tank that every player needs to go and, and push themselves past limits they haven’t seen.” Samuel mentioned himself that he had been regularly communicating with Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch, so it wasn’t a surprise that a return happened following the Pearsall injury. The 49ers need to improve their separation at wide receiver, which was where Pearsall was expected to contribute the most. But Shanahan has worked with Samuel’s skill set before and now has the task of finding ways to utilize him in the offense alongside Mike Evans.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: The Rams will fly into Australia the day before playing the 49ers
summary: We’re still a little over a month away from the San Francisco 49ers’ season opener against the Los Angeles Rams. If you’ve been away all summer, the game won’t be played in California. Instead, it’ll be the first-ever game in Australia. The way that each team is handling the travel schedule is vastly different. According […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 22: Sean McVay, head coach of the Los Angeles Rams, embraces Kyle Shanahan, head coach of the San Francisco 49ers, after a game at SoFi Stadium on September 22, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Kevork Djansezian/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re still a little over a month away from the San Francisco 49ers’ season opener against the Los Angeles Rams. If you’ve been away all summer, the game won’t be played in California. Instead, it’ll be the first-ever game in Australia . The way that each team is handling the travel schedule is vastly different. According to ESPN’s Dan Graziano , the Rams are waiting a day before the game to fly into Melbourne: The Rams’ Week 1 game is against the 49ers in the league’s first game in Australia. The Rams are handling the trip differently than the 49ers, flying in the day before the game and flying out right after. It’s similar to what they did for a game last year in London, when they arrived the morning of the game, beat the Jaguars and got right back on a plane to go home. The Rams actually had people from their organization fly from Los Angeles to Melbourne and back, tracking when and how much they felt the effects of the jet lag. They came to the conclusion that the best way to handle it would be to prepare at home, fly as close to the game as possible, let adrenaline carry them through the game and then fly right home and rest up on the back end. Their Week 2 game is on Monday night at home against the Giants . The idea of testing the potential effects makes a ton of sense. It sounds like the Rams are going to do their best to completely avoid any potential jet lag or distractions, making this as much of an “in and out” trip as it gets. Sean McVay said as much during the Rams trip to London last year: “We’re like SEAL Team 6. We’re in and out before you know what happened.” There’s roughly a 17-hour difference between the Pacific Time Zone and Melbourne. The 49ers will have plenty of time to get acclimated, as they plan on leaving a full nine days before kickoff. This offseason, head coach Kyle Shanahan said, “Usually when you travel with a 16-hour flight, you don’t want to get there the day before because you lose like a whole day there or two and you’re just messed up. If that’s accurate, the Rams’ plans could look foolish, unless they’re really banking on adrenaline.

title: 49ers’ new return man? Deebo Samuel was among the league leaders in 2025
summary: Special teams coordinator Brant Boyer spoke with the media on Monday. When asked how the competition for returners was going, he said, “I think [Jacob] Cowing, [Will] Pauling, and [Jordan] Watkins, all those guys are back there. Junior Bergen. There’s a big handful of guys, and hopefully they can make great decisions and catch the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 05: Deebo Samuel Sr. #1 of the Washington Commanders in action against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on October 05, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Special teams coordinator Brant Boyer spoke with the media on Monday. When asked how the competition for returners was going, he said, “I think [Jacob] Cowing, [Will] Pauling, and [Jordan] Watkins, all those guys are back there. Junior Bergen. There’s a big handful of guys, and hopefully they can make great decisions and catch the ball first and foremost. That’s important. General manager John Lynch said this past weekend that we’d see Samuel in the return game. Boyer stressed decision-making. He continued, saying, “It’s a matter of, can they make the right decisions? Can they block a gunner when they’re supposed to? Can they let a ball hit the ground when they’re supposed to? Can they go up and catch a fair catch when they’re supposed to? There’s a lot more that goes into it than just returning the ball. We’re trying to find the guy that has the whole package, that we can count on every week, that can catch the ball and make great decisions.” There isn’t much experience on the roster. All of Jacob Cowing’s stats came in 2024, when he returned 28 punts and a single kickoff. He’s the only one with returner experience. It seems like the punt return job is Cowing’s to lose. However, the addition of Deebo Samuel might mean Cowing has competition at kick returner. It might also make it more difficult for a player like Cowing to make the roster. Boyer spoke highly of Samuel: “Well, certainly when they told me that he was coming I was like, ‘Hell yeah. Let’s go.’ Because he is a difference maker. He’s obviously proven and he’s done it at a very, very high level. I’m really anxious, we were all talking about it, to get him in our scheme. I’ve watched him and really liked what he’s done throughout his career, liked him coming out of college. He’s a hell of a player and he’s really tough to tackle. He’s got speed to take it to the house all the time. Again, any time you can add a guy like that to the roster, you’re jumping up for joy as a special teams coach.” Samuel hasn’t returned a punt in his career, but does have 41 kickoff returns, with 32 of those coming in the previous two seasons. During his final season with the 49ers, Deebo averaged 31.3 yards per return, including a 60-yarder. Last season with the Commanders, Samuel was still over 30 yards per return and had a 69-yarder. Both of those would have been among the top 5 had Samuel had enough attempts to qualify. If the 49ers used Samuel to return in 2024, when the receiving room was thin, you’d think they’d give him the opportunity in 2026, with Mike Evans and De’Zhaun Stribling on the roster, no? Perhaps the team will see what Watkins, Pauling, and Bergen show in the preseason. If they aren’t up to par or look like they bring anything to the table, the fallback option is Deebo.

title: Ji’Ayir Brown says the previous 49ers schemes didn’t want football players. Raheem Morris does
summary: Steve Wilks, Nick Sorensen, Robert Saleh. One of those names is not like the others, though all three were the San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinators each of the last three years. Wilks and Sorensen were fired after one year while Saleh left in the offseason to become head coach of the Tennessee Titans. That should […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: Ji'Ayir Brown #27 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Steve Wilks, Nick Sorensen, Robert Saleh. One of those names is not like the others, though all three were the San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinators each of the last three years. Wilks and Sorensen were fired after one year while Saleh left in the offseason to become head coach of the Tennessee Titans. That should tell you the difference. 49ers safety Ji’Ayir Brown says all three had something in common: schemes lacking football players. The 49ers safety may have found his scheme in Raheem Morris, who succeeded Saleh as defensive coordinator. “Raheem is dope, bro.” Brown said when speaking to the media on Monday. “Super dope. He wants football players. Previous schemes we’ve been in haven’t been that, haven’t wanted that. Raheem wants you to play football. He wants instinctive players. He wants guys who can get out there and play ball and read the quarterback.” It’s no secret the 49ers and their fans had a common issue with Wilks and Sorensen. Saleh has his own criticisms, but there was no comparison between his defenses and the two coaches before him. According to Brown, Saleh’s scheme had some severe issues. “The scheme fits all of us,” Brown continued. “It’s been great to see us transition into this explosive, D-back unit.” Or maybe he has a point. Wilks had one of the most stacked defenses in the league—and somehow it had head-scratching brain farts every game. The less said about Sorensen, the better; he’s simply a guy in over his head. Then there’s Saleh. Did the 49ers defense improve? Oh yeah — even with the injuries. Those injuries really left the 49ers without a next man up of sorts. When a starter went down, things didn’t take a step back; they hit a massive stumbling block. A good example was when Nick Bosa went down with a torn ACL; the 49ers’ pass rush plummeted. Expected when losing a player like Bosa, but they really didn’t have a plan “B” of sorts. Brown isn’t going to point any fingers. “I’m not going to even go there,” Brown said. “What happened last year was what happened last year. Could things have been better? Of course. But I’m not going to hold nobody accountable to that. I’ll just hold myself accountable and take whatever comes with that. But what happened last year was last year.” Brown was seen as a possible starter in 2025, but lost the starting safety job in September to Marques Sigle . Shortly after the demotion, Brown said he was a top-5 player in the NFL. Whether you agree with top-5 or not, Brown did emerge as the season went on. His huge game against the Carolina Panthers in November definitely had everyone chatting. Unfortunately, Brown couldn’t stay consistent, and it led to an offseason where he feuded with former 49ers safety Donte Whitner of all people . The 49ers notched just six interceptions in 2025. Brown was tied with Deommodore Lenoir for having the most with two. He also had one forced fumble. In practice on Monday, Brown notched a pass breakup. On Saturday, Morris spoke of Brown’s rushing potential when there were injuries along the defensive line. Brown will be a player to watch. Not just because of the 49ers’ safety position, but because he may have finally found a scheme he can thrive in. He’s had his moments of excellence, but if Morris can help get some consistency, then he might finally be the top player he claims he is.

He might end up being more of a guy who creates sacks for someone else than one who racks them up personally — more pressures than finishes. What I’m confident of is his ability as a disruptor, even if it’s a bit role. I do know I saw him cook Colton McKivitz at least once on Monday. Another time, I saw him spin inside violently, forcing Dominick Puni to help. He and McKivitz ultimately drove Height into the ground, but it also meant Puni had to account for him. It was a proactive double team on a rookie. If people are having to double-team Height the way they double Nick Bosa or Osa Odighizuwa, that’s going to result in sacks and meaningful pressure elsewhere on the line. I’m legitimately all in on this kid as a pass rusher. He has a four-move bag I outlined in the draft guide that’s predicated on converting speed and hesitation……Good day for both starting corners. Deommodore Lenoir had at least a couple of breakups, including one on Jake Tonges. Renardo Green looked pretty good. I loved that he, Marques Sigle, and Dre Brown were all communicating together. That communication is fundamental to raising the defense’s ceiling. Green had a full clamp on Jordan Watkins in the red zone….. Tonges looks really good. I think he’s a great No. 2 receiving tight end I’d expect production from him regardless of George Kittle’s status. Jordan Watkins showed up from time to time and looked alright. There was one incredible catch from Brayden Willis: a back-shoulder, one-handed grab, defended by (I think) Patrick McMorris. That was the only time I really noticed Willis. Good stuff from Junior Bergen. Popped up in a lot of different places. Demarcus Robinson also had at least one nice grab early on….Keep an eye on Bryson Eason. He’s a hefty guy who packs some real punch with his hands. I think he has a route to make the team, especially with Gracen Halton not practicing.“ Mike Evans joins 49ers’ growing list of injuries despite team’s dialed-back camp (paywall) “Jaden Dugger was drafted in the fifth round to play linebacker. His versatility, however, was notable after he played linebacker, edge and safety at different points in his college career. Monday was the first time Dugger worked with the defensive line group, which was particularly shorthanded due to injury. Dugger recorded what would’ve been a sack in a live setting from a defensive end’s alignment.” Matt Maiocco’s 53-man 49ers roster projection 1.0 ahead of the 2026 NFL season “Cowing looks the most comfortable among all the candidates when he is fielding punts. Winning that job in the return game will lock him into one of those spots.….The last couple spots [on the defensive line] are wide open, and such players as Sample, Sebastian Valdez, Bryson Eason and James Thompson still have plenty of time to win their spots….There is good competition among the cornerbacks. Veteran Nate Hobbs is definitely right there for one of these spots, as is fourth-round draft pick Ephesians Prysock. Depending on how he looks in the two joint practices and three preseason games, Prysock could be a no-brainer to win a spot on the team. The 49ers might feel that way, anyway, because he was selected in the fourth round and has a lot of promise. But, right now, Luter is looking good as one of the backups behind the top four guys: Lenoir, Green, Stout and Jones.” Do the 49ers finally have a Trent Williams heir? Enrique Cruz Jr. is off to a good start (paywall) “Instead, the least experienced of them all, rookie Enrique Cruz Jr., bounded into the huddle like an eager golden retriever, and the second-team offense didn’t skip a beat. “Coach, who goes in?” Cruz recalled excitedly asking Chris Foerster. The offensive line coach’s quick response: “You! You go in!” The sequence ended up being a good way to get rid of Day 1 jitters, Cruz said. And it offered a glimpse at one of the rookie’s top qualities: He isn’t shy. “He has an infectious personality,” Cruz’s high school coach, Nick Hildreth, said. “He’s fun, he’s so outgoing, he’s so happy to be there. I’ve never seen him where he’s negative toward anybody, ever.”….. and though the two hit it off right away, there were some early obstacles. The first was Cruz fancied himself a basketball player. Even after Hildreth convinced him to give football a try, he informed his coach he was a wideout. “And I’m like, ‘You’re not a wideout,’” Hildreth told Cruz, who grew to 6 feet 5, 252 pounds before his senior season. “We did throw him the ball his senior year. He got the ball in his hands once.” Another problem was Cruz’s GPA, which fell as low as 1.4. His worst subject? Cruz laughs and admits it was Spanish — funny because his family’s from Puerto Rico and he speaks the language. “It was a different version of Spanish,” he said. “I’d be at my grandma’s house doing it, and my grandma would tell me it’s wrong, it’s the wrong term because it’s Puerto Rican Spanish and not Spanish Spanish. So it was pretty hard for me to learn.”….Hildreth also convinced Cruz to drop his beloved basketball for wrestling, a sport he’d never tried before but one that would make him a better offensive lineman. “It’s hard on the ego to be the biggest, baddest kid in the building and then go to the wrestling room and get beat up,” Hildreth said. Cruz truly took off as a junior. He was tall, powerful, long-limbed, and he could pull and wreak havoc on opposing linebackers. During the playoffs that year, Cruz caused a riot of euphoria on the Willowbrook sideline when he blocked a highly touted opponent out of the back of the end zone and into a snowbank. “That was the beginning of his coming-out party,” Hildreth said. By the time he graduated, his GPA was up to 3.0, and he’d gotten a scholarship from Syracuse. Hildreth essentially told Foerster that story when the 49ers assistant flew to Willowbrook to give Cruz a workout before the draft.“ 49ers star Nick Bosa shares why he feels faster after his 3rd ACL injury ”You learn something every time you do it, every year really, injury or not, you kind of learn how to prepare a certain way to be your best. When I came off of the one in 2020, it forced me to..I don’t know how to…

title: Titans need to break passing yards curse in 2026
summary: The Tennessee Titans have not fielded an effective passing offense in five seasons. That’s an extremely sad sentence to write, but it’s true. This past campaign, they ranked 30th as an offense in passing yards, averaging 166.1 per contest. They finished the 2024 campaign ranked 26th in passing yards under Brian Callahan and Will Levis, […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans Offensive Coordinator Brian Daboll addresses the media during his first press conference at Ascension Saint Thomas Sports Park in Nashville, Tenn., Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026. | DENNY SIMMONS / THE TENNESSEAN / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans have not fielded an effective passing offense in five seasons. That’s an extremely sad sentence to write, but it’s true. This past campaign, they ranked 30th as an offense in passing yards, averaging 166.1 per contest. They finished the 2024 campaign ranked 26th in passing yards under Brian Callahan and Will Levis, averaging 195.1 per game. They were 29th in 2023 (180.4/game), 30th in 2022 (171.4), 24th in 2021 (201.1), and 23rd in 2020 (228.3). That’s an unfathomable streak of consistently being a bottom-10 passing offense. The Titans invested significant offseason resources to hopefully change that in 2026. After hiring a defensive minded head coach in Robert Saleh, the Titans hired one of the most sought-after offensive coordinator candidates in Brian Daboll. Coach Daboll loved Cam Ward as a prospect and is legitimately excited to develop him this year. The Titans also invested big at wide receiver. They drafted Carnell Tate with the fourth overall pick and paid Wan’Dale Robinson $70 million in free agency. Both additions were approved by Daboll, and he’s expected to make them the focal point of his passing offense. The Titans are arguably deeper at wide receiver than they’ve ever been. They kept Calvin Ridley via a restructured contract as opposed to making him a salary cap casualty. They also have sophomores Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor. At tight end, they have the developing Gunnar Helm, and paid Daniel Bellinger $8 million per year in free agency. The Titans need to field a significantly more impactful aerial attack in 2026 than they have in several seasons. A lot of that will be decided by how Ward develops as a sophomore quarterback. Adding supporting pieces like Daboll, Tate, and Robinson should have a monumental impact. The Titans have the pieces in place to effectively pass the ball in 2026.

Call me biased but as I said in the draft process & since – I would still take JD5 over Caleb, who I view as a wild card, inconsistent roller coaster — Chris Russell AKA the 🐓🐓! (@Russellmania621) August 4, 2026 Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Training Camp Review: OL vs DL 1-on-1s The Washington Commanders had their first padded practice of training camp on Monday. There’s always a different level of hype and intensity when the pads come on for the first time and we finally get to see some physicality, especially in the trenches. Unfortunately, the team is still being very secretive with clips being posted online and fans in attendance being allowed to film, but some fans still posted a few clips One of the few clips I was able to find was a good one. It came from @AsiasAnalysis on twitter. She posted a clip of offensive line vs defensive line one-on-one drills. This is one of the best drills to watch when the pads come on so it was good to see a few reps. I’ll post the full clip from Asia first and then cut up each individual clip to break down in more detail. pic.twitter.com/gi5EtOJZV9 — Asia’s Analysis (@AsiasAnalysis) August 3, 2026 The first full rep we see is right tackle Josh Conerly Jr. against free agent signing Odafe Oweh . I wrote a few weeks ago about Conerly learning from Tunsil and you can see some improvements here, but still some things to work on. Oweh takes his first few steps up the field, challenging the edge. Conerly does a better job staying square compared to last year. His feet, hips and shoulders are much more square to the line of scrimmage than they were during the season last year. That’s a positive start. However, Oweh hits Conerly with a spin move. Conerly was guilty of giving up inside rushes a fair bit last year and part of the reason for that is that he often didn’t have his cleats in the ground at the point of contact. You can see here that as Oweh makes contact, Conerly is shuffling his inside foot backwards. Oweh works into his spin and if you pause the clip when you can see the full number 98 on Oweh’s back, you’ll see that both of Conerly’s feet are off the ground. That gives him no base to absorb any post. It’s a nice, tight spin from Oweh to get inside, but credit to Conerly for not giving up on the play. Conerly has the athletic ability to recover from bad situations and he does that here somewhat. He works to get his inside hand on Oweh’s chest to slow him down and try to delay the rush. Conerly leans on him and keeps a firm grip, enabling him to push Oweh down the line slightly. This would have bought the quarterback time to shuffle to his right and potentially scramble away from the pressure. Overall, it’s not an ideal rep from Conerly but one that shows some significant improvements with regards to staying square, while also showing there’s still some work to go, which we expect of all second year players. On the other side of the ball, it was a nice rush from Oweh that clearly generated plenty of pressure and would have forced the quarterback off the spot. With his athleticism, Oweh would have had a decent chance of breaking free and chasing down many quarterbacks too. I wrote about this clip from @AsiasAnalysis of Commanders OL vs DL 1-on-1s yesterday. Some fun reps, broke each one down: https://t.co/ib7afy3TBY https://t.co/Or5OUS41RF — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 4, 2026 Commanders Roundtable Commanders notes: McCaffrey stands out; defense brings the heat Luke McCaffrey — The Biggest Winner of the Day If you weren’t talking about Luke McCaffrey before today, you will be now. He was the standout of the practice. McCaffrey hauled in multiple deep catches, the most eye-catching of which was a 40-plus yard seam route out of the slot where Daniels put the ball right on him in traffic, splitting Mike Sainristil and Jeremy Reaves with a dime that had everyone on the sideline taking notice. McCaffrey caught it cleanly and didn’t get touched until the five-yard line on the run after the catch. The middle of the field was his territory all day. He added another deep grab later in practice — another 40-ish yard shot down the seam — and the combination of his speed, his hands, and Daniels’ willingness to trust him over the top is a matchup that defensive coordinators around the NFC are going to have a problem with. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Training camp notebook | Jayden Daniels shines in strong practice for offense The depth at the tight end position continues to get more looks, and the players are stepping up with more positive plays in the passing game. Colson Yankoff has gotten most of the attention and had a nice catch from Marcus Mariota during team drills. But Lawrence Cager might have had the catch of the day near the end of practice making a leaping grab in the middle of the field with Daniels under center. It feels like most of the tight end room is with Okonkwo, John Bates and Ben Sinnott at the top of the position, but players like Yankoff and Cager are making strong cases for the Commanders to keep four tight ends on the roster. The Commanders are in the second day of a three-day practice stretch, and Quinn described it as “powering up.” That means the workload and intensity of practices are supposed to increase by the day, and he wants to see players push themselves. Wednesday will be the last practice before the players take a day off, so the players should expect to go through their most competitive and challenging practice of camp so far. title: What gives WR Jaden Bradley a shot to earn Commanders 53-man roster spot
summary: As training camp battles get underway, two things seem to be written in stone about the Commanders’ wide receiver group.  Terry McLaurin has a lock on the WR1 position. And rookie third-round pick Antonio Williams will have every opportunity to compete for a position high on the depth chart. After those two, most of the […]
full_text: As training camp battles get underway, two things seem to be written in stone about the Commanders’ wide receiver group. Terry McLaurin has a lock on the WR1 position. And rookie third-round pick Antonio Williams will have every opportunity to compete for a position high on the depth chart. After those two, most of the final positions on the depth chart are up for grabs. The team’s two recent draft picks, Luke McCaffrey and Jaylin Lane, are virtual locks to make the final 53-man roster, if for no other reason than their value in the return game. Neither has yet proved to be a reliable second or third receiving option. They will have to compete for playing time on offense, but it would be shocking if either isn’t active on opening day. That leaves one or two roster spots up for grabs, depending on whether the Commanders keep five or six receivers. The competition for the remaining roster spot(s) at receiver features a host of characters, including cheap 2026 free-agent additions Dyami Brown and Van Jefferson, returning veteran Treylon Burks, 2025 UDFAs Jacoby Jones and Nick Nash, and this year’s UDFA signees, Jaden Bradley and Chris Hilton Jr. The remaining wild card in the mix is the possibility that the Commanders could sign another free agent, such as Stefon Diggs or Keenan Allen. A quick reader poll: Until another signing is announced, which is by no means guaranteed, there is a prime opportunity for a player currently on the margin to claim a roster spot through a standout performance in training camp and the preseason. One reason why Jaden Bradley could be that guy is his better than expected ability to catch the football. It might seem a strange thing to say, but catching the football is an underrated skillset in wide receivers. Every NFL draft cycle, without fail, some receiver shoots up draft boards after running a fast 40-yard dash at the combine. But when was the last time that a receivers shot up boards because scouts suddenly noticed, late in the process, that he was really good at coming down with the football? A few months after the draft, when players finally take the field, some late round pick or UDFA invariably emerges as a viable starting receiver. One thing that most of these hidden gems at receiver frequently have in common is being really good at catching the football. The truth is, it doesn’t matter how much separation a speedy receiver can create if he doesn’t make the catch when he’s targeted. On the other hand, elite catch phase execution can make up for a lot of deficiencies in athletic testing. The first stat that comes to mind when we think about catching ability is reception rate (Rec %). Unfortunately though, reception rate tells us very little about catching ability because that is drowned out by a major confounding variable, Average Depth of Target (ADOT). Even the most casual football fan will appreciate that it is easier to complete short passes than long passes. As a result, reception rate depends very heavily on the route tree that a receiver runs. In order to compare two wide receivers in a meaningful way, for example Commanders’ 2026 third-round draft pick Antonio Williams (76.4% reception rate, ADOT 7.7 yds) and UDFA Jaden Bradley (61.7% reception rate, ADOT 16.3 yds), they would need to have run a similar depth of routes. In this case, they didn’t. Superficially, it might appear that Williams was better at catching the ball because his reception rate was higher. But that could just be a byproduct of his average target being less than half as deep as Bradley’s. In fact, many previous analyses I have done have shown that ADOT explains around 40% of the variance in reception rate at both the NCAA and NFL levels. Statisticians call that level of effect a dominating influence. In order to see the effects of receiving skills, we need to have some way to factor out the confounding effect of ADOT. My attempt to solve that problem is what first caused Jaden Bradley to cross my radar. Although I didn’t realize it at the time. To explain what I mean, let’s revisit some analysis I did for the roundup of WR draft prospects I published before the 2026 draft. Catch Rate Over Expectation (CROE) Two years ago, I developed a metric which I called Catch Rate Over Expectation (CROE) to adjust reception rate for ADOT. In mathematical terms, it is simply the residual of the regression of reception rate on ADOT. If you have no idea what that means, don’t worry. You don’t really need to. And I will walk through it below for those who are interested. All you really need to know is that it measures an individual receiver’s catch rate relative to the expectation for an average receiver based on ADOT alone. There is another metric popularized in fantasy football circles called Catch Rate Over Expected, which shares the same acronym. That one is an attempt to tease out catching ability from all of the other variables which contribute to reception rate, including separation. Consequently, the fantasy football version gives the erroneous impression that receivers who excel at creating separation aren’t very good at catching the football. My version of CROE is actually a lot simpler and makes more sense. What we want to know is how likely a receiver is to come down with the ball when targeted, no matter how he gets it done, without being fooled into thinking that receivers with shorter route trees have better ball skills. And that’s what it achieves. To illustrate how CROE works, the following graph plots reception rate against ADOT for all the draft eligible FBS WRs in 2026 who ran 100 or more routes. As expected, there is a strong trend for reception rate to decline as ADOT increases. The regression line (often called the trend line), shown in blue, tracks the central tendency of the scatter of points. This essentially shows the average, or “expected”, value of reception rate at each value of ADOT. As a predictive variable, ADOT explains 40.8% of the variance in reception rate. The remaining 59.2% is referred to as “unexplained variance”. It reflects a variety of factors, including separation, ball tracking, and catching ability, as well as QB accuracy and strength of coverage. The blue line represents the expected reception rate, based on ADOT alone. Receivers at points above the line have better than expected reception rates. The vertical distance between a WR’s point and the regression line, measured in units of catch rate (%), is that WR’s Catch Rate Over Expectation (CROE). The red dotted line indicates CROEs of +7.5%. Over 81% of qualifying WRs in the FBS fell below that line. The 42 receivers above the red line are the best pass catchers in the conference. Four individual players are highlighted in the graph. Titans’ fourth overall pick, Carnell Tate , had the highest CROE in the draft class (20.75%). He is an absolute freak at catching the football, as well as a number of other receiving productivity metrics . Three future Commanders sit on either side of the red line, which puts them right on the cusp between very good and elite. Third-round pick Antonio Williams will get plenty of attention and opportunities in training camp. The rest of this article will mainly focus on Jaden Bradley, who fill face more of an uphill climb. I think he will have a legitimate shot at earning a roster spot because of the receiving ability he demonstrated in his breakout senior season. Chris Hilton Jr, gets a mention at the end because he stood out in this metric. He will have a steeper climb than Bradley. title: Bill Croskey-Merritt committed to being an asset in Commanders pass game
summary: Commanders running back Bill Croskey-Merritt wasn’t involved much in the pass game last season. He had just nine catches for 68 yards on 13 targets, stats that show a lack of production, opportunity and (let’s just say it) trust from the coaching staff to use the rookie in those situations.   That wasn’t a massive […]
full_text: Commanders running back Bill Croskey-Merritt wasn’t involved much in the pass game last season. He had just nine catches for 68 yards on 13 targets , stats that show a lack of production, opportunity and (let’s just say it) trust from the coaching staff to use the rookie in those situations. That wasn’t a massive shock, considering Croskey-Merritt didn’t do much receiving in college, either. He had just seven receptions for New Mexico in 2023 , his last full collegiate season after odd eligibility issues essentially nullified his 2024 campaign at Arizona. The Commanders pushed him to improve as a receiver and a pass protector in 2026, and are testing him in those areas during training camp. “They want me to be able to do more,” Croskey-Merritt said in a press conference after Tuesday’s camp practice. “The more you can do, the better. They know I can do it. I just have to put more of it on film. There’s always something you can get better at. I just want to go out show I can do whatever is needed.” LIVE: RB Bill Croskey-Merritt speaks to the media after practice https://t.co/L0RpIp1wev — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 4, 2026 Croskey-Merritt had a productive rookie year despite a clear focus on rushing, with 805 yards and eight touchdowns on 175 carries. He had some blowup games and some subdued efforts in 2025. He showed real promise as a runner, with a style that should fit well with the zone rushing concepts expected of new coordinator David Blough’s scheme. Well-rounded play is essential to staying on the field in the NFL, so there was an obvious desire to get better as a receiver. Croskey-Merritt believed it was a matter of opportunity over skill, but has set out to prove he can do it all while holding onto the ball. Bill going through some ball security drills pic.twitter.com/LePzfxRVok — Zach Selby (@ZachSelbyWC) August 4, 2026 He worked hard during the offseason to get bigger and stronger – that’ll certainly help in pass protection – and be a trusted target in the passing game. Look at those arms on Bill Croskey-Merritt 💪💪 Bill got bigger! pic.twitter.com/eOAKApr2GV — Scott Abraham (@Scott7news) August 4, 2026 “I always felt like it was slept on,” Croskey-Merritt said. “I feel like it comes natural for me, and it’s something I definitely want to show. I can do more than just run the ball. I want to be able to catch out of the backfield, block and run. I just want to be a jack of all trades.” That means being right on technique and the details of his assignment. His talent is unquestioned. It’s about building trust in areas where he didn’t have as much in 2025. Does that mean Croskey-Merritt’s competing to be Washington’s featured, every-down back? Probably not. The Commanders have a well-balanced running back room with juice coming from several different players. Veteran free-agenct acquisition Rachaad White has long been a quality receiver out of the backfield who can be an efficient runner. Sixth-round rookie Kaytron Allen enters the chat following an A-plus career at Penn State, bringing a physical rushing style to the unit and could be valuable in short-yardage situations. Jeremy McNichols and Jerome Ford are also battling for a roster spot as depth components. Croskey-Merritt enters his second season with confidence stemming from a productive offseason. “They had a plan for me and I went at it 100%. I trusted the process and it’s paying off. I don’t feel like I slowed down any. I feel stronger. I feel like I’m ready to go and in the best shape of my life right now. “…When the ball’s coming my way, just make the most of it. I feel like I have been doing that well so far. I want to get better every day.”

title: Commanders Camp Talk: Dan Quinn, Javon Kinlaw and Bill Croskey-Merritt
summary: Tuesday marks Day 5 of Washington Commanders training camp in Ashburn, VA. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of today’s practice. Javon Kinlaw and Bill Croskey-Merritt are scheduled for Q&As after practice, along with players getting interviewed on the field. Quinn said this three-day block (Monday-Wednesday) is about powering up, stacking […]
full_text: Tuesday marks Day 5 of Washington Commanders training camp in Ashburn, VA. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of today’s practice. Javon Kinlaw and Bill Croskey-Merritt are scheduled for Q&As after practice, along with players getting interviewed on the field. Quinn said this three-day block (Monday-Wednesday) is about powering up, stacking and fixing any issues with what’s been installed. They’ll be running longer drives in practice, putting more stress on the secondary and getting a better look at the wide receivers in space. Quinn was asked about several of the free agents Washington signed this year including Fabian Moreau, who was signed today to replace a retiring Ahkello Witherspoon . The head coach said Washington liked the former third-round pick’s versatility. Moreau is also familiar with defensive coordinator Daronte Jones from their time together on the Vikings the last two seasons. Quinn also praised LB Leo Chenal’s winning standards and is very high on the Commanders big offseason signing, EDGE Odafe Oweh. The competition at left guard is on, and Quinn said that Chris Paul has dropped 20 pounds since last season. He said the new offense will run more zone and playaction, and Brandon Coleman has “always been quick off the spot”. He also talked about Jayden Daniels’ red-zone touch, and said, “That’s not luck.” Rookie receiver Antonio Williams is further along as a rookie than Luke McCaffrey was, but Quinn noted McCaffrey had recently switched positions from quarterback. He described Jaylin Lane as more of a returner who added to the receiving room later. full_text: The Washington Commanders have added another veteran cornerback to the roster. Rasul Douglas joined the team in early July , and Washington’s former third-round pick, Fabian Moreau, was the latest addition to the secondary. The team announced the signing on Tuesday morning. The Commanders are missing another Day 2 pick at training camp with Trey Amos still recovering from a broken fibula from his rookie season. Amos was reportedly dealing with some soft tissue soreness that landed him on the active/PUP list. The Commanders also announced the corresponding roster move, CB Ahkello Witherspoon has been placed on the reserve/retired list. We have made the following roster moves: – Signed CB Fabian Moreau – Placed CB Ahkello Witherspoon on the Reserve/Retired List pic.twitter.com/2SmO98Sv2T — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 4, 2026 Moreau was taken in the third round of the 2017 NFL draft and he spent his first four seasons with Washington, with 18 starts. Moreau signed with the Falcons after his rookie contract ended, and has been with four teams over the last five seasons since leaving Washington. He spent the last two seasons with the Vikings, but didn’t start game for them, and only played 28.2% of the snaps on defense last season. He reunites with Commanders new DC Daronte Jones who was the Vikings’ defensive backs coach/pass game coordinator. He’s expected to provide depth at the position group, which has been fortified by recent signings. full_text: The Daily Slop — August 4, 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles WUSA9 ‘Them boys are coming’ | Washington defenders going after the ball, even after the whistle Early on, you can tell this Daronte Jones defense is not going to make it easy for offenses to hang onto the ball. Several times Monday, Commanders defenders were trying to punch or rip the ball out of the ball carrier’s hands. Sometimes after the whistle. “Yeah, definitely like even after the whistle they’re going at the ball,” said tight end Chig Okonkwo. “I mean one time today, you know, [K’Lavon Chaisson] got me after the whistle. Them boys are coming and it’s just nice to, you know, have that competition that just raises up, raises up another level of competition.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Washington Post (paywall) Commanders’ offense gets cooking and other observations from Monday’s practice Overall, it was easily the best practice the offense has had in camp thus far. Daniels was on the money, and the pass catchers did a better job of creating separation. The downside: The offensive line continued to have issues both in pass protection and the run game. As has been the case throughout training camp, the defensive line outperformed its counterpart. The run defense was stout throughout practice, and the running backs didn’t have much room to create. The defensive line did a good job of maintaining gap integrity, while the linebackers were quick to trigger and make plays close to the line of scrimmage. In the passing game, the defensive line was able to win frequently off the edge while also creating a consistent push up the middle of the pocket. Oweh credited defensive coordinator Daronte Jones for making it clear when players can go all-in on the pass rush and giving them freedom to improvise along the way. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Daronte Jones’ brought constant heat, but Jayden Daniels and new-look offense flashed high-end creativity on Day 1 in pads David Blough’s hands-on energy: Offensive Coordinator David Blough is an active, hands-on coach. Throughout practice, you could see him engaged in drills, dropping back into coverage, or pulling a player aside to talk one-on-one. To begin practice, the WRs engaged in light pass-and-catch drills. Blough used what looked like a padded pole to punch at the ball and try to provoke a fumble. He seems like a guy with real attention to detail. Defense wins Day 1: If I were to declare a winner today, I would give it to the defense. On many occasions, they penetrated the gaps and took away any potential for positive yardage on runs. In this same Red Zone series, Javon Kinlaw broke through the line and “sacked” Daniels. The defense provided sticky coverage, and while Daniels tried to buy time, it was to no avail. Personnel wrinkles: The offense will provide fans (and opposing defenses) a lot of eye candy with pre-snap motion. The Commanders ran a lot of 12-personnel sets today and moved both tight ends in pre-snap motion. It’s an interesting wrinkle that wasn’t present last year. On defense, I was surprised to see Frankie Luvu at the Mike position. He spent a good amount of time there, which allowed other LBs, including Styles, to blitz off the edge. Sinnott’s versatile role: Sinnott will be used creatively this season. Today, we saw him as an H-Back and a true fullback in I-formation. I can see why he is excited for a fresh start under Blough. Long after practice wrapped up, Sam Hartman stayed on the field to throw extra routes to Sinnott, Ryan Cracraft, and others. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Training camp notebook | Sonny Styles stands out during first padded practice The first drill was indicative of how the practice went for both sides of the ball. Players were competing on every play, and each unit had some positive moments. Right after Styles’ tackle on Croskey-Merritt, Marcus Mariota connected with the running back for a touchdown. Perhaps the best catch of the day came when the starting offense was on the field, as Jayden Daniels connected with Terry McLaurin in the back corner of the end zone for the score, despite Mike Sainristil providing tight coverage. [R]ookie Joshua Josephs was one of the more entertaining players to watch today. Josephs’ athleticism shone on Monday, as he was all over the field making plays. He batted down a pass from Daniels early in the day, and he showed impressive speed during pass protection drills. It’s still unclear where he fits on the depth chart and how many snaps he’ll get, but there have been signs of his potential. A lot of people were wondering how rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams would look with the pads on after getting open and creating separation in the first three days of camp. The answer is that he looked basically the same and continued to find ways of getting open. He had two touchdowns today, one of which came on the last play of two-minute drills. Williams practiced mostly with the second group today, but that could change soon because of how impressive the rookie has looked against defensive backs. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Good and Not So Good From Commanders’ First Padded Practice The Not So Good Kaliakmanis appearing in this section for another interception after being picked off in each of the previous two open practices is not a good look. Turnovers in three consecutive practices are hard to defend or dismiss for a seventh-round quarterback trying to take reps from Sam Hartman as a developmental quarterback. Rookies are expected to make mistakes, but throwing interceptions every day will never be acceptable and is worth tracking. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Wire 4 standouts from Commanders’ first padded practice CB Mike Sainristil Sainristil was playing inside and outside on Monday. While he did allow the touchdown to McLaurin early in practice, it was strong coverage. He was beaten by a terrific throw. Sainristil got his revenge later, breaking up a pair of plays in the red zone. It’s been a good camp so far for Sainristil. Confidence is everything. Washington needs a strong bounce-back year from Sainristil, and he seems up to the task . To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Pro Football Focus Offensive Guard Rankings: The top 32 players ahead of the 2026 NFL season 10. Sam Cosmi , Washington Commanders Cosmi returned from a knee injury midway through last season and brought his trademark stability back to Washington‘s offensive line. Though he appeared in only nine games, his 76.3 PFF grade ranked 10th among qualified guards. Cosmi allowed just 11 pressures and two sacks over those nine games, and his 72.3 PFF run-blocking grade was another strong mark. It’s reasonable to expect an even stronger season in 2026, assuming he stays healthy. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig (paywall) Odafe Oweh’s evolution mirrors Commanders defense’s fast start in padded practice “I came in as a run defender,” said the 31st overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. “I’ve had zero sacks, so people forget that.” Oweh isn’t referencing a quarter, a half, a game or even a month of football.vHis final season at Penn State ended without recording a single sack. Mentioning that eyebrow-raising stat served two purposes. First, it reminded everyone that stopping the run was once the foundation of his game, even if his pass-rushing success has since overshadowed it. You don’t get drafted in the first round without a sack if there aren’t other aspects worthy of praise. “The run game was what I hung my hat on at first,” he said during his post-practice media availability. title: 2026 Arizona Cardinals training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Cardinals training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day, following all the action. The Arizona Cardinals ' camp is at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, and Cardinals reporter Josh Weinfuss has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Cardinals camp. We will update this file often. How will Arizona's quarterback situation shake out with  Jacoby Brissett  back on a reworked contract? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest on the Cardinals 
 
 Tyler Allgeier 'building' relationship with rookie RB Jeremiyah Love 
 Source: Cardinals' Brissett guaranteed $15.5M in reworked deal 
 Cardinals TE Trey McBride walks back dig at Arizona fanbase 
 Sweat (knee) among four Cards added to PUP list 
 With deal done, Brissett can focus on Cardinals' playbook 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 Thursday night's Hall of Fame game will not just be a run-through for the players, it will also be the first time the Cardinals' coaching staff will have a chance to be together during a game.

 "I think that's another great thing for us to have this game, to just get a little quick dry run-through on how game day operations go, just from time management, all that stuff," offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett said. "I think it's going to be great for all of us and there'll be some ups and downs and you work through those and grow every day."

 Hackett said he'll be in the booth watching the action unfold from above but with new coach Mike LaFleur calling the plays and quarterback coach Matt Schaub handling Carson Beck , Hackett will be able to help whoever needs help. But that'll also be part of this staff's first time together: Figuring out his role in all of it.

 More observations: 

 
 Even though Josh Sweat hasn't practiced this camp and there isn't a set timeline for his return, defensive coordinator Nick Rallis said Tuesday that Sweat is "locked in" with meetings and post-practice tape. 
 

 
 Monday, Aug. 3 
 Deep balls were the theme of the day for the Cardinals as Jacoby Brissett ,  Gardner Minshew II  and Carson Beck put on an aerial display.

 Brissett unleashed a bomb to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who, after letting a deep ball earlier in practice go off his fingertips, came down with a diving grab that would have gained more than 50 yards.

 Beck showed off his deep ball, hitting fellow rookie Reggie Virgil on a beautiful pass. On another deep shot, Beck froze two defenders in the second level before finding a receiver who made the catch a step in front of a defender.

 More observations from the day:  

 
 Tight end Trey McBride was banged up briefly after he was hit in the middle of the field. He went down and was slow to get up but later returned to the offensive drills. 
 The tip drill paid off for the defense on two different plays Monday. On one, defensive lineman  Zachary Carter  tipped a pass by Minshew and L.J. Collier came down with it. On another play, defensive lineman  Roy Lopez  batted down a Beck pass. 
 The catch of the day came from Virgil, who made an impressive one-handed catch in mid-air as he was falling to the ground on a pass from Beck along the sideline. 
 

 

 Sunday, Aug. 2 
 Jacoby Brissett continues to get more and more comfortable with the offense, as was evident Sunday.
 He had seven drives with the first-team offense, totaling 29 snaps, and finished 13-for-16 passing with two interceptions.

 The first was by defensive back Sean Murphy-Bunting , who jumped the route in front of Michael Wilson for the pick. The second was by second-year linebacker Cody Simon . Brissett's other incompletion was an overthrow.

 Overall, though, Brissett looked to be better in command of what's being asked of him. He didn't have a completion to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who was the intended target on Simon's interception, but Brissett did find a favorite receiver in tight end Trey McBride , who caught all six of the targets thrown his way.

 Back-up quarterback  Gardner Minshew II  was 9-for-13 passing and Carson Beck was 9-for-12 passing. While Beck wasn't consistent with his deep passes, he completed a couple of passes while he was off-balance, showcasing poise in the pocket.

 

 More observations from the day: 

 
 Second-year defensive lineman Walter Nolen III said the discomfort with his left knee during Friday's practice -- the same knee that ended his rookie season in 2025 -- was just a little hiccup. He said he wasn't concerned when it happened. He told himself he needed to slow down. 
 With the Cardinals' third block (every four days of practice is considered a block) of training camp starting Sunday, rookie running back Jeremiyah Love got the first snap of 11-on-11 with the first-team offense. Until Sunday, that was reserved for Tyler Allgeier . 
 Ihmir Smith-Marsette , who had been one of the surprise standouts of training camp thus far, left practice with a trainer and did not return. 
 Devin Duvernay , the lightning quick return specialist, showed he can be a factor as a receiver, as well. During the second-team, red zone 11-on-11, he caught a pass from Minshew on the right side, stopped in his tracks and reversed course to lose the defensive back and score a touchdown. 
 
 

 Friday, July 31 
 Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love showed off his highly lauded pass-catching ability on Friday in a play that also highlighted his quickness and shiftiness.

 During one of Arizona's 11-on-11 sessions, Love lined up in the backfield but then sidestepped to the right enough to take off from the slot at the snap. He then put a stutter step and a cut on second-year linebacker Cody Simon that left Simon in Love's dust. Love then cut inside and caught a pass from quarterback Jacoby Brissett .

 Even though it was a small sample size, Love is pleased with his role in the Cardinals' passing game thus far.

 "I like that they're trying to utilize me in ways that benefit me," he said. "I'm a guy that loves to get out in space. If I get out in space, I feel like I can make a play against whoever, whether it's linebacker, safety, I can make a play."

 More observations from the day: 

 
 Defensive back Joey Blount left the practice and walked to the locker room alongside a trainer on Friday. He missed the last 16 games with a neck injury last season. 
 With all the talk of Love and Tyler Allgeier splitting reps on the field and being close off it, as Allgeier said this week, after Allgeier scored a touchdown in practice on Friday, Love, who wasn't in on the play, ran straight to Allgeier to congratulate him on the play. 
 Cornerback Will Johnson took exception with left tackle Paris Johnson Jr . kicking out wide to block him on a screen pass to Michael Wilson for a touchdown, and a scuffle ensued. It wasn't about the Michigan (where Will went)-Ohio State (where Paris went) rivalry, though. "I think it was more about being a 300-pound lineman trying to finish a corner late," Johnson said. "Like, what are you doing? Do that to a d-lineman. Then you can talk s---." 
 

 

 

 Thursday, July 30 
 Second-year right guard Isaiah Adams has begun taking steps to show that the glimpses of promise last season are more like the norm now, offensive line coach Justin Frye said Thursday.

 "He's doing some really good things right now that he's never done because of the technique and the things that is carry over, those are becoming more habitual," Frye said.

 Adams, who faced instant competition for the starting job when Arizona drafted Chase Bisontis in the second round, has started to…
